Collections — Lists, Sets, Maps & Arrays

Read-only interfaces over mutable JVM collections — which to pick and what each operation costs.

  • jvm
  • android
  • kotlin >=2.0
  • jvm >=17
  • Kotlin/JVM (the standard library)

Sources: Collections overview — Kotlin docs

Pick the container

The defaults keep insertion order — `mutableSetOf` and `mutableMapOf` are linked hash collections.

NeedUseWhy
ordered listList<T> / mutableListOf()an ArrayList underneath; List is a read-only view
membership, dedupeSet<T> / mutableSetOf()LinkedHashSet: O(1) contains, insertion order
key → valueMap<K, V> / mutableMapOf()LinkedHashMap; hashMapOf() drops the order for a little speed
sorted keyssortedMapOf() / java.util.TreeMapO(log n), range queries
queue or stackArrayDeque<T>O(1) at both ends
priority queuejava.util.PriorityQueueO(log n) offer and poll
primitives in bulkIntArray, DoubleArray…int[] underneath — no boxing

What operations cost

The JVM implementations behind the Kotlin interfaces.

TypeLookupInsertRemove
ArrayListO(1) by index, O(n) by valueO(1)* at the end, O(n) elsewhereO(1) last, O(n) other
LinkedHashSet / LinkedHashMapO(1) averageO(1) averageO(1) average
TreeMap / TreeSetO(log n)O(log n)O(log n)
ArrayDequeO(1) by indexO(1)* at either endO(1) at either end
PriorityQueueO(1) peekO(log n)O(log n) poll, O(n) by value

Read-only is not immutable

`List` hides the mutators; the object underneath can still change through another reference.

fun main() {
    val readOnly: List<Int> = listOf(3, 1, 2)
    val mutable = readOnly.toMutableList()      // a copy you may change
    mutable += 4
    println("$readOnly $mutable")

    val view: List<Int> = mutable               // a read-only VIEW of the same list
    mutable.clear()
    println(view.size)
}
Result
[3, 1, 2] [3, 1, 2, 4]
0
Setup
  1. A Kotlin 2.x compiler (kotlinc) and JDK 17 or later
  2. Save as main.kt; run kotlinc main.kt -include-runtime -d main.jar && java -jar main.jar

Ran with kotlinc 2.2.20, JVM 17.0.15 on 2026-11-11: the output matched the result shown.

Maps and sets

`getValue` throws on a missing key; `[]` returns null; set algebra reads as infix words.

fun main() {
    val counts = mutableMapOf<String, Int>()
    for (word in "the cat and the hat".split(" ")) {
        counts[word] = counts.getOrDefault(word, 0) + 1
    }
    println(counts)
    println(counts.getValue("the") to ("dog" in counts))

    val a = setOf(1, 2, 3)
    val b = setOf(2, 3, 4)
    println("${a union b} ${a intersect b} ${a subtract b}")
}
Result
{the=2, cat=1, and=1, hat=1}
(2, false)
[1, 2, 3, 4] [2, 3] [1]

Keys need value equality

A `data class` generates `equals` and `hashCode`; a plain class compares by identity.

data class Point(val x: Int, val y: Int)
class Cell(val x: Int, val y: Int)

fun main() {
    println(setOf(Point(1, 1), Point(1, 1)).size)
    println(setOf(Cell(1, 1), Cell(1, 1)).size)
}

ArrayDeque and primitive arrays

`ArrayDeque` is the queue and the stack; `IntArray` is `int[]` with no boxing.

fun main() {
    val queue = ArrayDeque<String>()
    queue.addLast("a")
    queue.addLast("b")
    queue.addFirst("urgent")
    println("${queue.removeFirst()} ${queue.removeLast()} $queue")

    val primes = intArrayOf(2, 3, 5, 7)
    println(primes.sum())
}
Result
urgent b [a]
17

Pitfalls

Where Kotlin differs from Swift's value-type collections.

  • Collections are references: val ys = xs aliases a MutableList. Copy with toList() / toMutableList().
  • list.removeAt(0) in a loop is O(n²) — use ArrayDeque.
  • Mutating a collection while iterating it throws ConcurrentModificationException; use removeAll { } or iterate a copy.
  • Expose List, Set, Map from APIs; keep the Mutable* type private.
  • List<Int> boxes every element; IntArray does not — it matters for large numeric data.

Transform and fold

`sumOf` says the intent; `fold` is the general form.

data class Order(val id: Int, val customer: String, val total: Int)

fun main() {
    val orders = listOf(Order(1, "ana", 30), Order(2, "bo", 12), Order(3, "ana", 8))
    println(orders.filter { it.total >= 10 }.map { it.id })
    println(orders.sumOf { it.total })
    println(orders.fold(0) { acc, o -> acc + o.total })
}

Group, index, count, partition

Groups keep the order in which keys first appear.

data class Person(val name: String, val team: String)

fun main() {
    val people = listOf(Person("Ana", "web"), Person("Bo", "data"), Person("Cy", "web"))
    println(people.groupBy({ it.team }, { it.name }))
    println(people.associateBy { it.name }.getValue("Bo").team)
    println(people.groupingBy { it.team }.eachCount())
    val (web, others) = people.partition { it.team == "web" }
    println("${web.size} ${others.size}")
}
Result
{web=[Ana, Cy], data=[Bo]}
data
{web=2, data=1}
2 1

Sort by several keys

Comparators compose: `compareByDescending { }.thenBy { }`. Sorting is stable.

data class Player(val name: String, val score: Int)

fun main() {
    val players = listOf(Player("cy", 7), Player("ana", 9), Player("bo", 7))
    val ranked = players.sortedWith(compareByDescending<Player> { it.score }.thenBy { it.name })
    println(ranked.joinToString(" ") { "${it.name}:${it.score}" })
    println("${players.maxBy { it.score }.name} ${players.minByOrNull { it.score }?.name}")
}
Result

Chunk, window, dedupe, zip

All built in.

fun main() {
    println((1..5).chunked(2))
    println((1..4).windowed(3))
    println(listOf("b", "a", "b", "c", "a").distinct())
    println(listOf("a", "b", "c").zip(listOf(1, 2)))     // stops at the shorter
    println(listOf(1, 2, 4, 7).zipWithNext { a, b -> b - a })
}

Lazy pipelines with sequences

A sequence runs each element through the whole chain and stops as soon as `take` is satisfied.

fun main() {
    var squared = 0
    val firstOddSquares = generateSequence(1) { it + 1 }
        .map { squared++; it * it }
        .filter { it % 2 == 1 }
        .take(3)
        .toList()
    println("$firstOddSquares after $squared squares")
}
Result
[1, 9, 25] after 5 squares

Strings — Standard Operations

UTF-16 `Char`s underneath, graphemes on screen — search, split, slice, compare, fold, normalize, build, format and match text correctly on the JVM.

  • jvm
  • android
  • kotlin >=2.2
  • jvm >=21
  • android API 26+ (named regex groups)
  • Kotlin/JVM standard library and the JDK's java.text

Sources: Strings — Kotlin docs · kotlin.text — Kotlin standard library API · java.text.BreakIterator — Java SE 21 API · java.text.Collator — Java SE 21 API · java.util.regex.Pattern — Java SE 21 API

I want to…

The standard call for each everyday job, and the trap that comes with it.

I want to…KotlinWatch out
know if text contains a wordcontains(x, ignoreCase = true), startsWith, endsWithaccent-sensitive: "Émile" does not contain "emile" — normalize or collate first
find where it isindexOf, lastIndexOf, indexOfFirst { }-1 when absent; the index counts UTF-16 Chars, not characters
split into fieldssplit(";"), split(",", limit = 2), lines()keeps empty fields: "a,,b".split(",") is [a, , b], and "".split(",") is [""], not []
split into what a reader seesBreakIterator.getCharacterInstance() / getWordInstance(locale)toList() and chunked(1) break emoji and accents apart
joinjoinToString(", ", prefix, postfix) { transform }builds one string; no need for a StringBuilder by hand
trimtrim(), trimStart(), trimEnd(), trim('-')Kotlin's trim() uses isWhitespace (Unicode); Java's String.trim() only strips <= U+0020
replacereplace("-", " ") (all), replaceFirst, replace(regex, "…"), replace(regex) { m -> }in replace(regex, "…") $1 and \ are special; the lambda's result is used literally
cut a known prefixremovePrefix, removeSuffix, substringBefore('@'), substringAfterLast('/')substringBefore returns the whole string when the delimiter is missing
pad or repeatpadStart(8, '0'), padEnd, repeat(3)counts Chars, so emoji and combining marks misalign columns
take a piecetake(n), substring(a, b), slice(range), last()can cut a surrogate pair in half — check isHighSurrogate() or cut on graphemes
measure for storageencodeToByteArray().size (UTF-8 bytes)a database column, an HTTP header or a push payload limits bytes: the family emoji is 8 Chars but 18 bytes
sort for peoplesortedWith(Collator.getInstance(locale))sorted() compares UTF-16 units: "Zoe" < "adam", and Å lands after z everywhere
change caseuppercase() (invariant), uppercase(locale) for displayJava's String.toUpperCase() (an error in Kotlin 2.1+, still in Java code) uses the default locale: "title" becomes "TİTLE" on a Turkish device
count charactersgraphemes via BreakIteratorlength counts UTF-16 units; codePointCount counts code points — neither is what a user sees

Char, code point, grapheme, byte — and slicing safely

Count and cut on graphemes whenever a person will see the result (length limits, truncation, initials), and on UTF-8 bytes whenever storage or a protocol sets the limit.

import java.text.BreakIterator

fun graphemes(text: String): List<String> {
    val boundaries = BreakIterator.getCharacterInstance().apply { setText(text) }
    val result = mutableListOf<String>()
    var start = boundaries.first()
    var end = boundaries.next()
    while (end != BreakIterator.DONE) {
        result += text.substring(start, end)
        start = end
        end = boundaries.next()
    }
    return result
}

fun truncateForDisplay(name: String, max: Int): String {
    val parts = graphemes(name)
    return if (parts.size <= max) name else parts.take(max).joinToString("") + "…"
}

fun main() {
    // The family emoji is three emoji glued by ZERO WIDTH JOINER (U+200D).
    // ë is either one code point (U+00EB) or e + COMBINING DIAERESIS (U+0308).
    val family = "\uD83D\uDC69\u200D\uD83D\uDC69\u200D\uD83D\uDC67"
    val samples = mapOf(
        "plain" to "Ana",
        "family" to family,
        "composed" to "Zo\u00EB",
        "decomposed" to "Zoe\u0308",
    )
    for ((label, text) in samples) {
        val codePoints = text.codePointCount(0, text.length)
        val utf8Bytes = text.encodeToByteArray().size     // what a byte-limited column or header sees
        println(
            "${label.padEnd(10)} chars ${text.length}  code points $codePoints" +
                "  graphemes ${graphemes(text).size}  UTF-8 bytes $utf8Bytes",
        )
    }

    val display = "Zo\u00EB $family family"
    println("take(5) ends inside a surrogate pair: ${display.take(5).last().isHighSurrogate()}")
    println(truncateForDisplay(display, 5))
}
Result

family     chars 8  code points 5  graphemes 1  UTF-8 bytes 18
composed   chars 3  code points 3  graphemes 3  UTF-8 bytes 4
decomposed chars 4  code points 4  graphemes 3  UTF-8 bytes 5

Search, split, trim, replace, pad

Parsing one line of a CSV-ish export — the calls you use every day, and what each returns at the edges.

fun main() {
    val line = "  1042 ; Ana Lima ;  ana.lima@example.com ; paid  "
    val (id, name, email, status) = line.split(";").map { it.trim() }

    println(name.contains("lima", ignoreCase = true))          // search
    println(name.indexOf("Lima") to name.indexOf("Silva"))      // -1 when absent
    println(email.substringBefore('@') + " | " + email.substringAfter('@'))
    println("ORD-" + id.padStart(8, '0'))                      // pad
    println(status.uppercase().padEnd(8, '.') + "|")

    println("a,,b,".split(","))                                 // empty fields are kept
    println("a,,b,".split(",").filter { it.isNotEmpty() })
    println("2026-11-16T10:00".split("-", limit = 2))           // stop after the first cut
    println("one\ntwo\r\nthree".lines())                        // any line ending

    println(email.substringBefore('@').replace('.', ' ')        // replace every match
        .split(' ').joinToString(" ") { it.replaceFirstChar(Char::titlecase) })
    println("Order 1042 shipped".removePrefix("Order ").removeSuffix(" shipped"))
    println("--draft--".trim('-'))
    println("missing".substringBefore('@'))                     // delimiter absent: whole string
}

Compare and sort by locale

`Collator` sorts the way a reader of that language expects; `compareTo` and `sorted()` compare UTF-16 units.

import java.text.Collator
import java.util.Locale

fun main() {
    val customers = listOf("Zoë", "zoe", "Ångström", "Adam", "Örjan", "Émile", "eva")

    println(customers.sorted())                                  // code units: capitals first, accents last
    println(customers.sortedWith(String.CASE_INSENSITIVE_ORDER)) // still puts accented letters last

    val english = Collator.getInstance(Locale.ENGLISH)
    println(customers.sortedWith(english))
    val swedish = Collator.getInstance(Locale.forLanguageTag("sv-SE"))
    println(customers.sortedWith(swedish))                       // Å and Ö come after Z in Swedish

    println("Zoe".compareTo("zoe", ignoreCase = true) == 0)
    println("straße".equals("STRASSE", ignoreCase = true))       // false: compares one char at a time

    val accentBlind = Collator.getInstance(Locale.FRENCH).apply { strength = Collator.PRIMARY }
    println(accentBlind.compare("Émile", "emile") == 0)          // a search match, not an identity
}
Result
[Adam, Zoë, eva, zoe, Ångström, Émile, Örjan]

[Adam, Ångström, Émile, eva, Örjan, zoe, Zoë]
[Adam, Émile, eva, zoe, Zoë, Ångström, Örjan]

false

Case conversion with a Locale, and normalization

Use `uppercase()` / `lowercase()` (invariant) for identifiers and keys, `uppercase(locale)` for text a person reads, and NFC before comparing.

import java.text.Normalizer
import java.util.Locale

// A Latin-script search key: strip the combining accents U+0300–U+036F that follow a Latin letter, then
// recompose — so Cyrillic й and ї, whose breve and diaeresis are in that range too, stay letters.
// Letters with no decomposition (đ, ł, ø, ß) stay as they are.
// To match rather than build a key, prefer a PRIMARY-strength Collator (see Compare and sort).
fun searchKey(text: String): String {
    val decomposed = Normalizer.normalize(text, Normalizer.Form.NFD)
    val withoutAccents = decomposed.replace(Regex("(?<=\\p{IsLatin})[\\u0300-\\u036F]+"), "")
    return Normalizer.normalize(withoutAccents, Normalizer.Form.NFC).lowercase()
}

fun main() {
    val turkish = Locale.forLanguageTag("tr-TR")
    println("title".uppercase())              // invariant (Locale.ROOT): right for keys and enums
    println("title".uppercase(turkish))       // dotted capital İ: right for a Turkish heading
    println("TITLE".lowercase(turkish))       // dotless ı
    println("straße".uppercase())             // one Char becomes two

    val composed = "Caf\u00E9"             // é as one code point (NFC)
    val decomposed = "Cafe\u0301"          // e + COMBINING ACUTE ACCENT (NFD)
    println(composed == decomposed)
    println(Normalizer.normalize(decomposed, Normalizer.Form.NFC) == composed)

    println(searchKey("Émile Zoë") == searchKey("emile zoe"))
    // The dakuten in が (U+3099) and the virama in हिन्दी (U+094D) are not Latin accents: they survive.
    println(searchKey("がっこう") + " " + searchKey("हिन्दी"))
    println(searchKey("Đà Nẵng") + " " + searchKey("Йошкар-Ола Київ"))
}

Building strings efficiently

Both print the same CSV; `+=` in a loop copies the whole string every pass, `buildString` and `joinToString` append into one buffer.

Concatenation in a loop
data class Order(val id: Int, val customer: String, val totalCents: Long)

fun toCsv(orders: List<Order>): String {
    var csv = "id,customer,total\n"
    for (order in orders) {
        csv += order.id.toString() + "," + order.customer + "," +
            (order.totalCents / 100).toString() + "." +
            (order.totalCents % 100).toString().padStart(2, '0') + "\n"   // a new String each time
    }
    return csv
}

fun main() {
    val orders = listOf(Order(1042, "Ana Lima", 12990), Order(1043, "Bo Chen", 1500))
    print(toCsv(orders))
}
buildString and joinToString
data class Order(val id: Int, val customer: String, val totalCents: Long)

fun money(cents: Long) = "${cents / 100}.${(cents % 100).toString().padStart(2, '0')}"

fun toCsv(orders: List<Order>): String = buildString {
    appendLine("id,customer,total")
    orders.joinTo(this, separator = "") { "${it.id},${it.customer},${money(it.totalCents)}\n" }
}

fun main() {
    val orders = listOf(Order(1042, "Ana Lima", 12990), Order(1043, "Bo Chen", 1500))
    print(toCsv(orders))
}

Templates, raw strings and String.format with a Locale

Templates for code-side text; `trimIndent`/`trimMargin` for multi-line literals; `format` only with an explicit `Locale`.

import java.util.Locale

data class Order(val id: Int, val customer: String, val totalCents: Long)

fun main() {
    val order = Order(1042, "Ana Lima", 123456)
    println("Order #${order.id} for ${order.customer.uppercase()}")   // any expression in ${}

    val receipt = """
        Order:    #${order.id}
        Customer: ${order.customer}
        Coupon:   ${'$'}5 off
    """.trimIndent()                                                 // drops the common indent
    println(receipt)

    val query = """
        |SELECT id, total
        |  FROM orders
        | WHERE customer = ?
    """.trimMargin()                                                 // keeps indent after the '|'
    println(query)

    val json = $$"""{"price": "$12", "id": $${order.id}}"""          // Kotlin 2.2+: only $$ interpolates
    println(json)

    val amount = order.totalCents / 100.0
    println(String.format(Locale.US, "%,.2f", amount))
    println(String.format(Locale.GERMANY, "%,.2f", amount))
    println("%-10s|%6d|".format(Locale.ROOT, "Ana", 42))              // column layout for logs
}

Regex: named groups, findAll, replace with a lambda

Raw strings keep patterns readable, `findAll` is lazy, and `matches` needs the whole input while `containsMatchIn` accepts any part.

fun main() {
    val log = """
        2026-11-16 ORD-1042 paid 129.90
        2026-11-16 ORD-1043 refunded 15.00
        2026-11-17 ORD-1044 paid 42.00
    """.trimIndent()
    val entry = Regex("""(?<date>\d{4}-\d{2}-\d{2}) (?<id>ORD-\d+) (?<status>\w+) (?<amount>\d+\.\d{2})""")

    for (match in entry.findAll(log)) {
        println("${match.groups["id"]?.value} ${match.groups["status"]?.value}")
    }
    val paid = entry.findAll(log)
        .filter { it.groups["status"]?.value == "paid" }
        .sumOf { it.groups["amount"]!!.value.toBigDecimal() }
    println("paid: $paid")

    // A quoted local part, or a run without spaces or list punctuation (so +tags and non-ASCII);
    // a comma or semicolon may join addresses, and the sentence's final punctuation is never taken.
    val email = Regex("""("[^"\r\n]*"|[^\s@,;<>()"]+)@([^\s@,;<>()"]+?)(?=[.,;!?)>]?(?:[\s,;]|$))""")
    val texts = listOf(
        "Write to ana+shop@example.com, josé@exemplo.pt or bo-chen@example.org.",
        "Mail ana@example.com,bo@example.org now; To: \"ana lima\"@example.com",
    )
    for (text in texts) {
        val masked = email.replace(text) { match ->
            val (user, domain) = match.destructured
            "${user.trimStart('"').first()}***@$domain"            // the lambda's result is used literally
        }
        println(masked)
    }

    println(Regex("""\d{3}""").matches("1042"))                 // false: matches() is anchored
    println(Regex("""\d+""").containsMatchIn("ORD-1042"))
    println(Regex("""\d+""").find("ORD-1042")?.range)
    println("v1.2.3".split(Regex.fromLiteral(".")))              // a literal dot, not "any char"
}

Catastrophic backtracking, measured

Counting the engine's reads on JDK 21 shows a nested quantifier growing roughly with n² (the JDK memoizes the loop), a backreference after it growing about 16-fold per four extra letters, and the possessive form growing linearly.

// Counts how often the regex engine reads the input: a deterministic measure of its work.
class CountingInput(private val text: String) : CharSequence {
    var reads = 0L
        private set
    override val length: Int get() = text.length
    override fun get(index: Int): Char {
        reads++
        return text[index]
    }
    override fun subSequence(startIndex: Int, endIndex: Int) = text.subSequence(startIndex, endIndex)
    override fun toString() = text
}

fun reads(regex: Regex, input: String): Long = CountingInput(input).also { regex.matches(it) }.reads

fun main() {
    val nested = Regex("""^(\p{L}+ ?)*$""")            // nested quantifiers: the JDK memoizes the loop
    val withBackreference = Regex("""^(\p{L}+ ?)*\1$""") // a backreference turns the memo off
    val possessive = Regex("""^(?:\p{L}++ ?)*+$""")      // never gives characters back

    // A near-miss: n letters, then a character the pattern cannot accept.
    for (n in listOf(10, 14, 18, 22)) {
        val nearMiss = "a".repeat(n) + "!"
        println(
            "n=$n  nested ${reads(nested, nearMiss)}  backreference ${reads(withBackreference, nearMiss)}" +
                "  possessive ${reads(possessive, nearMiss)}",
        )
    }
}
Result
n=10  nested 185  backreference 5649  possessive 14
n=14  nested 343  backreference 90553  possessive 18
n=18  nested 549  backreference 1449057  possessive 22
n=22  nested 803  backreference 23185161  possessive 26

Long input: StackOverflowError, possessive quantifiers and a length cap

A repeated group recurses once per repetition, so long input throws `StackOverflowError` — an `Error` that `catch (e: Exception)` misses — while the possessive form and a length cap stay safe, and `\p{L}` instead of the ASCII-only `\w` accepts real names.

// A display name: words that start with a letter, then letters, combining marks, apostrophes or
// hyphens, with single spaces between.
const val TAIL = """[\p{L}\p{M}'’-]"""

val asciiOnly = Regex("""^\w+(?: \w+)*$""")            // \w is [a-zA-Z0-9_] unless (?U) is set
val backtracking = Regex("""^\p{L}$TAIL*(?: \p{L}$TAIL*)*$""")     // right answers, a stack frame per word
val possessive = Regex("""^\p{L}$TAIL*+(?: \p{L}$TAIL*+)*+$""")   // same language, no backtracking

const val MAX_NAME = 200

fun isValidName(input: String) = input.length <= MAX_NAME && possessive.matches(input)

fun main() {
    val names = listOf("José Lima", "Zoë", "李 小龍", "O'Brien", "Anne-Marie", "Ana  Lima", "", "-")
    println("ascii only:  " + names.map { asciiOnly.matches(it) })
    println("possessive:  " + names.map { possessive.matches(it) })

    // 50,000 one-letter words: the repeated group recurses once per word.
    val pasted = "a ".repeat(50_000).trim()
    for ((label, regex) in listOf("backtracking" to backtracking, "possessive" to possessive)) {
        // runCatching catches Throwable; a catch (e: Exception) would let the Error through.
        val outcome = runCatching { regex.matches(pasted) }
        println("$label: ${outcome.getOrNull() ?: outcome.exceptionOrNull()!!::class.simpleName}")
    }
    println("isValidName (capped at $MAX_NAME): ${isValidName(pasted)}")
}
Result
ascii only:  [false, false, false, false, false, false, false, false]
possessive:  [true, true, true, true, true, false, false, false]
backtracking: StackOverflowError
possessive: true
isValidName (capped at 200): false

Pitfalls worth saying out loud

The bugs that ship most often.

  • length, take(n) and substring work on UTF-16 Chars and cut emoji and accents; reversed() keeps surrogate pairs but swaps flags (🇵🇹 becomes 🇹🇵) and detaches accents and ZWJ parts. Use BreakIterator for anything a user sees.
  • toUpperCase() / toLowerCase() no longer compile in Kotlin 2.1+, but Java's String.toUpperCase() still uses the default locale: on a Turkish device "id" becomes "İD" — watch Java interop.
  • uppercase() / lowercase() are locale-invariant — right for keys; pass uppercase(locale) for display text.
  • String.format("%.2f", x) or "%.2f".format(x) without a Locale prints 1,50 in Germany — fine on screen, broken in a CSV, a URL or SQL. Pass Locale.ROOT for machine text.
  • Sorting names with sorted() or compareTo: code-unit order, wrong in every language. Use a Collator for the user's locale.
  • Two strings that look equal may differ (NFC vs NFD). Normalize input at the boundary before comparing, hashing or storing as a key.
  • Concatenating in a loop is quadratic. Use buildString, joinToString or a StringBuilder.
  • \w and \b are ASCII-only in Java regexes: José fails \w+. Use \p{L} (letters) and \p{M} (marks), or the (?U) flag.
  • A user-supplied pattern, a backreference after a nested group, or a repeated group over pasted text can hang or crash a thread. Escape with Regex.escape, cap the length, prefer possessive ++ / *+.
  • Prefer raw strings """…""" for regexes and multi-line text: no double escaping, and trimIndent() keeps the code indented.

Serialization — kotlinx.serialization, JSON & Friends

@Serializable models and Json configuration, names, missing and null fields, unknown keys, dates and enums, sealed polymorphism, custom serializers and JsonElement, generic envelopes, errors and validation, and how it compares to Moshi, Gson and Jackson.

  • jvm
  • android
  • kotlinx-serialization-json
  • kotlin >=2.4
  • kotlinx-serialization >=1.13
  • jvm >=17
  • Kotlin/JVM with the kotlinx.serialization compiler plugin

Sources: Kotlin serialization — Kotlin docs · Kotlin Serialization Guide — kotlinx.serialization on GitHub · kotlinx.serialization API reference

Codable → kotlinx.serialization

The same compile-time codec idea; the configuration lives on one `Json` instance instead of on the encoder each call.

Swiftkotlinx.serializationNote
struct Order: Codable@Serializable data class Orderthe compiler plugin generates the serializer — no reflection
JSONEncoder() / JSONDecoder()Json / Json { … }build the configured instance once and reuse it
CodingKeys raw value@SerialName("unit_price")per property, per enum entry, per sealed subclass
.convertFromSnakeCasenamingStrategy = JsonNamingStrategy.SnakeCaseglobal, and applied to @SerialName values too — use a separate Json for an API whose keys break the convention
optional property / decodeIfPresentval bio: String? = nulla property is optional only when it has a default
dateDecodingStrategykotlin.time.Instant (built in) or a KSerializer for java.time.Instant@Serializable(with = …) on the property or @file:UseSerializers
enum Status: String, Codable@Serializable enum class + @SerialNameunknown values fail unless coerced to a default
enum with associated valuessealed interface + classDiscriminatora "type" field picks the subclass
init(from:) / encode(to:)KSerializer<T> or JsonTransformingSerializerfor wire shapes that do not match the model
DecodingErrorSerializationExceptiona subclass of IllegalArgumentException

Encode, decode and name the keys

Use `@SerialName` for one key that differs and a naming strategy for an API that is snake_case throughout — the strategy rewrites `@SerialName` values too.

import kotlinx.serialization.*
import kotlinx.serialization.json.*

@Serializable
data class LineItem(
    val sku: String,
    val quantity: Int,
    @SerialName("unit_price_cents") val unitPriceCents: Long,
)

@Serializable
data class Order(val id: String, val customer: String, val items: List<LineItem>)

@Serializable
data class Shipment(
    val orderId: String,
    @SerialName("carrierSCAC") val carrier: String,      // the naming strategy rewrites this one too
    val trackingNumber: String,
    val estimatedDays: Int,
)

@OptIn(ExperimentalSerializationApi::class)
val snakeCaseApi = Json { namingStrategy = JsonNamingStrategy.SnakeCase }   // build once, reuse

fun main() {
    val order = Order("A-1041", "Ada", listOf(LineItem("BOOK-7", 2, 1299)))
    val text = Json.encodeToString(order)
    println(text)
    println(Json.decodeFromString<Order>(text) == order)

    val body = """{"order_id":"A-1041","carrier_scac":"UPSN","tracking_number":"1Z999","estimated_days":3}"""
    val shipment = snakeCaseApi.decodeFromString<Shipment>(body)
    println(shipment)
    println(snakeCaseApi.encodeToString(shipment.copy(estimatedDays = 2)))
}
Result
{"id":"A-1041","customer":"Ada","items":[{"sku":"BOOK-7","quantity":2,"unit_price_cents":1299}]}

Shipment(orderId=A-1041, carrier=UPSN, trackingNumber=1Z999, estimatedDays=3)
{"order_id":"A-1041","carrier_scac":"UPSN","tracking_number":"1Z999","estimated_days":2}

Missing, null, defaults — and unknown keys

Strict is the default: an unknown key or a `null` for a non-null property fails, until you opt into leniency per `Json` instance.

import kotlinx.serialization.*
import kotlinx.serialization.json.*

@Serializable
data class Profile(
    val id: String,                      // required: no default
    val displayName: String = "Guest",   // may be missing
    val bio: String? = null,             // may be missing or null
    val newsletter: Boolean = false,
)

val tolerant = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true; coerceInputValues = true }

@OptIn(ExperimentalSerializationApi::class)
val compact = Json { encodeDefaults = true; explicitNulls = false }

fun firstLine(e: Exception) = e.message?.lineSequence()?.first()

fun main() {
    println(Json.decodeFromString<Profile>("""{"id":"u1"}"""))
    try {
        Json.decodeFromString<Profile>("""{"id":"u2","theme":"dark"}""")
    } catch (e: SerializationException) {
        println("strict: ${firstLine(e)}")
    }
    // A newer server added "theme" and sends null for a field we default: accept both.
    println(tolerant.decodeFromString<Profile>("""{"id":"u3","displayName":null,"theme":"dark"}"""))

    val profile = Profile("u4")
    println(Json.encodeToString(profile))       // defaults are not written
    println(Json { encodeDefaults = true }.encodeToString(profile))
    println(compact.encodeToString(profile))    // defaults written, nulls left out
}
Result
Profile(id=u1, displayName=Guest, bio=null, newsletter=false)

Profile(id=u3, displayName=Guest, bio=null, newsletter=false)

Dates with a KSerializer

Prefer `kotlin.time.Instant`, which is built in; for `java.time`, `BigDecimal` or `UUID` write a `KSerializer` that throws `SerializationException` on bad input.

import java.time.Instant
import java.time.format.DateTimeParseException
import kotlinx.serialization.*
import kotlinx.serialization.descriptors.*
import kotlinx.serialization.encoding.*
import kotlinx.serialization.json.Json

object InstantIso8601 : KSerializer<Instant> {
    override val descriptor = PrimitiveSerialDescriptor("java.time.Instant", PrimitiveKind.STRING)

    override fun serialize(encoder: Encoder, value: Instant) = encoder.encodeString(value.toString())

    override fun deserialize(decoder: Decoder): Instant {
        val text = decoder.decodeString()
        return try {
            Instant.parse(text)
        } catch (e: DateTimeParseException) {             // a decoding error, not a crash
            throw SerializationException("'$text' is not an ISO-8601 instant", e)
        }
    }
}

@Serializable
data class OrderEvent(val orderId: String, @Serializable(with = InstantIso8601::class) val at: Instant)

fun main() {
    val text = Json.encodeToString(OrderEvent("A-1041", Instant.parse("2026-11-18T14:05:00Z")))
    println(text)
    println(Json.decodeFromString<OrderEvent>(text).at.epochSecond)

    try {
        Json.decodeFromString<OrderEvent>("""{"orderId":"A-1041","at":"yesterday"}""")
    } catch (e: SerializationException) {                 // the caller's one decoding-error branch
        println("rejected: ${e.message}")
    }
}
Result
{"orderId":"A-1041","at":"2026-11-18T14:05:00Z"}
1795010700
rejected: 'yesterday' is not an ISO-8601 instant

Enums, and values the app does not know yet

Name each entry with `@SerialName`, and give the property a default with `coerceInputValues` so a status added on the server next month does not crash today's app.

import kotlinx.serialization.*
import kotlinx.serialization.json.Json

@Serializable
enum class OrderStatus {
    @SerialName("pending") PENDING,
    @SerialName("shipped") SHIPPED,
    @SerialName("delivered") DELIVERED,
    UNKNOWN,                                              // never sent; the fallback
}

@Serializable
data class OrderUpdate(val orderId: String, val status: OrderStatus = OrderStatus.UNKNOWN)

val api = Json { coerceInputValues = true }               // an unknown enum value becomes the default

fun main() {
    println(api.encodeToString(OrderUpdate("A-1041", OrderStatus.SHIPPED)))

    val newer = """{"orderId":"A-1041","status":"returned"}"""
    println(api.decodeFromString<OrderUpdate>(newer))

    try {
        Json.decodeFromString<OrderUpdate>(newer)
    } catch (e: SerializationException) {
        println("strict: ${e.message?.lineSequence()?.first()}")
    }
}

Sealed polymorphism and the class discriminator

A sealed hierarchy is closed and needs no registration; the discriminator key names the subclass by its `@SerialName`.

import kotlinx.serialization.*
import kotlinx.serialization.json.*

@Serializable
sealed interface PaymentEvent { val orderId: String }

@Serializable @SerialName("authorized")
data class Authorized(override val orderId: String, val amountCents: Long) : PaymentEvent

@Serializable @SerialName("captured")
data class Captured(override val orderId: String) : PaymentEvent

@Serializable @SerialName("refunded")
data class Refunded(override val orderId: String, val reason: String) : PaymentEvent

val payments = Json { classDiscriminator = "kind" }    // the API's name for the type field

fun describe(event: PaymentEvent): String = when (event) {   // exhaustive: no else branch
    is Authorized -> "${event.orderId}: authorized ${event.amountCents} cents"
    is Captured -> "${event.orderId}: captured"
    is Refunded -> "${event.orderId}: refunded (${event.reason})"
}

fun main() {
    val events: List<PaymentEvent> = listOf(Authorized("A-1041", 2598), Refunded("A-1041", "damaged"))
    val text = payments.encodeToString(events)
    println(text)
    payments.decodeFromString<List<PaymentEvent>>(text).forEach { println(describe(it)) }
    try {
        payments.decodeFromString<PaymentEvent>("""{"kind":"disputed","orderId":"A-1041"}""")
    } catch (e: SerializationException) {
        println(e.message?.lineSequence()?.first())
    }
}

A custom serializer, and JsonElement for dynamic shapes

Keep a free-form part as `JsonObject` and decode it once you know its shape; use a `KSerializer` when the wire format and the model disagree.

import java.math.BigDecimal
import kotlinx.serialization.*
import kotlinx.serialization.descriptors.*
import kotlinx.serialization.encoding.*
import kotlinx.serialization.json.*

/** The API sends money as a decimal string ("25.98"); the app counts cents as a Long. */
object DecimalStringCents : KSerializer<Long> {
    override val descriptor = PrimitiveSerialDescriptor("DecimalStringCents", PrimitiveKind.STRING)
    override fun serialize(encoder: Encoder, value: Long) =
        encoder.encodeString(BigDecimal.valueOf(value, 2).toPlainString())
    override fun deserialize(decoder: Decoder): Long =
        BigDecimal(decoder.decodeString()).movePointRight(2).longValueExact()   // "25.999" fails
}

@Serializable
data class Refund(val orderId: String, @Serializable(with = DecimalStringCents::class) val amountCents: Long)

@Serializable
data class Webhook(val type: String, val data: JsonObject)   // the shape of data depends on type

val lenient = Json { ignoreUnknownKeys = true }              // built once, not per webhook

fun main() {
    val body = """{"type":"refund.created",""" +
        """"data":{"orderId":"A-1041","amountCents":"25.98","note":"partial"}}"""
    val hook = Json.decodeFromString<Webhook>(body)
    when (hook.type) {
        "refund.created" -> println(lenient.decodeFromJsonElement<Refund>(hook.data))
        else -> println("ignored ${hook.type}")
    }
    println(hook.data["note"]?.jsonPrimitive?.contentOrNull)
    val reply = buildJsonObject { put("received", true); put("type", hook.type) }
    println(reply)
    println(Json.encodeToString(Refund("A-1042", 500)))
}
Result
Refund(orderId=A-1041, amountCents=2598)
partial
{"received":true,"type":"refund.created"}
{"orderId":"A-1042","amountCents":"5.00"}

Generic wrappers: Page<T>

A generic `@Serializable` class takes its type argument's serializer; pass it explicitly where `T` is not reified.

import kotlinx.serialization.*
import kotlinx.serialization.json.*

@Serializable
data class Page<T>(val items: List<T>, val nextCursor: String? = null)

@Serializable
data class Customer(val id: String, val name: String)

@Serializable
data class Order(val id: String, val totalCents: Long)

// Reified: the compiler finds Page<T>'s serializer at the call site.
inline fun <reified T> decodePage(body: String): Page<T> = Json.decodeFromString(body)

// Not reified (a converter, a cache keyed by type): build the serializer from its parts.
fun <T> decodePage(body: String, item: KSerializer<T>): Page<T> =
    Json.decodeFromString(Page.serializer(item), body)

fun main() {
    val customers = decodePage<Customer>("""{"items":[{"id":"c1","name":"Ada"}],"nextCursor":"c1"}""")
    println(customers)
    val orders = decodePage("""{"items":[{"id":"A-1041","totalCents":2598}]}""", Order.serializer())
    println("${orders.items.single().id}, last page: ${orders.nextCursor == null}")
    println(Json.encodeToString(Page(listOf(Customer("c2", "Grace")), nextCursor = "c2")))
}
Result
Page(items=[Customer(id=c1, name=Ada)], nextCursor=c1)
A-1041, last page: true
{"items":[{"id":"c2","name":"Grace"}],"nextCursor":"c2"}

Report a bad payload, and validate after decoding

Decoding proves the shape; an `init` block with `require` proves the values — and it runs during decoding too.

import kotlinx.serialization.*
import kotlinx.serialization.json.*

@Serializable
data class SignUp(val email: String, val age: Int, val password: String) {
    init {
        require('@' in email) { "email must contain @" }
        require(age in 13..130) { "age must be between 13 and 130" }
        require(password.length >= 12) { "password must have at least 12 characters" }
    }
    override fun toString() = "SignUp(email=$email, age=$age, password=***)"   // never log it
}

sealed interface Parsed<out T> {
    data class Valid<T>(val value: T) : Parsed<T>
    data class Invalid(val reason: String) : Parsed<Nothing>
}

fun parseSignUp(body: String): Parsed<SignUp> =
    try {
        Parsed.Valid(Json.decodeFromString<SignUp>(body))
    } catch (e: SerializationException) {        // before IllegalArgumentException: it is one
        Parsed.Invalid("malformed: ${e.message?.lineSequence()?.first()}")
    } catch (e: IllegalArgumentException) {      // a require() in init
        Parsed.Invalid("invalid: ${e.message}")
    }

fun main() {
    println(parseSignUp("""{"email":"ada@example.com","age":36,"password":"correct-horse-battery"}"""))
    println(parseSignUp("""{"email":"ada@example.com","password":"correct-horse-battery"}"""))
    println(parseSignUp("""{"email":"ada@example.com","age":"36y","password":"correct-horse-battery"}"""))
    println(parseSignUp("""{"email":"ada.example.com","age":36,"password":"correct-horse-battery"}"""))
}
Result
Valid(value=SignUp(email=ada@example.com, age=36, password=***))
Invalid(reason=malformed: Field 'age' is required for type with serial name 'SignUp', but it was missing at path: $)
Invalid(reason=malformed: Unexpected JSON token at offset 36: Unexpected symbol 'y' in numeric literal at path: $.age)
Invalid(reason=invalid: email must contain @)

A binary format: ProtoBuf with @ProtoNumber

The same `@Serializable` classes encode to compact ProtoBuf, where field numbers — not names — are the contract between versions.

import kotlinx.serialization.*
import kotlinx.serialization.json.Json
import kotlinx.serialization.protobuf.*

@OptIn(ExperimentalSerializationApi::class)
@Serializable
data class OrderMessage(
    @ProtoNumber(1) val id: String,
    @ProtoNumber(2) val totalCents: Long,                  // money as integer cents, never a Double
    @ProtoNumber(3) val skus: List<String> = emptyList(),
    @ProtoNumber(4) val giftNote: String? = null,          // added in v2: optional, so v1 still decodes
)

@OptIn(ExperimentalSerializationApi::class)
@Serializable
data class OrderMessageV1(@ProtoNumber(1) val id: String, @ProtoNumber(2) val totalCents: Long)

@OptIn(ExperimentalSerializationApi::class)
fun main() {
    val order = OrderMessage("A-1041", 2598, listOf("BOOK-7", "PEN-2"), giftNote = "Happy birthday")
    val bytes = ProtoBuf.encodeToByteArray(order)
    println("${bytes.size} bytes of protobuf, ${Json.encodeToString(order).length} of JSON")
    println(ProtoBuf.decodeFromByteArray<OrderMessage>(bytes) == order)
    println(ProtoBuf.decodeFromByteArray<OrderMessageV1>(bytes))       // an old reader skips fields 3 and 4
    val v1 = ProtoBuf.encodeToByteArray(OrderMessageV1("A-1042", 500))
    println(ProtoBuf.decodeFromByteArray<OrderMessage>(v1))            // a new reader fills the defaults
    val cutAtField = bytes.copyOf(bytes.size - 16)                   // the giftNote field is gone
    println(ProtoBuf.decodeFromByteArray<OrderMessage>(cutAtField))    // no error: silently a default
    try {
        ProtoBuf.decodeFromByteArray<OrderMessage>(bytes.copyOf(bytes.size - 4))
    } catch (e: RuntimeException) {                     // not always a SerializationException
        println("cut mid-field: ${e::class.simpleName}")
    }
}
Result

Prints that 42 bytes of ProtoBuf carry what takes 87 characters of JSON, that the round trip is equal, that a v1 reader skips fields 3 and 4 and a v2 reader fills their defaults — and that a payload cut at a field boundary decodes without error, while one cut mid-field throws IndexOutOfBoundsException.

Setup
  1. Gradle: the kotlin("plugin.serialization") plugin, kotlinx-serialization-json:1.13.0 and org.jetbrains.kotlinx:kotlinx-serialization-protobuf:1.13.0
  2. Save as main.kt in that project and run it; the ProtoBuf format is marked @ExperimentalSerializationApi

Pitfalls worth saying out loud

Most decoding bugs are configuration, not code.

  • Building Json { … } inside a function you call per request — it is meant to be built once and shared; keep one instance per API.
  • Turning on ignoreUnknownKeys, coerceInputValues and isLenient everywhere — leniency hides contract drift. Be lenient only for responses from servers that evolve, strict for anything you produce.
  • Encoding a subclass through its own static type: encodeToString(Authorized(…)) writes no discriminator. Encode through the sealed type (encodeToString<PaymentEvent>(…)).
  • Catching IllegalArgumentException before SerializationException — the second is a subclass of the first, so its branch never runs.
  • A property is optional only if it has a default; String? without = null is still required.
  • Assuming strict Json checks JSON types: it still decodes "36" into an Int. Validate the values you care about in init, or with a custom serializer.
  • Catching only SerializationException: a custom serializer, the built-in kotlin.time.Instant one, or a truncated ProtoBuf payload can throw other IllegalArgumentExceptions or IndexOutOfBoundsException — map them all to one decoding error.
  • Keep wire models separate from domain models when the API is ugly: decode into OrderDto, validate, then map to Order.
  • Treat every payload as untrusted: decode, then require the ranges, then cap sizes (body.length, list counts) before you allocate on them.
  • R8 keeps generated serializers for plain @Serializable classes; check the library's R8 notes when you look serializers up by KClass or use @Polymorphic registrations.

Sequential vs concurrent

Calls are sequential by default; `async` makes concurrency explicit.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlin.time.measureTime

suspend fun load(name: String): String {
    delay(100)                             // suspends; the thread is free meanwhile
    return name
}

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val sequential = measureTime { load("user"); load("posts") }
    val concurrent = measureTime {
        val user = async { load("user") }
        val posts = async { load("posts") }
        println("${user.await()} ${posts.await()}")
    }
    // about 200 ms against about 100 ms; compared, not printed, so a busy machine cannot change the output
    println("concurrent took well under the sequential time: ${concurrent < sequential * 0.75}")
}
Result
user posts
concurrent took well under the sequential time: true

Structured fan-out

`coroutineScope` waits for every child and fails if one fails — the TaskGroup of Kotlin.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*

suspend fun thumbnail(id: Int): String {
    delay(10L * (4 - id))                  // later ids finish first
    return "thumb-$id"
}

suspend fun thumbnails(ids: List<Int>): Map<Int, String> = coroutineScope {
    ids.map { id -> async { id to thumbnail(id) } }   // all start now
        .awaitAll()                                   // results in INPUT order
        .toMap()
}

fun main() = runBlocking {
    println(thumbnails(listOf(1, 2, 3)))
}
Result
{1=thumb-1, 2=thumb-2, 3=thumb-3}

Failure propagation and supervision

A failing child cancels its siblings in `coroutineScope`; in `supervisorScope` each child fails alone.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*

fun main() = runBlocking {
    try {
        coroutineScope {
            launch { delay(1_000); println("never printed: cancelled by its sibling") }
            launch { delay(10); error("boom") }
        }
    } catch (e: IllegalStateException) {
        println("caught ${e.message}")
    }

    val results = supervisorScope {
        val a = async { delay(10); 1 }
        val b = async<Int> { throw IllegalArgumentException("bad input") }
        listOf(runCatching { a.await() }, runCatching { b.await() })
    }
    println(results.map { r -> r.getOrElse { it.message } })
}
Result
caught boom
[1, bad input]

Cancellation and timeouts

Cancellation is cooperative: every suspension point checks it, and `finally` runs like Swift's `defer`.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val ticks = Channel<Int>()
    val job = launch {
        try {
            repeat(10) { i ->
                ticks.send(i)
                delay(100)                     // a suspension point: where cancellation lands
            }
        } finally {
            println("cleanup")
        }
    }
    repeat(3) { println("tick ${ticks.receive()}") }
    job.cancelAndJoin()                        // e.g. the screen went away after three ticks

    val result = withTimeoutOrNull(150) { delay(1_000); "done" }
    println("timeout -> $result")
}
Result
tick 0
tick 1
tick 2
cleanup
timeout -> null

CPU work off the caller's thread

`withContext(Dispatchers.Default)` moves the work; a loop without suspension must call `ensureActive()` to stay cancellable.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*

suspend fun countPrimes(limit: Int): Int = withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
    var count = 0
    for (n in 2..limit) {
        ensureActive()
        if ((2..Math.sqrt(n.toDouble()).toInt()).none { n % it == 0 }) count++
    }
    count
}

fun main() = runBlocking {
    println(countPrimes(10_000))
}
Result
1229

Bridging callbacks and futures

`suspendCancellableCoroutine` is `withCheckedContinuation`; `CompletableFuture.await()` ships in coroutines-core.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.future.await
import java.util.concurrent.CompletableFuture
import kotlin.coroutines.resume

fun fetchTheme(callback: (String) -> Unit) {          // a callback API you do not own
    Thread { Thread.sleep(20); callback("dark") }.start()
}

suspend fun fetchTheme(): String = suspendCancellableCoroutine { cont ->
    fetchTheme { value -> cont.resume(value) }
}

fun main() = runBlocking {
    println(fetchTheme())
    println(CompletableFuture.supplyAsync { 6 * 7 }.await())
}
Result
dark
42

Swift concurrency → coroutines

The concepts map one to one; the defaults differ.

SwiftKotlinDifference
async letasync { } + await()needs a scope; async is a builder, not a keyword
withThrowingTaskGroupcoroutineScope { map { async { } }.awaitAll() }same structured semantics
Task { }scope.launch { }always launched in an explicit scope
Task.detachedGlobalScope.launchdiscouraged for the same reasons
Task.checkCancellation()ensureActive()CancellationException must be rethrown, never swallowed
withCheckedContinuationsuspendCancellableCoroutineresuming twice throws IllegalStateException
@MainActorDispatchers.Main / withContext(Dispatchers.Main)a dispatcher, not a compiler-checked isolation domain

Rules

What reviewers flag first.

  • runBlocking inside a coroutine or on the Android main thread blocks the thread it runs on.
  • catch (e: Exception) around a suspend call swallows CancellationException — rethrow it, or catch narrower types.
  • Launch in a scope with a lifetime (viewModelScope, lifecycleScope, your own CoroutineScope), never GlobalScope.
  • Make suspend functions main-safe: they switch dispatcher themselves with withContext.

Two pointers

On sorted input, move the pointer that brings the sum closer. O(n), O(1) space.

fun pairWithSum(sorted: List<Int>, target: Int): Pair<Int, Int>? {
    var lo = 0
    var hi = sorted.lastIndex
    while (lo < hi) {
        val sum = sorted[lo] + sorted[hi]
        when {
            sum == target -> return lo to hi
            sum < target -> lo++
            else -> hi--
        }
    }
    return null
}

fun main() = println("${pairWithSum(listOf(1, 3, 4, 6, 9), 10)} ${pairWithSum(listOf(1, 2), 7)}")

(0, 4) null

Sliding window

Longest substring without repeats — grow the right edge, jump the left past the last repeat. O(n).

fun longestUnique(s: String): Int {
    val lastSeen = HashMap<Char, Int>()
    var start = 0
    var best = 0
    for ((i, ch) in s.withIndex()) {
        val prev = lastSeen[ch]
        if (prev != null && prev >= start) start = prev + 1
        lastSeen[ch] = i
        best = maxOf(best, i - start + 1)
    }
    return best
}

fun main() = println("${longestUnique("abcabcbb")} ${longestUnique("pwwkew")}")

Binary search — built in and lower bound

The built-in finds some match; the lower bound finds the first index not less than the target.

fun lowerBound(xs: List<Int>, target: Int): Int {
    var lo = 0
    var hi = xs.size
    while (lo < hi) {
        val mid = (lo + hi) ushr 1
        if (xs[mid] < target) lo = mid + 1 else hi = mid
    }
    return lo
}

fun main() {
    val xs = listOf(1, 3, 3, 5, 8)
    println("${xs.binarySearch(5)} ${xs.binarySearch(4)}")    // 4 is missing: -(3) - 1
    println("${lowerBound(xs, 3)} ${lowerBound(xs, 4)} ${lowerBound(xs, 9)}")
}

Heap — top k

A min-heap of size k keeps the k largest; its root is the smallest of them. O(n log k).

import java.util.PriorityQueue

fun topK(xs: List<Int>, k: Int): List<Int> {
    val heap = PriorityQueue<Int>()
    for (x in xs) {
        heap.offer(x)
        if (heap.size > k) heap.poll()
    }
    return heap.sortedDescending()
}

Breadth-first search on a grid

BFS finds shortest paths in unweighted graphs; `ArrayDeque` makes each dequeue O(1).

fun shortestPath(grid: List<String>, from: Pair<Int, Int>, to: Pair<Int, Int>): Int {
    val dist = hashMapOf(from to 0)
    val queue = ArrayDeque(listOf(from))
    while (queue.isNotEmpty()) {
        val cell = queue.removeFirst()
        val here = dist.getValue(cell)
        if (cell == to) return here
        val (r, c) = cell
        for ((dr, dc) in listOf(1 to 0, -1 to 0, 0 to 1, 0 to -1)) {
            val next = r + dr to c + dc
            val (nr, nc) = next
            if (nr !in grid.indices || nc !in grid[nr].indices || grid[nr][nc] == '#' || next in dist) continue
            dist[next] = here + 1
            queue.addLast(next)
        }
    }
    return -1
}

fun main() = println(shortestPath(listOf("..#.", ".##.", "...."), 0 to 0, 0 to 3))

Hash map: counting, grouping, memory of the past

Unsorted two-sum, anagram groups and the first non-repeating character — remember what you have seen, in O(n) hash operations and O(n) space.

fun twoSumUnsorted(xs: IntArray, target: Int): Pair<Int, Int>? {
    val indexOf = HashMap<Int, Int>()                   // value -> where it was seen
    for ((i, x) in xs.withIndex()) {
        indexOf[target - x]?.let { return it to i }       // near Int.MAX_VALUE, compute in Long
        indexOf[x] = i
    }
    return null
}

fun main() {
    println(twoSumUnsorted(intArrayOf(7, 2, 11, 15, 4), 6))

    // Grouping: a canonical key per group (sorting each word adds O(L log L) per word);
    // groupBy keeps first-seen order (LinkedHashMap).
    val words = listOf("listen", "silent", "enlist", "google", "gogole", "cat")
    println(words.groupBy { it.toCharArray().sorted().joinToString("") }.values)

    // Counting: groupingBy().eachCount() builds the frequency map in one pass.
    val text = "swiss"
    val counts = text.groupingBy { it }.eachCount()
    println("$counts first unique: ${text.firstOrNull { counts[it] == 1 }}")
}

Prefix sums & difference arrays

Daily revenue: any range total in O(1) after O(n) prep, subarrays summing to k, and many range updates in O(1) each.

// Revenue in cents: Long, because an Int sum silently wraps past 2^31 (about $21M).
fun prefixSums(xs: IntArray): LongArray {
    val prefix = LongArray(xs.size + 1)                 // prefix[i] = sum of the first i
    for (i in xs.indices) prefix[i + 1] = prefix[i] + xs[i]
    return prefix
}

/** How many contiguous runs sum to exactly k? Prefix sums + a hash map, O(n). */
fun subarraysSummingTo(xs: IntArray, k: Long): Int {
    val seen = hashMapOf(0L to 1)                       // prefix value -> times seen
    var running = 0L
    var total = 0
    for (x in xs) {
        running += x
        total += seen[running - k] ?: 0
        seen[running] = (seen[running] ?: 0) + 1
    }
    return total
}

/** "Add v to every day from l to r" many times: O(1) per update, one O(n) pass at the end. */
fun applyRangeAdds(days: Int, updates: List<Triple<Int, Int, Long>>): LongArray {
    val diff = LongArray(days + 1)
    for ((l, r, v) in updates) {
        diff[l] += v
        diff[r + 1] -= v
    }
    var running = 0L
    return LongArray(days) { running += diff[it]; running }
}

fun main() {
    val prefix = prefixSums(intArrayOf(3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2))
    fun rangeSum(from: Int, to: Int) = prefix[to + 1] - prefix[from]     // inclusive, O(1)
    println("days 2..5 = ${rangeSum(2, 5)}")
    println(subarraysSummingTo(intArrayOf(1, 2, 3, -2, 2), 3))
    println(applyRangeAdds(5, listOf(Triple(0, 2, 10L), Triple(1, 4, 5L))).toList())
}

Sort then sweep: intervals

A room's bookings merged into busy blocks, and the number of rooms the day needs — sorting first makes both a linear scan.

data class Booking(val start: Int, val end: Int)

fun busyBlocks(bookings: List<Booking>): List<Booking> {
    val merged = mutableListOf<Booking>()
    for (b in bookings.sortedBy { it.start }) {
        val last = merged.lastOrNull()
        if (last != null && b.start <= last.end) {
            merged[merged.lastIndex] = last.copy(end = maxOf(last.end, b.end))   // overlap: extend
        } else {
            merged += b
        }
    }
    return merged
}

/** Sweep line: +1 at each start, -1 at each end. Ends sort first on a tie: a room frees up for the next. */
fun roomsNeeded(bookings: List<Booking>): Int {
    val events = bookings.flatMap { listOf(it.start to +1, it.end to -1) }
        .sortedWith(compareBy({ it.first }, { it.second }))
    var inUse = 0
    var peak = 0
    for ((_, delta) in events) {
        inUse += delta
        peak = maxOf(peak, inUse)
    }
    return peak
}

fun main() {
    val day = listOf(Booking(9, 10), Booking(13, 15), Booking(9, 12), Booking(12, 13), Booking(16, 17))
    println(busyBlocks(day))
    println("rooms: ${roomsNeeded(day)}")
}

Stack & monotonic stack

Validate the brackets in a template, and for each day count the days until a warmer one — both O(n) with an ArrayDeque.

fun isBalanced(s: String): Boolean {
    val openerOf = mapOf(')' to '(', ']' to '[', '}' to '{')
    val open = ArrayDeque<Char>()
    for (ch in s) {
        when (ch) {
            in openerOf.values -> open.addLast(ch)
            in openerOf.keys -> if (open.removeLastOrNull() != openerOf[ch]) return false
        }
    }
    return open.isEmpty()
}

/** Indices wait on a stack whose temperatures decrease; a warmer day pops and answers them. */
fun daysUntilWarmer(temps: IntArray): IntArray {
    val answer = IntArray(temps.size)
    val waiting = ArrayDeque<Int>()
    for (i in temps.indices) {
        while (waiting.isNotEmpty() && temps[waiting.last()] < temps[i]) {
            val day = waiting.removeLast()
            answer[day] = i - day
        }
        waiting.addLast(i)
    }
    return answer
}

fun main() {
    println("${isBalanced("{ \"items\": [1, (2)] }")} ${isBalanced("([)]")} ${isBalanced("((")}")
    println(daysUntilWarmer(intArrayOf(73, 74, 75, 71, 69, 72, 76, 73)).toList())
    // The same skeleton: stock span, largest rectangle in a histogram, trapping rain water.
}

Fast & slow pointers on a linked list

A playlist chained by next pointers: find its middle, and detect a corrupted chain that loops — O(n) time, O(1) space.

class Node(val value: Int, var next: Node? = null)

fun middle(head: Node?): Node? {
    var slow = head
    var fast = head
    while (fast?.next != null) {
        slow = slow?.next
        fast = fast.next?.next
    }
    return slow
}

fun hasCycle(head: Node?): Boolean {
    var slow = head
    var fast = head
    while (fast?.next != null) {
        slow = slow?.next
        fast = fast.next?.next
        if (slow === fast) return true                  // identity, not equality
    }
    return false
}

fun linked(vararg values: Int): Node? = values.reversed().fold(null as Node?) { next, v -> Node(v, next) }

fun main() {
    val playlist = linked(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)
    println("middle=${middle(playlist)?.value} cycle=${hasCycle(playlist)}")
    println("middle of an even list: ${middle(linked(1, 2, 3, 4))?.value}")   // the second of the two
    val second = Node(2)
    val looping = Node(1, second)
    second.next = Node(3, next = second)                       // a corrupted chain: 3 points back at 2
    println("cycle=${hasCycle(looping)}")
}
Result
middle=3 cycle=false
middle of an even list: 3
cycle=true

In-place reversal of a linked list

Reverse the play-next queue without allocating — three pointers in one pass, the building block of reverse-in-groups and palindrome checks.

class Node(val value: Int, var next: Node? = null)

/** Turns each node's `next` to point backwards. O(n) time, O(1) extra space. */
fun reverse(head: Node?): Node? {
    var previous: Node? = null
    var current = head
    while (current != null) {
        val next = current.next                          // remember the rest before cutting the link
        current.next = previous
        previous = current
        current = next
    }
    return previous
}

fun linked(vararg values: Int): Node? = values.reversed().fold(null as Node?) { next, v -> Node(v, next) }

fun Node?.values() = generateSequence(this) { it.next }.map { it.value }.toList()

fun main() {
    println(reverse(linked(1, 2, 3, 4, 5)).values())
    println("${reverse(linked(7)).values()} ${reverse(null).values()}")
}

Trees: DFS and BFS

A binary search tree of product prices: in-order DFS gives sorted output, BFS gives levels, and validity needs bounds passed down.

class TreeNode(val value: Int, val left: TreeNode? = null, val right: TreeNode? = null)

// Recursion depth = tree height: a degenerate tree of ~20k nodes (prices inserted in sorted order)
// overflows the stack — walk it with an explicit ArrayDeque stack there.
fun inorder(node: TreeNode?, out: MutableList<Int> = mutableListOf()): List<Int> {
    if (node != null) {
        inorder(node.left, out)
        out += node.value
        inorder(node.right, out)
    }
    return out
}

fun levels(root: TreeNode?): List<List<Int>> {
    val result = mutableListOf<List<Int>>()
    var level = listOfNotNull(root)
    while (level.isNotEmpty()) {
        result += level.map { it.value }
        level = level.flatMap { listOfNotNull(it.left, it.right) }
    }
    return result
}

/** Compare against the allowed range, not just the parent. Long bounds so Int.MIN_VALUE still fits. */
fun isValidBst(node: TreeNode?, low: Long = Long.MIN_VALUE, high: Long = Long.MAX_VALUE): Boolean {
    if (node == null) return true
    val v = node.value.toLong()
    return low < v && v < high && isValidBst(node.left, low, v) && isValidBst(node.right, v, high)
}

fun main() {
    val prices = TreeNode(8,
        left = TreeNode(3, TreeNode(1), TreeNode(6, TreeNode(4), TreeNode(7))),
        right = TreeNode(10, right = TreeNode(14, TreeNode(13))))
    println(inorder(prices))
    println(levels(prices))
    val broken = TreeNode(5, TreeNode(1), TreeNode(6, TreeNode(3), TreeNode(7)))   // 3 sits right of 5
    println("${isValidBst(prices)} ${isValidBst(broken)}")
}

Graphs: BFS and DFS

Degrees of separation between two users by BFS and every service hit by a failing one by DFS, both in O(V + E).

typealias Graph = Map<String, List<String>>

/** BFS: the first time a person is reached is by the fewest hops — shortest in an unweighted graph. */
fun degreesBetween(friends: Graph, from: String, to: String): Int? {
    val distance = hashMapOf(from to 0)
    val queue = ArrayDeque(listOf(from))
    while (queue.isNotEmpty()) {
        val person = queue.removeFirst()
        if (person == to) return distance.getValue(person)
        for (friend in friends[person].orEmpty()) {
            if (friend in distance) continue
            distance[friend] = distance.getValue(person) + 1
            queue.addLast(friend)
        }
    }
    return null
}

/** Iterative DFS with an explicit stack: a deep graph cannot overflow the call stack. */
fun affectedBy(dependents: Graph, failing: String): Set<String> {
    val seen = HashSet<String>()
    val stack = ArrayDeque(listOf(failing))
    while (stack.isNotEmpty()) {
        val service = stack.removeLast()
        if (seen.add(service)) dependents[service].orEmpty().forEach(stack::addLast)
    }
    return (seen - failing).toSortedSet()
}

fun main() {
    val friends = mapOf("ana" to listOf("ben", "cy"), "ben" to listOf("ana", "dee"), "cy" to listOf("ana"),
        "dee" to listOf("ben", "eve"), "eve" to listOf("dee"), "fay" to emptyList())
    println("${degreesBetween(friends, "ana", "eve")} ${degreesBetween(friends, "ana", "fay")}")
    val dependents = mapOf("db" to listOf("orders", "users"), "orders" to listOf("checkout"),
        "users" to listOf("checkout", "profile"), "search" to listOf("checkout"))
    println(affectedBy(dependents, "db"))
}

Topological sort

The order to build Gradle modules so each comes after what it depends on — Kahn's algorithm in O(V + E), which also detects a cycle.

/** Returns null when the dependencies contain a cycle. */
fun buildOrder(dependsOn: Map<String, List<String>>): List<String>? {
    val modules = (dependsOn.keys + dependsOn.values.flatten()).toSortedSet()
    val waitingOn = modules.associateWith { dependsOn[it].orEmpty().size }.toMutableMap()
    val unblocks = HashMap<String, MutableList<String>>()
    for ((module, deps) in dependsOn) for (dep in deps) unblocks.getOrPut(dep) { mutableListOf() } += module

    val ready = ArrayDeque(modules.filter { waitingOn[it] == 0 })
    val order = mutableListOf<String>()
    while (ready.isNotEmpty()) {
        val module = ready.removeFirst()
        order += module
        for (next in unblocks[module].orEmpty()) {
            waitingOn[next] = waitingOn.getValue(next) - 1
            if (waitingOn[next] == 0) ready.addLast(next)
        }
    }
    return if (order.size == modules.size) order else null     // leftovers are on a cycle or wait on one
}

fun main() {
    val project = mapOf(
        ":app" to listOf(":feature-cart", ":core-ui"),
        ":feature-cart" to listOf(":core-network", ":core-ui"),
        ":core-ui" to listOf(":core-model"),
        ":core-network" to listOf(":core-model"),
    )
    println(buildOrder(project))
    println(buildOrder(mapOf(":a" to listOf(":b"), ":b" to listOf(":a"))))
}

Backtracking

Every set of gift cards that pays an order exactly, and every order of delivery stops — choose, explore, un-choose, and prune early.

fun exactCombinations(cards: List<Int>, total: Int): List<List<Int>> {
    require(cards.all { it > 0 }) { "card values must be positive" }   // the `break` pruning relies on it
    val sorted = cards.sorted()
    val result = mutableListOf<List<Int>>()
    val chosen = mutableListOf<Int>()
    fun explore(start: Int, remaining: Int) {
        if (remaining == 0) { result += chosen.toList(); return }
        for (i in start until sorted.size) {
            if (sorted[i] > remaining) break                       // sorted: nothing later fits either
            if (i > start && sorted[i] == sorted[i - 1]) continue  // same value, same subtree
            chosen += sorted[i]                                    // choose
            explore(i + 1, remaining - sorted[i])                  // explore
            chosen.removeAt(chosen.lastIndex)                      // un-choose
        }
    }
    explore(0, total)
    return result
}

fun <T> routes(stops: List<T>): List<List<T>> {
    val result = mutableListOf<List<T>>()
    val route = mutableListOf<T>()
    val used = BooleanArray(stops.size)
    fun explore() {
        if (route.size == stops.size) { result += route.toList(); return }
        for (i in stops.indices) {
            if (used[i]) continue
            used[i] = true; route += stops[i]
            explore()
            route.removeAt(route.lastIndex); used[i] = false
        }
    }
    explore()
    return result
}

fun main() {
    println(exactCombinations(listOf(10, 1, 2, 7, 6, 1, 5), 8))
    println(routes(listOf("A", "B", "C")))
}

Dynamic programming

Fewest coins for change (1-D), edit distance for "did you mean" (2-D), and a memoised count when the recurrence reads better top-down.

/** dp[a] = fewest coins making a. O(amount × coins). -1 when impossible. */
fun fewestCoins(coins: IntArray, amount: Int): Int {
    val dp = IntArray(amount + 1) { if (it == 0) 0 else Int.MAX_VALUE }
    for (a in 1..amount) {
        for (c in coins) if (c <= a && dp[a - c] != Int.MAX_VALUE) dp[a] = minOf(dp[a], dp[a - c] + 1)
    }
    return if (dp[amount] == Int.MAX_VALUE) -1 else dp[amount]
}

/** dp[i][j] = edits turning the first i chars of a into the first j of b. */
fun editDistance(a: String, b: String): Int {
    val dp = Array(a.length + 1) { IntArray(b.length + 1) }
    for (i in 0..a.length) dp[i][0] = i                        // delete everything
    for (j in 0..b.length) dp[0][j] = j                        // insert everything
    for (i in 1..a.length) {
        for (j in 1..b.length) {
            dp[i][j] = if (a[i - 1] == b[j - 1]) dp[i - 1][j - 1]
            else 1 + minOf(dp[i - 1][j], dp[i][j - 1], dp[i - 1][j - 1])   // delete, insert, substitute
        }
    }
    return dp[a.length][b.length]
}

/** Paths through an r × c grid moving right or down. Long: the count outgrows Int quickly. */
fun gridPaths(r: Int, c: Int, memo: MutableMap<Pair<Int, Int>, Long> = HashMap()): Long =
    if (r == 1 || c == 1) 1
    else memo.getOrPut(r to c) { gridPaths(r - 1, c, memo) + gridPaths(r, c - 1, memo) }

fun main() {
    println("${fewestCoins(intArrayOf(1, 5, 10, 25), 63)} ${fewestCoins(intArrayOf(2), 3)}")
    println("${editDistance("kitten", "sitting")} ${editDistance("recieve", "receive")}")
    println(gridPaths(17, 17))
}

6 -1
3 2
601080390

Union-Find (disjoint set)

Cables between routers: which cable closes a loop and how many separate networks remain, in near O(1) per operation.

class UnionFind(size: Int) {
    private val parent = IntArray(size) { it }
    private val rank = IntArray(size)
    var components = size
        private set

    fun find(x: Int): Int {
        if (parent[x] != x) parent[x] = find(parent[x])    // path compression
        return parent[x]
    }

    /** False when a and b were already connected — the new edge is redundant. */
    fun union(a: Int, b: Int): Boolean {
        val ra = find(a)
        val rb = find(b)
        if (ra == rb) return false
        when {                                              // union by rank keeps trees shallow
            rank[ra] < rank[rb] -> parent[ra] = rb
            rank[ra] > rank[rb] -> parent[rb] = ra
            else -> { parent[rb] = ra; rank[ra]++ }
        }
        components--
        return true
    }
}

fun main() {
    val networks = UnionFind(6)
    for ((a, b) in listOf(0 to 1, 1 to 2, 3 to 4, 2 to 0, 4 to 5)) {
        if (!networks.union(a, b)) println("cable $a-$b closes a loop")
    }
    println("networks=${networks.components}")
    println("0~2 ${networks.find(0) == networks.find(2)}, 0~5 ${networks.find(0) == networks.find(5)}")
}
Result
cable 2-0 closes a loop
networks=2
0~2 true, 0~5 false

Trie (prefix tree)

Autocomplete for a search box: completions of a prefix in O(prefix + results), whatever the dictionary size.

class Trie {
    private class Node {
        val children = sortedMapOf<Char, Node>()            // sorted: completions come out alphabetical
        var isWord = false
    }

    private val root = Node()

    fun insert(word: String) {
        var node = root
        for (ch in word) node = node.children.getOrPut(ch) { Node() }
        node.isWord = true
    }

    private fun find(prefix: String): Node? {
        var node = root
        for (ch in prefix) node = node.children[ch] ?: return null
        return node
    }

    fun complete(prefix: String, limit: Int = 5): List<String> {
        val out = mutableListOf<String>()
        fun collect(node: Node, path: StringBuilder) {
            if (out.size == limit) return
            if (node.isWord) out += path.toString()
            for ((ch, child) in node.children) {
                path.append(ch)
                collect(child, path)
                path.setLength(path.length - 1)
            }
        }
        find(prefix)?.let { collect(it, StringBuilder(prefix)) }
        return out
    }
}

fun main() {
    val products = Trie()
    listOf("kotlin", "kotlinx", "kodein", "koin", "ktor", "java").forEach(products::insert)
    println("${products.complete("ko")} ${products.complete("kt")} ${products.complete("sw")}")
}
Result

Bit manipulation & cyclic sort

Feature flags packed in an Int, the one unpaired id, and the lowest ticket number not yet issued — O(1) extra space each.

// An Int holds 32 flags (test with `!= 0`); `1 shl 32 == 1` because the shift count wraps —
// use Long and `1L shl n` for up to 64.
const val DARK_MODE = 1 shl 0
const val OFFLINE = 1 shl 1
const val BETA = 1 shl 2

fun IntArray.swap(i: Int, j: Int) {
    val t = this[i]
    this[i] = this[j]
    this[j] = t
}

/**
 * Cyclic sort: put each value v in 1..n at index v - 1, then the first misfit is the answer.
 * It reorders `tickets` in place (that is the O(1) space): pass `tickets.copyOf()` to keep the original.
 */
fun lowestUnissued(tickets: IntArray): Int {
    var i = 0
    while (i < tickets.size) {
        val home = tickets[i] - 1
        if (home in tickets.indices && tickets[home] != tickets[i]) tickets.swap(i, home) else i++
    }
    return (tickets.indices.firstOrNull { tickets[it] != it + 1 } ?: tickets.size) + 1
}

fun main() {
    var flags = DARK_MODE or BETA
    println("beta=${(flags and BETA) != 0} offline=${(flags and OFFLINE) != 0} set=${flags.countOneBits()}")
    flags = flags and BETA.inv()                                   // clear one flag
    println("flags=${flags.toString(2)} lowest=${(OFFLINE or BETA).takeLowestOneBit()}")
    val isPowerOfTwo = { x: Int -> x > 0 && (x and (x - 1)) == 0 }  // x and (x - 1) drops the lowest bit
    println("powers of two: ${listOf(64, 96).map(isPowerOfTwo)}")

    println("unpaired id: ${intArrayOf(4, 1, 2, 1, 2).reduce { acc, id -> acc xor id }}")  // pairs cancel
    val items = listOf("a", "b", "c")                              // every subset as a bitmask (< 31 items)
    val subsets = (0 until (1 shl items.size)).map { mask ->
        items.filterIndexed { i, _ -> (mask shr i) and 1 == 1 }
    }
    println(subsets)

    println("${lowestUnissued(intArrayOf(3, 4, -1, 1))} ${lowestUnissued(intArrayOf(1, 2, 3))}")
}

Working a problem out loud

The habits that matter more than the language.

  • State the brute force and its cost first, then the bottleneck the better pattern removes.
  • Name the edge cases before coding: empty input, one element, duplicates, Int overflow.
  • (lo + hi) / 2 can overflow on huge indices — ushr 1 or lo + (hi - lo) / 2.
  • List<Int> boxes; for tight numeric loops prefer IntArray.

Streaming & Time-Series Patterns

Unbounded data, bounded memory: windows, sketches, rate limits and backpressure — in plain Kotlin and over Flow and Channel.

  • jvm
  • android
  • kotlin >=2.0
  • jvm >=17
  • Kotlin/JVM (the standard library and java.util)

Sources: Asynchronous Flow — Kotlin docs · Channels — Kotlin docs · kotlinx-coroutines-test — API reference · kotlin.time — Kotlin API reference

The constraints that define the field

Every card below is an answer to one of these.

  • You see each item once, in order, and cannot keep them all — so answers are incremental, approximate, or windowed.
  • Bounded memory is the whole game: O(1) or O(window), never O(stream).
  • Time is two things: event time (when it happened) and processing time (when you saw it). They diverge, and a watermark is how you decide a window is complete.
  • Exact vs approximate — a sketch trades a few percent of accuracy for orders of magnitude of memory. Say the error bound out loud.
  • In Kotlin a stream is a Flow (cold, suspending — the collector's pace *is* the backpressure), a Channel (a hot, bounded queue between coroutines) or a Sequence (synchronous pull, for files and replays).
  • Inject the clock. TimeSource with TestTimeSource for plain code, runTest virtual time for flows — every example here is deterministic that way.

Windowing a stream

Almost every streaming requirement is one of these windows plus a lateness policy.

WindowShapeAnswersGroup by
Tumblingfixed size, no overlap: [0, 60s), [60s, 120s)orders per minute, a billing periodt - Math.floorMod(t, size)
Hoppingfixed size advancing by a smaller hop; an event is in size / hop windowsa 5-minute error rate refreshed every 10 severy hop start in (t - size, t]
Sessionper key, closed by a gap of inactivitya user's visit, a burst of typingkey, extended while the next event is within the gap
Count (sliding)the last n eventsthe average of the last 100 requestsposition: a ring buffer
Late eventsits window has already closed: window end ≤ watermark (highest event time − allowed lateness)what happens to a delayed uploaddrop and count, hold longer, or reopen the window and re-emit

Tumbling windows with a watermark

Revenue per minute by event time — a window closes once the watermark passes its end, so a delayed order still counts, up to the allowed lateness.

import java.util.TreeMap

data class Order(val atMs: Long, val cents: Long)                // atMs: event time
data class Window(val startMs: Long, var orders: Int = 0, var cents: Long = 0)

class TumblingWindows(private val sizeMs: Long, private val latenessMs: Long) {
    private val open = TreeMap<Long, Window>()                   // window start -> running totals
    private var watermark = Long.MIN_VALUE                       // highest event time − allowed lateness
    var late = 0
        private set

    /** Adds an order; returns the windows the advancing watermark closed, oldest first. */
    fun add(order: Order): List<Window> {
        val start = order.atMs - Math.floorMod(order.atMs, sizeMs)
        if (start + sizeMs <= watermark) {                       // already final: count it, never reopen
            late++
            return emptyList()
        }
        open.getOrPut(start) { Window(start) }.apply { orders++; cents += order.cents }
        watermark = maxOf(watermark, order.atMs - latenessMs)
        return closeWhile { startMs -> startMs + sizeMs <= watermark }
    }

    fun flush(): List<Window> = closeWhile { true }              // end of stream: all open windows are final

    private fun closeWhile(due: (startMs: Long) -> Boolean): List<Window> {
        val closed = mutableListOf<Window>()
        while (open.isNotEmpty() && due(open.firstKey())) closed += open.pollFirstEntry().value
        return closed
    }
}

fun main() {
    val perMinute = TumblingWindows(sizeMs = 60_000, latenessMs = 10_000)
    fun show(w: Window) = "[${w.startMs / 1000}s, +60s) count ${w.orders}, ${w.cents} cents"
    val arrivals = listOf(5 to 1200L, 20 to 800L, 58 to 450L, 62 to 2000L, 50 to 300L, 75 to 990L,
        130 to 1500L, 55 to 700L)                                // (second, cents), in arrival order
    for ((second, cents) in arrivals) {
        for (w in perMinute.add(Order(second * 1000L, cents))) println("after ${second}s: ${show(w)}")
    }
    for (w in perMinute.flush()) println("at the end: ${show(w)}")
    println("late orders dropped: ${perMinute.late}")
}
Result

after 130s: [60s, +60s) count 2, 2990 cents
at the end: [120s, +60s) count 1, 1500 cents
late orders dropped: 1

Ring buffer — a fixed-size sliding window

A rolling average of the last k request latencies in O(1) per event and O(k) memory.

class RingBuffer<T>(val capacity: Int) {
    private val slots = arrayOfNulls<Any>(capacity)
    private var head = 0
    var size = 0
        private set

    /** Appends, and returns the element that fell out of the window, if any. */
    @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
    fun add(element: T): T? {
        val evicted = if (size == capacity) slots[head] as T else null
        slots[head] = element
        head = (head + 1) % capacity
        if (size < capacity) size++
        return evicted
    }

    @Suppress("UNCHECKED_CAST")
    fun toList(): List<T> = List(size) { slots[(head - size + it + capacity) % capacity] as T }
}

class MovingAverage(window: Int) {
    private val window = RingBuffer<Double>(window)
    private var sum = 0.0

    fun add(latencyMs: Double): Double {
        window.add(latencyMs)?.let { sum -= it }   // slide: subtract what left, never re-sum
        sum += latencyMs
        return sum / window.size
    }

    fun samples() = window.toList()
}

fun main() {
    val average = MovingAverage(window = 3)
    println(listOf(120.0, 80.0, 100.0, 420.0, 110.0).map(average::add))
    println(average.samples())
}
Result
[120.0, 100.0, 100.0, 200.0, 210.0]
[100.0, 420.0, 110.0]
