Make illegal states unrepresentable

Three independent fields allow eight combinations and the screen means four; a sealed interface has exactly four, and `when` proves you handled them.

Flags
data class CheckoutState(
    val isPaying: Boolean = false,
    val receiptId: String? = null,
    val error: String? = null,
)

fun render(state: CheckoutState): String = when {
    state.isPaying -> "spinner"
    state.error != null -> "error: ${state.error}"
    state.receiptId != null -> "paid: ${state.receiptId}"
    else -> "pay button"
}

fun main() {
    var state = CheckoutState()
    println(render(state))
    state = state.copy(isPaying = true)
    println(render(state))
    state = state.copy(isPaying = false, error = "card declined")
    println(render(state))
    state = state.copy(error = null, receiptId = "R-77")   // forget error = null and it shows "error"
    println(render(state))
}
Sealed
sealed interface CheckoutState {
    data object Idle : CheckoutState
    data object Paying : CheckoutState
    data class Paid(val receiptId: String) : CheckoutState
    data class Failed(val reason: String) : CheckoutState
}

fun render(state: CheckoutState): String = when (state) {   // a fifth state will not compile until handled
    CheckoutState.Idle -> "pay button"
    CheckoutState.Paying -> "spinner"
    is CheckoutState.Paid -> "paid: ${state.receiptId}"
    is CheckoutState.Failed -> "error: ${state.reason}"
}

fun main() {
    val journey = listOf(
        CheckoutState.Idle,
        CheckoutState.Paying,
        CheckoutState.Failed("card declined"),
        CheckoutState.Paid("R-77"),
    )
    journey.map(::render).forEach(::println)
}
Result
pay button
spinner
error: card declined
paid: R-77

Immutability: val, read-only views and copy

`val` fixes the reference, `List` hides the mutators — neither makes the data immutable; snapshot with `toList()` at a boundary and change values with `copy`.

data class Cart(val items: List<String>, val coupon: String? = null)

fun main() {
    val backing = mutableListOf("mug")
    val readOnly: List<String> = backing          // a read-only VIEW of the same list
    backing += "lamp"
    println(readOnly)                             // sees the change

    val snapshot = backing.toList()               // a copy: later changes do not reach it
    backing += "desk"
    println(snapshot)

    val cart = Cart(items = listOf("mug"))
    val withCoupon = cart.copy(coupon = "WELCOME5")
    val withLamp = withCoupon.copy(items = withCoupon.items + "lamp")   // `+` returns a new list
    println(cart)
    println(withLamp)

    // A read-only reference can be cast back: never trust List to mean "nobody will change it".
    val sneaky = readOnly as? MutableList<String>
    println("cast back to MutableList: ${sneaky != null}, size ${readOnly.size}")
}
Result
[mug, lamp]
[mug, lamp]
Cart(items=[mug], coupon=null)
Cart(items=[mug, lamp], coupon=WELCOME5)
cast back to MutableList: true, size 3

Laziness and memoization: Sequence, lazy, a cache

A `Sequence` runs each element through the whole chain and stops at `take`, `by lazy` computes once on first read, and this `memoize` is for pure functions only and is unbounded and single-threaded (use `ConcurrentHashMap.computeIfAbsent` or an LRU cache when shared).

data class Product(val sku: String, val priceCents: Long)

class SalesReport(private val orderTotals: List<Long>) {
    val total: Long by lazy {                                  // thread-safe by default
        println("computing total")
        orderTotals.sum()
    }
}

fun <A, R> memoize(compute: (A) -> R): (A) -> R {
    val cache = HashMap<A, R>()
    return { key -> cache.getOrPut(key) { compute(key) } }
}

fun main() {
    var priced = 0
    val firstPremium = (1..1_000_000).asSequence()
        .map { Product("P-$it", it * 7L % 10_000).also { priced++ } }   // nothing runs yet
        .filter { it.priceCents > 9_000 }
        .take(2)
        .toList()                                                        // the terminal step pulls
    println("${firstPremium.map(Product::sku)} after pricing $priced of 1000000")

    val report = SalesReport(listOf(4200, 1500))
    println(report.total)
    println(report.total)

    var quotes = 0                                                      // only here to show the cache hits
    val shippingQuote = memoize { postcode: String ->
        quotes++
        if (postcode.startsWith("75")) 0L else 590L
    }
    println(listOf("75001", "69001", "75001", "69001").map(shippingQuote))
    println("computed $quotes quotes for 4 lookups")
}
Result
[P-1286, P-1287] after pricing 1287 of 1000000
computing total
5700
5700
[0, 590, 0, 590]
computed 2 quotes for 4 lookups

tailrec, inline and reified: three compiler keywords

`tailrec` turns self-recursion into a loop; `inline` pastes a lambda into the caller (no allocation, non-local `return`); `reified` keeps a type argument at run time.

// tailrec: the recursive call is the last thing the function does, so it compiles to a loop.
tailrec fun rootCategory(id: String, parentOf: Map<String, String>): String {
    val parent = parentOf[id] ?: return id
    return rootCategory(parent, parentOf)
}

// forEach is inline, so this `return` leaves firstOutOfStock itself.
fun firstOutOfStock(stock: Map<String, Int>): String? {
    stock.forEach { (sku, quantity) -> if (quantity == 0) return sku }
    return null
}

// reified works only in an inline function: the type is substituted at each call site.
inline fun <reified T> Map<String, Any>.valueAs(key: String): T? = this[key] as? T

fun main() {
    val deepTree = (1 until 100_000).associate { "c$it" to "c${it - 1}" }   // c99999 -> ... -> c0
    println(rootCategory("c99999", deepTree))           // without tailrec: StackOverflowError
    println(firstOutOfStock(mapOf("mug" to 3, "lamp" to 0, "desk" to 0)))

    val remoteConfig: Map<String, Any> = mapOf("retries" to 3, "region" to "eu-west-1")
    val retries = remoteConfig.valueAs<Int>("retries")
    val wrongType = remoteConfig.valueAs<Int>("region")          // a String: safely null, not a crash
    println("$retries $wrongType")
}
Result
c0
lamp
3 null

Trade-offs to say out loud

The answers that show you have used FP in production, not just read about it.

  • Pure functions and immutable data classes are safe to share across coroutines and threads with no locks — the reason Compose and StateFlow want immutable state.
  • A sealed type with an exhaustive when turns a forgotten case into a compile error — the highest-value FP idea in everyday Kotlin.
  • Every List operator allocates a new list. For long chains over large data, or when you stop early, use asSequence(); for a handful of elements, plain lists are faster.
  • Read-only is not immutable: a List parameter may be a MutableList someone else changes. Copy at boundaries, or use kotlinx.collections.immutable for persistent collections.
  • Curried, point-free code fights the language — Kotlin favours named functions, trailing lambdas and named arguments; partially apply with a lambda, as in the function-values card.
  • inline copies the body into every call site — keep inline functions small; reified ones cannot be called from Java.
  • runCatching catches everything, including CancellationException in coroutines — rethrow it, or catch the specific exception instead.
  • Arrow (Either, Raise, optics) is the library for typed functional errors; adopt it as a team decision, not in one file.

Architectural Approaches

MVVM, MVI and clean layers on Android and the JVM — a view model, a reducer, a use case, an offline-first repository, navigation and a composition root, all in plain Kotlin and run; Hilt as the one Android excerpt.

  • jvm
  • android
  • kotlinx-coroutines-core
  • kotlin >=2.0
  • kotlinx-coroutines >=1.10
  • jvm >=17
  • Kotlin/JVM with kotlinx.coroutines; on Android the same classes sit behind `ViewModel` and Hilt

The common approaches compared

Name the data flow, where the logic lives and how you test it; the acronym is the least important part.

ApproachData flowWhere logic livesTestabilityBest for
MVC (Activity as controller)view ⇄ controller ⇄ model, both waysthe Activity/Fragment, next to the frameworklow: needs a device or Robolectricprototypes, a single screen
MVPview calls presenter; presenter calls a View interface backpresenter (plain Kotlin)high, but the interface is boilerplate and the presenter dies on rotationlegacy View-system codebases
MVVMview observes StateFlow; calls view-model functionsview model, which survives configuration changeshigh: plain Kotlin with a fake repositorymost Compose and View apps
MVIintents → a pure reducer → one immutable statethe reducer; effects outside itvery high: the reducer is a functioncomplex screens, many interacting inputs
Clean / hexagonalUI → domain ← data; dependencies point inwarduse cases and entities, free of Androidvery highlong-lived products, shared KMP domains

MVVM done properly

The view model exposes one read-only `StateFlow` of a sealed UI state, cancels a load that a newer one supersedes, and takes its scope and repository call from outside, so it runs as plain Kotlin (on Android it extends `ViewModel` and launches in `viewModelScope`); it maps only `IOException`, so any other exception still crashes it until you wrap the call with the next card's `uiStateOf`.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import java.io.IOException

sealed interface OrdersUiState {
    data object Loading : OrdersUiState
    data class Loaded(val orderIds: List<String>) : OrdersUiState
    data class Failed(val message: String) : OrdersUiState
}

class OrdersViewModel(private val scope: CoroutineScope, private val fetchIds: suspend () -> List<String>) {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow<OrdersUiState>(OrdersUiState.Loading)
    val state: StateFlow<OrdersUiState> = _state.asStateFlow()
    private var loadJob: Job? = null

    fun load() {
        loadJob?.cancel()                                        // a newer load supersedes an older one
        _state.value = OrdersUiState.Loading
        loadJob = scope.launch {
            _state.value = try {
                OrdersUiState.Loaded(fetchIds())
            } catch (e: IOException) {                           // anything else crashes: see uiStateOf
                OrdersUiState.Failed("Couldn't load orders. Check your connection.")
            }
        }
    }
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    var calls = 0
    val viewModel = OrdersViewModel(backgroundScope) {          // a fake repository call
        val call = ++calls                                       // which call this answer belongs to
        delay(if (call == 1) 500 else 100)                       // the first answer is slow
        if (call == 3) throw IOException("timeout")
        listOf("A-$call")
    }
    backgroundScope.launch { viewModel.state.collect { println(it) } }

    for (gapMs in listOf(10L, 1_000L, 1_000L)) {                 // three refreshes: 10 ms, then 1 s apart
        viewModel.load()
        advanceTimeBy(gapMs)
    }
}
Result
Loading
Loaded(orderIds=[A-2])
Loading
Failed(message=Couldn't load orders. Check your connection.)

View-model failures: map the expected, report the rest

One policy shared by every view model turns offline into the screen's own message, reports every other exception, and lets `CancellationException` through, so a superseded load is never shown or reported as a failure.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import java.io.IOException

sealed interface UiState<out T> {
    data object Loading : UiState<Nothing>
    data class Loaded<T>(val value: T) : UiState<T>
    data class Failed(val message: String) : UiState<Nothing>
}

data class FailureMessages(val offline: String, val unexpected: String = "Something went wrong. Try again.")

// The catch chain of model-errors (Kotlin Engineering Best Practices), ending in UI state.
suspend fun <T> uiStateOf(
    messages: FailureMessages,
    report: (Throwable) -> Unit,
    load: suspend () -> T,
): UiState<T> = try {
    UiState.Loaded(load())
} catch (e: CancellationException) {
    throw e
} catch (e: IOException) {
    UiState.Failed(messages.offline)
} catch (e: Exception) {
    report(e)
    UiState.Failed(messages.unexpected)
}

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val orders = FailureMessages(offline = "Couldn't load orders. Check your connection.")
    val report: (Throwable) -> Unit = { println("reported: $it") }    // on Android: the crash reporter

    println(uiStateOf(orders, report) { listOf("A-1", "A-2") })
    println(uiStateOf(orders, report) { throw IOException("timeout") })
    println(uiStateOf(orders, report) { error("malformed order JSON") })

    val screen = launch {
        val state = uiStateOf(orders, report) {
            delay(10_000)
            listOf("A-3")
        }
        println(state)
    }
    yield()
    screen.cancelAndJoin()                                     // the user left: nothing printed or reported
    println("cancelled: ${screen.isCancelled}")
}
Result
Loaded(value=[A-1, A-2])
Failed(message=Couldn't load orders. Check your connection.)
reported: java.lang.IllegalStateException: malformed order JSON
Failed(message=Something went wrong. Try again.)
cancelled: true

MVI: unidirectional flow without a library

Intents go up, one immutable state comes down, and the only code that changes state is a pure reducer — so a list of intents replays a session.

import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*

data class CartState(val items: Map<String, Int> = emptyMap(), val couponApplied: Boolean = false) {
    val count: Int get() = items.values.sum()
}

sealed interface CartIntent {
    data class Add(val sku: String) : CartIntent
    data class Remove(val sku: String) : CartIntent
    data object ApplyCoupon : CartIntent
}

fun reduce(state: CartState, intent: CartIntent): CartState = when (intent) {
    is CartIntent.Add -> state.copy(items = state.items + (intent.sku to (state.items[intent.sku] ?: 0) + 1))
    is CartIntent.Remove -> {
        val left = (state.items[intent.sku] ?: 0) - 1
        state.copy(items = if (left > 0) state.items + (intent.sku to left) else state.items - intent.sku)
    }
    CartIntent.ApplyCoupon -> state.copy(couponApplied = true)
}

class CartStore(initial: CartState = CartState()) {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(initial)
    val state: StateFlow<CartState> = _state.asStateFlow()
    fun dispatch(intent: CartIntent) = _state.update { reduce(it, intent) }   // atomic compare-and-set
}

fun main() {
    val session = listOf(CartIntent.Add("mug"), CartIntent.Add("mug"), CartIntent.Add("lamp"),
                         CartIntent.Remove("mug"), CartIntent.ApplyCoupon)
    val store = CartStore()
    session.forEach(store::dispatch)
    println(store.state.value)
    println(session.runningFold(CartState(), ::reduce).map { it.count })   // replay, no store needed
}
Result
CartState(items={mug=1, lamp=1}, couponApplied=true)
[0, 1, 2, 3, 2, 2]

The clean core: a use case and the repository it declares

The domain owns the interface and the outcomes and the data layer (or a test fake) implements it, so dependencies point inward.

import java.time.Instant

enum class OrderStatus { PLACED, SHIPPED, CANCELLED }

data class Order(val id: String, val status: OrderStatus, val cancelledAt: Instant? = null)

interface OrderRepository {                                    // declared BY the domain
    suspend fun order(id: String): Order?
    suspend fun save(order: Order)
}

sealed interface CancelResult {
    data class Cancelled(val order: Order) : CancelResult
    data class NotCancellable(val status: OrderStatus) : CancelResult
    data object NotFound : CancelResult
}

class CancelOrderUseCase(private val orders: OrderRepository, private val now: () -> Instant) {
    suspend operator fun invoke(id: String): CancelResult {
        val order = orders.order(id) ?: return CancelResult.NotFound
        if (order.status != OrderStatus.PLACED) return CancelResult.NotCancellable(order.status)
        val cancelled = order.copy(status = OrderStatus.CANCELLED, cancelledAt = now())
        orders.save(cancelled)
        return CancelResult.Cancelled(cancelled)
    }
}

class FakeOrderRepository(vararg seed: Order) : OrderRepository {   // the outer ring: data layer or test
    private val rows = seed.associateBy { it.id }.toMutableMap()
    override suspend fun order(id: String) = rows[id]
    override suspend fun save(order: Order) {
        rows[order.id] = order
    }
}

suspend fun main() {
    val repository = FakeOrderRepository(Order("A-1", OrderStatus.PLACED), Order("A-2", OrderStatus.SHIPPED))
    val cancelOrder = CancelOrderUseCase(repository, now = { Instant.parse("2026-11-16T09:30:00Z") })

    listOf("A-1", "A-2", "Z-9").forEach { println(cancelOrder(it)) }
    println(repository.order("A-1")?.status)
}
Result
Cancelled(order=Order(id=A-1, status=CANCELLED, cancelledAt=2026-11-16T09:30:00Z))
NotCancellable(status=SHIPPED)
NotFound
CANCELLED

Offline-first: the database is the single source of truth

The UI only ever observes local storage; the network only ever writes into it — so a failed refresh leaves the screen on the cached data instead of an error.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import java.io.IOException

data class Order(val id: String, val status: String)

class OrderDao {                                             // on Android: a Room DAO returning Flow
    private val rows = MutableStateFlow<List<Order>>(emptyList())

    fun observeAll(): Flow<List<Order>> = rows

    fun upsert(orders: List<Order>) = rows.update { current ->
        (current.associateBy { it.id } + orders.associateBy { it.id }).values.toList()
    }
}

fun interface OrderApi { suspend fun fetchRecent(): List<Order> }

class OfflineFirstOrderRepository(private val dao: OrderDao, private val api: OrderApi) {
    val orders: Flow<List<Order>> = dao.observeAll()         // reads: always local

    // Writes: network -> database (scheduled by WorkManager on Android).
    suspend fun refresh(): Result<Unit> = try {
        dao.upsert(api.fetchRecent())
        Result.success(Unit)
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        Result.failure(e)                                    // keep the cause: the caller decides
    }
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    val dao = OrderDao().apply { upsert(listOf(Order("A-1", "placed"))) }   // cached last session
    var online = false
    val api = OrderApi {
        if (!online) throw IOException("offline")
        listOf(Order("A-1", "shipped"), Order("A-2", "placed"))
    }
    val repository = OfflineFirstOrderRepository(dao, api)
    backgroundScope.launch { repository.orders.collect { println("screen shows $it") } }
    runCurrent()

    println("refresh: ${repository.refresh()}")
    online = true
    println("refresh: ${repository.refresh()}")
    runCurrent()
}
Result
screen shows [Order(id=A-1, status=placed)]
refresh: Failure(java.io.IOException: offline)
refresh: Success(kotlin.Unit)
screen shows [Order(id=A-1, status=shipped), Order(id=A-2, status=placed)]

Navigation as its own concern

Screens say where to go through a `Navigator`; one object owns the back stack as observable state — the shape Navigation Compose's type-safe routes and Navigation 3's back-stack list expect.

import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*

sealed interface Route {
    data object OrderList : Route
    data class OrderDetail(val orderId: String) : Route
    data object Checkout : Route
}

fun interface Navigator { fun navigate(route: Route) }   // all a view model may know

class BackStackNavigator(start: Route) : Navigator {     // the single owner of the back stack
    private val _backStack = MutableStateFlow(listOf(start))
    val backStack: StateFlow<List<Route>> = _backStack.asStateFlow()

    override fun navigate(route: Route) = _backStack.update { it + route }

    fun back(): Boolean {                                  // called by the system back handler
        if (_backStack.value.size == 1) return false       // let the system close the app
        _backStack.update { it.dropLast(1) }
        return true
    }
}

class OrderListViewModel(private val navigator: Navigator) {   // decides WHERE, not HOW
    fun onOrderTapped(orderId: String) = navigator.navigate(Route.OrderDetail(orderId))
}

fun main() {
    val navigator = BackStackNavigator(Route.OrderList)
    OrderListViewModel(navigator).onOrderTapped("A-1")
    navigator.navigate(Route.Checkout)
    println(navigator.backStack.value)
    println("${navigator.back()} ${navigator.back()} ${navigator.back()} ${navigator.backStack.value}")

    val recorded = mutableListOf<Route>()
    OrderListViewModel { recorded.add(it) }.onOrderTapped("A-2")   // a test fake is one lambda
    println(recorded)
}
Result
[OrderList, OrderDetail(orderId=A-1), Checkout]
true true false [OrderList]
[OrderDetail(orderId=A-2)]

Dependency injection by hand: a composition root

A container built once (in `Application.onCreate`) holds app-wide instances and factories for per-screen ones; everything else just takes constructor parameters.

fun interface OrderApi { fun fetch(id: String): String }

class RemoteOrderApi(private val baseUrl: String) : OrderApi {
    override fun fetch(id: String) = "GET $baseUrl/orders/$id"   // stands in for an HTTP call
}

class OrderRepository(private val api: OrderApi) {
    fun order(id: String) = api.fetch(id)
}

class OrderDetailViewModel(private val orderId: String, private val repository: OrderRepository) {
    fun load() = repository.order(orderId)
}

// The composition root: the only class that knows concrete types and lifetimes.
class AppContainer(baseUrl: String) {
    private val api: OrderApi = RemoteOrderApi(baseUrl)
    val orderRepository: OrderRepository by lazy { OrderRepository(api) }      // one per app

    fun orderDetailViewModel(orderId: String) =                                // one per screen
        OrderDetailViewModel(orderId, orderRepository)
}

// On Android, ShopApp : Application() holds `val container by lazy { AppContainer(BuildConfig.API_URL) }`;
// BuildConfig holds only non-secret configuration such as a base URL.
fun main() {
    val container = AppContainer(baseUrl = "https://api.example.com")
    println(container.orderDetailViewModel("A-1").load())
    println(container.orderDetailViewModel("A-2").load())
    println(container.orderRepository === container.orderRepository)

    val fakeApi = OrderApi { id -> "fake $id" }                       // a test builds its own graph
    val underTest = OrderDetailViewModel("A-1", OrderRepository(api = fakeApi))
    println(underTest.load())
}
Result
GET https://api.example.com/orders/A-1
GET https://api.example.com/orders/A-2
true
fake A-1

DI by hand, Hilt or Koin

The classes stay the same — constructor parameters — whichever wires them; only the composition root changes.

ApproachHow the graph is declaredWhen errors show upBest for
By handan AppContainer class: constructors, by lazy for singletons, factory functions per screencompile time — it is ordinary codesmall and medium apps, libraries, Kotlin Multiplatform
Hilt@Inject constructor, @Module + @InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class) with @Binds/@Provides, @HiltViewModel, @AndroidEntryPointcompile time: Dagger validates the graph (KSP)Android apps — Google's recommended library; Hilt 2.59 or later with AGP 9, 2.57.x with AGP 8
Koina Kotlin DSL: module { single<OrderApi> { RemoteOrderApi(getProperty("API_URL")) }; viewModelOf(::OrdersViewModel) }at run time, unless a test covers the graph with verify() (JVM) or androidVerify(), or Koin's compiler plugin checks itfast setup, Kotlin Multiplatform, teams avoiding annotation processing
Dagger 2hand-written @Component interfaces and modulescompile timeJVM servers and existing Dagger codebases

The same graph with Hilt, ending in Compose

Bind each interface once in a module and provide what you do not own, so the view model gets its repository by constructor and the screen collects state with the lifecycle.

@HiltAndroidApp
class ShopApp : Application()

@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
abstract class DataModule {
    @Binds @Singleton
    abstract fun bindOrderRepository(impl: OfflineFirstOrderRepository): OrderRepository

    @Binds abstract fun bindOrderApi(impl: HttpOrderApi): OrderApi    // HttpOrderApi: an @Inject constructor
}

@Module
@InstallIn(SingletonComponent::class)
object DatabaseModule {
    @Provides @Singleton
    fun provideOrderDao(@ApplicationContext context: Context): OrderDao =
        Room.databaseBuilder(context, ShopDatabase::class.java, "shop.db").build().orderDao()
}

class OfflineFirstOrderRepository @Inject constructor(
    private val dao: OrderDao,
    private val api: OrderApi,
) : OrderRepository {
    override val orders: Flow<List<Order>> = dao.observeAll()     // refresh() as in the offline-first card
}

@HiltViewModel
class OrdersViewModel @Inject constructor(repository: OrderRepository) : ViewModel() {
    val state: StateFlow<OrdersUiState> = repository.orders
        .map<List<Order>, OrdersUiState> { orders -> OrdersUiState.Loaded(orders.map { it.id }) }
        .stateIn(viewModelScope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), OrdersUiState.Loading)
}

@AndroidEntryPoint
class MainActivity : ComponentActivity() {
    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        setContent { OrdersRoute() }
    }
}

@Composable
fun OrdersRoute(viewModel: OrdersViewModel = hiltViewModel()) {
    val state by viewModel.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    OrdersScreen(state)                                // a stateless composable: state in, events out
}
Result

Hilt builds the graph at compile time; the orders screen gets a view model scoped to its navigation destination (or, without navigation, to the activity) that survives rotation, and stops collecting five seconds after it leaves the screen.

How to answer "which architecture would you use?"

Constraints first, invariants second, acronym last.

  • Start with the constraints: team size, app lifetime, offline needs, how much state is shared across screens, Compose or Views, KMP or not.
  • Name the invariants: one source of truth per piece of data, state down and events up, no logic in composables, a domain that compiles without Android, navigation owned in one place.
  • Then pick the lightest shape that gives them — usually Google's layering with MVVM (UI state holders → optional use cases → repositories), MVI for screens with many interacting inputs.
  • Mention the seams that matter more than the name: constructor injection, a sealed UI state, repositories that expose Flow, and a fake for every interface.
  • Say what you would not do: a use case that only forwards one repository call, a module per layer on a five-screen app, or a framework for MVI before a reducer function has hurt.
  • Avoid an acronym with no trade-off — and avoid a ViewModel that holds a Context, a View or a NavController: it outlives them.

Kotlin Engineering Best Practices

The habits that make Kotlin on Android and the JVM survive a second year and a second engineer — conventions, errors, null safety, logging, configuration, coroutines, performance and hygiene, with the runnable parts run.

  • jvm
  • android
  • kotlin >=2.0
  • jvm >=17
  • Kotlin/JVM (the standard library and kotlinx.coroutines); the same code runs on Android

Sources: Coding conventions — Kotlin docs · Null safety — Kotlin docs · Best practices for coroutines in Android — Android Developers · App performance guide — Android Developers

The ten that matter most

If you say nothing else in a review, say these.

  • Make illegal states unrepresentable. A sealed interface beats three Booleans and a nullable error.
  • val, read-only types and data classes by default. A var or a MutableList in a public signature is a decision to justify.
  • Inject dependencies through the constructor — the clock, the dispatchers, the network, the database. Nothing reaches for a singleton.
  • Keep the public surface small. internal for module details, explicit API mode in libraries; public is a promise.
  • Errors are designed. Sealed results for expected failures, exceptions for bugs, and never swallow CancellationException.
  • No !!. Give every Java value a declared nullability at the boundary, and handle absence where it is meaningful.
  • One source of truth per piece of state, exposed as a read-only StateFlow by exactly one owner.
  • Structured concurrency. Every coroutine belongs to a scope with a lifecycle; no GlobalScope, no fire-and-forget.
  • Tests are part of the change. If it is hard to test, the design is telling you something.
  • Measure before optimising — Macrobenchmark, Baseline Profiles and a system trace on the lowest-end device you support.

Conventions that matter in review, documented with KDoc

Properties instead of getters, top-level functions instead of `Utils` objects, read-only exposure of mutable state, string templates — and KDoc on what the caller must know.

Java in Kotlin syntax
import java.util.ArrayList
import java.util.Locale

class OrderUtils {
    companion object {
        fun formatPrice(cents: Long): String =
            "EUR " + (cents / 100) + "." + String.format(Locale.ROOT, "%02d", cents % 100)
    }
}

class Order(id: String) {
    private var mId: String = id
    private var mLines: ArrayList<Long> = ArrayList()

    fun getId(): String { return mId }
    fun getLines(): ArrayList<Long> { return mLines }        // callers can mutate it
    fun getTotal(): Long {
        var total = 0L
        for (i in 0 until mLines.size) total = total + mLines.get(i)
        return total
    }
}

fun main() {
    val order = Order("A-1")
    order.getLines().add(1200)
    order.getLines().add(350)
    println(order.getId() + ": " + OrderUtils.formatPrice(order.getTotal()))
}
Idiomatic Kotlin
import java.util.Locale

/**
 * An order being built at the till.
 *
 * Lines are added only through [addLine], so [totalCents] is always consistent.
 */
class Order(val id: String) {
    private val lines = mutableListOf<Long>()

    /** A snapshot of the line prices in cents: callers cannot reach the backing list. */
    val lineCents: List<Long> get() = lines.toList()

    val totalCents: Long get() = lines.sum()

    /** @throws IllegalArgumentException if [priceCents] is not positive. */
    fun addLine(priceCents: Long) {
        require(priceCents > 0) { "price must be positive, was $priceCents" }
        lines += priceCents
    }
}

/**
 * Formats [cents] for receipts.
 *
 * @return the amount with its currency, for example `EUR 15.50`.
 */
fun formatPrice(cents: Long): String = "EUR %d.%02d".format(Locale.ROOT, cents / 100, cents % 100)

/** The old `Int` API: callers get a warning, and the IDE offers the replacement as a quick-fix. */
@Deprecated("Prices are Long cents", ReplaceWith("formatPrice(cents.toLong())"))
fun formatPrice(cents: Int): String = formatPrice(cents.toLong())

fun main() {
    val order = Order("A-1").apply {
        addLine(1200)
        addLine(350)
    }
    println("${order.id}: ${formatPrice(order.totalCents)}")
}
Result
A-1: EUR 15.50

Model errors at the boundary, and never swallow cancellation

Translate expected exceptions into a sealed domain error in one place, keep and report the unexpected ones whole, and rethrow `CancellationException` before any broad `catch` or a cancelled coroutine keeps running.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import java.io.IOException

sealed interface SyncError {
    data object Offline : SyncError
    data class Unexpected(val cause: Throwable) : SyncError         // the exception itself: stack and cause
}

sealed interface SyncResult {
    data class Synced(val count: Int) : SyncResult
    data class Failed(val error: SyncError) : SyncResult
}

// report: the crash reporter in production, e.g. Firebase.crashlytics.recordException(e).
// The same chain ending in UI state: view-model-error-policy in the Architectural Approaches sheet.
class OrderSync(private val report: (Throwable) -> Unit) {
    suspend fun sync(fetch: suspend () -> List<String>): SyncResult = try {
        SyncResult.Synced(fetch().size)
    } catch (e: CancellationException) {
        throw e                                                       // cancellation is not an error
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        SyncResult.Failed(SyncError.Offline)                          // expected: nothing to report
    } catch (e: Exception) {
        report(e)                                                     // unexpected: someone must see it
        SyncResult.Failed(SyncError.Unexpected(e))
    }
}

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val orderSync = OrderSync(report = { println("reported: $it") })

    println(orderSync.sync { listOf("A-1", "A-2") })
    println(orderSync.sync { throw IOException("no route to host") })
    println(orderSync.sync { error("malformed order JSON") })

    val screen = launch {
        orderSync.sync {
            delay(10_000)
            emptyList()
        }
        println("still running after cancel")                   // printed if cancellation were swallowed
    }
    yield()
    screen.cancelAndJoin()
    println("cancelled cleanly: ${screen.isCancelled}")
}
Result
Synced(count=2)
Failed(error=Offline)
reported: java.lang.IllegalStateException: malformed order JSON
Failed(error=Unexpected(cause=java.lang.IllegalStateException: malformed order JSON))
cancelled cleanly: true

Null-safety discipline: no `!!`, no unchecked platform types

A Java method returns a platform type (`String!`) the compiler will not check; give it a nullability the moment it enters Kotlin, and turn absence into a branch instead of a crash.

Crashes later
import java.util.Properties

class Session { var userId: String? = null }

fun greeting(session: Session, settings: Properties): String {
    val name = settings.getProperty("display.name")       // String! from Java: unchecked
    val shortName = name.trim()                            // NPE when the key is missing
    return "Hi " + shortName + " (" + session.userId!!.uppercase() + ")"   // NPE when signed out
}

fun main() {
    val settings = Properties().apply { setProperty("display.name", " Ada ") }
    val session = Session().apply { userId = "u-42" }
    println(greeting(session, settings))
}
Handled at the boundary
import java.util.Properties

class Session { var userId: String? = null }

fun greeting(session: Session, settings: Properties): String {
    val name: String = settings.getProperty("display.name")?.trim() ?: "there"   // declared, defaulted
    val userId = session.userId ?: return "Hi $name (signed out)"          // a local val: smart-castable
    return "Hi $name (${userId.uppercase()})"
}

fun main() {
    val settings = Properties().apply { setProperty("display.name", " Ada ") }
    val session = Session().apply { userId = "u-42" }
    println(greeting(session, settings))
}
Result
Hi Ada (U-42)

Logging: structured events, lazy messages, redacted by type

Log an event name with key–value fields and the `Throwable` itself, build expensive messages only when the level is on, and let PII types redact themselves (on Android behind `Log` or Timber, on the JVM behind SLF4J).

enum class Level { DEBUG, INFO, WARN, ERROR }

class Logger(
    private val tag: String,
    private val minLevel: Level,
    private val sink: (line: String, error: Throwable?) -> Unit,     // in production: Log.e(tag, line, error)
) {
    fun log(level: Level, event: String, vararg fields: Pair<String, Any?>, error: Throwable? = null) {
        if (level < minLevel) return
        val rendered = fields.joinToString(" ") { (key, value) -> "$key=$value" }
        sink("${level.name} [$tag] $event $rendered", error)         // the Throwable itself, with its stack
    }

    fun debug(event: String, details: () -> String) {               // the lambda runs only if DEBUG is on
        if (Level.DEBUG >= minLevel) sink("DEBUG [$tag] $event ${details()}", null)
    }
}

@JvmInline
value class Email(val value: String) {
    override fun toString() = value.take(2) + "***@" + value.substringAfter('@')   // logs never see it whole
}

fun main() {
    // Only this demo sink shortens the Throwable to one line, so the output is reproducible.
    val printSink = { line: String, error: Throwable? ->
        println(line + (error?.let { " error=$it cause=${it.cause}" } ?: ""))
    }
    val log = Logger("sync", minLevel = Level.INFO, sink = printSink)   // release builds: INFO and up
    var expensiveDumps = 0

    log.log(Level.INFO, "sync_started", "user" to Email("ada@example.com"), "orders" to 3)
    log.debug("payload") {
        expensiveDumps++
        "a 2 MB JSON dump"
    }
    val failure = IllegalStateException("sync failed", java.io.IOException("timeout"))
    log.log(Level.ERROR, "sync_failed", "attempt" to 2, error = failure)
    println("debug messages built: $expensiveDumps")
}
Result
INFO [sync] sync_started user=ad***@example.com orders=3
ERROR [sync] sync_failed attempt=2 error=java.lang.IllegalStateException: sync failed cause=java.io.IOException: timeout
debug messages built: 0

Configuration, secrets and feature flags

Parse configuration once at startup and fail with every problem at once; wrap secrets so they never print; give each flag a default, an owner and a removal date.

@JvmInline
value class Secret(val value: String) {
    override fun toString() = "Secret(****)"
}

data class AppConfig(val apiBaseUrl: String, val apiKey: Secret, val requestTimeoutMs: Long)

// env: System.getenv() on a server. On Android, BuildConfig holds only non-secret configuration
// (a base URL, public ids): a server secret never ships inside an APK.
fun loadConfig(env: Map<String, String>): AppConfig {
    val problems = mutableListOf<String>()
    fun required(key: String): String {
        val value = env[key]
        if (value.isNullOrBlank()) problems += "$key is missing"
        return value.orEmpty()
    }
    val baseUrl = required("API_BASE_URL")
    val apiKey = required("API_KEY")
    if (baseUrl.isNotEmpty() && !baseUrl.startsWith("https://")) problems += "API_BASE_URL must use https"
    val rawTimeout = env["REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS"]
    val timeoutMs = rawTimeout?.toLongOrNull()
    if (rawTimeout != null && timeoutMs == null) problems += "REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS is not a number"
    check(problems.isEmpty()) { "invalid configuration: ${problems.joinToString("; ")}" }
    return AppConfig(baseUrl, Secret(apiKey), timeoutMs ?: 10_000)
}

enum class Flag(val default: Boolean, val owner: String, val removeBy: String) {
    NEW_CHECKOUT(default = false, owner = "payments", removeBy = "2027-01"),
    OFFLINE_CART(default = true, owner = "orders", removeBy = "2026-12"),
}

class FeatureFlags(private val remote: Map<Flag, Boolean>) {          // remote config, cached on disk
    fun isEnabled(flag: Flag): Boolean = remote[flag] ?: flag.default
}

fun main() {
    println(loadConfig(mapOf("API_BASE_URL" to "https://api.example.com", "API_KEY" to "test-key-123")))

    val broken = mapOf("API_BASE_URL" to "http://api.example.com", "REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS" to "abc")
    println(runCatching { loadConfig(broken) }.exceptionOrNull()?.message)

    val flags = FeatureFlags(remote = mapOf(Flag.NEW_CHECKOUT to true))
    println(Flag.entries.map { "${it.name}=${flags.isEnabled(it)}" })
}
Result
AppConfig(apiBaseUrl=https://api.example.com, apiKey=Secret(****), requestTimeoutMs=10000)
invalid configuration: API_KEY is missing; API_BASE_URL must use https; REQUEST_TIMEOUT_MS is not a number
[NEW_CHECKOUT=true, OFFLINE_CART=true]
Setup

Coroutines: injected dispatchers, main-safe functions, structured work

A suspend function moves its own blocking work with an injected dispatcher, so any caller (the main thread included) can call it, and parallel children inside `withContext` — or `coroutineScope` when no switch is needed — cancel each other on failure.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*

class ReceiptRepository(
    private val io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO,             // injected: a test passes its own
    private val corrupted: Set<String> = emptySet(),
) {
    // Main-safe and structured: withContext waits for every child, and one failure cancels the rest.
    suspend fun loadReceipts(ids: List<String>): List<String> = withContext(io) {
        ids.map { id -> async { readReceipt(id) } }.awaitAll()
    }

    private suspend fun readReceipt(id: String): String {
        delay(if (id in corrupted) 50 else 100)                       // stands in for a disk or database read
        check(id !in corrupted) { "receipt $id is corrupt" }
        return "receipt $id"
    }
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    val io = StandardTestDispatcher(testScheduler)                    // virtual time, no real threads
    val repository = ReceiptRepository(io, corrupted = setOf("A-9"))

    println(repository.loadReceipts(listOf("A-1", "A-2", "A-3")))
    println("after $currentTime ms of virtual time: the three reads ran in parallel")

    try {
        repository.loadReceipts(listOf("A-1", "A-9"))
    } catch (e: IllegalStateException) {
        println("${e.message} at $currentTime ms: A-1 was cancelled, not awaited")
    }
}
Result
[receipt A-1, receipt A-2, receipt A-3]
after 100 ms of virtual time: the three reads ran in parallel
receipt A-9 is corrupt at 150 ms: A-1 was cancelled, not awaited

Performance checklist

In rough order of how often each one is the actual culprit.

SymptomLook atFix
Janky scrollinga system trace (Perfetto), recomposition counts in the Layout Inspectorstable keys in lazy lists, immutable UI state, work moved off the main thread
Allocation in hot pathsthe memory profiler's allocation trackingprimitive arrays (IntArray) over List<Int> boxing, reused buffers, buildString, no lambdas allocated per frame
Long collection chainsa microbenchmarkasSequence() for large inputs or early exit; plain lists for small ones
Higher-order helpers in loopsthe bytecode (Show Kotlin Bytecode)inline small functions that take lambdas — the standard library's already are
Slow cold startMacrobenchmark StartupTimingMetricBaseline Profiles, lazy initialization, no disk or network in Application.onCreate
Large or slow release buildthe APK AnalyzerR8 with isMinifyEnabled = true and minimal keep rules; shrink resources
I/O on the main threadStrictMode in debug buildswithContext(ioDispatcher) inside the repository, with Dispatchers.IO injected — not at every call site
Memory growthLeakCanary, heap dumpsno Activity, View or Context held by a ViewModel or singleton; bounded caches
Regressions after a changebenchmarks in CIa Macrobenchmark or Microbenchmark that fails when the number moves

Project hygiene

What a healthy Kotlin repository has, so reviews can be about design.

AreaPractice
Formattingktlint or ktfmt, applied by a Gradle task and a pre-commit hook — never argued about in review
Static analysisdetekt with a committed configuration, and a baseline file for legacy findings only
Android Lintlint { warningsAsErrors = true } on CI, with a baseline for what predates the rule
Compiler warningskotlin { compilerOptions { allWarningsAsErrors.set(true) } } — a warning nobody fixes is one everybody ignores
Public APIkotlin { explicitApi() } in library modules, and a binary-compatibility check for published ones
Dependenciesa version catalog, Renovate or Dependabot pull requests, and Gradle dependency verification for the supply chain
Testsunit tests on every pull request (./gradlew test); instrumented and screenshot tests on merge or nightly
CIbuild, lint, detekt and tests on every pull request, with the build cache and configuration cache on; aim for under ten minutes
ReleasesR8 on, the mapping file uploaded for crash deobfuscation, versionCode from CI, a tag per release
OwnershipCODEOWNERS per module so reviews route themselves

A five-minute review checklist — accessibility, localization and privacy included

Cheap if checked as you go; expensive as a retrofit.

  • Correctness — what happens on empty, null, error, cancellation, process death (SavedStateHandle) and a slow network?
  • Concurrency — which scope owns this coroutine, which dispatcher runs it, and is the function main-safe?
  • Surface and naming — does this need to be public? Can I tell what it does from the call site alone?
  • Tests — is there one test that fails if the core behaviour regresses, using fakes and virtual time?
  • Accessibility — a contentDescription (or null for decoration) on every icon, touch targets of at least 48 dp, text in sp that survives 200% font scale, rows merged with Modifier.semantics(mergeDescendants = true) {}, and one pass with TalkBack — see Accessibility on Android.
  • Localization — every user-visible string in resources with placeholders and plurals (pluralStringResource), no sentences built by concatenation, numbers and dates formatted for the user's locale, and a run under the en-XA and ar-XB pseudolocales for truncation and RTL — see Localization & Internationalization.
  • Privacy — no PII or tokens in logs or crash reports, permissions asked in context, tokens in Keystore-backed storage, no secrets in BuildConfig, and the Play data-safety form still true — see Security, Authentication & Privacy.
  • Size — is the diff reviewable? Under about 400 lines gets a real review; over that gets a rubber stamp.
  • Review the design before the syntax; formatting and style are the linters' job.

Swift idea → Kotlin

Close cousins, with a different default for classes (final) and for equality (`==` calls `equals`).

SwiftKotlinWatch out
Optional<T>, ?., ??, guard letT?, ?., ?:, ?: return!! is the force unwrap; Java types arrive as platform types (T!)
enum with associated valuessealed interface + data class caseswhen is exhaustive over a sealed type
structdata class (with vals)a reference type: copy() instead of value semantics
protocol + extensioninterface + extension functionsextensions are resolved statically
generics where<T : Bound>, where T : A, T : Bdeclaration-site variance: out / in
throwsunchecked exceptionsnothing in the signature says a function throws
defertry { } finally { }, use { }use closes a Closeable

Null safety

Nullability is part of the type. `?.` short-circuits, `?:` supplies a default — or returns early.

data class Address(val city: String?)
data class User(val name: String, val address: Address?)

fun cityOf(user: User): String {
    val city = user.address?.city ?: return "no city for ${user.name}"   // like guard let … else
    return city.uppercase()                                              // smart cast: String here
}

fun main() {
    val user = User("Ana", address = null)
    println(user.address?.city ?: "unknown city")
    println(cityOf(user))
    println(cityOf(User("Bo", Address("lima"))))
}
Result
unknown city
no city for Ana
LIMA

Sealed hierarchies and when

A new case breaks compilation at every `when` that does not handle it.

sealed interface Shape
data class Circle(val radius: Double) : Shape
data class Rect(val width: Double, val height: Double) : Shape

fun area(s: Shape): Double = when (s) {
    is Circle -> Math.PI * s.radius * s.radius
    is Rect -> s.width * s.height               // smart cast: s is a Rect here
}

fun main() {
    println(area(Rect(2.0, 3.0)))
    println(Math.round(area(Circle(1.0)) * 100) / 100.0)
}
Result
6.0
3.14

Generics, bounds and variance

`out T` marks a producer, so a `Source<Int>` is a `Source<Number>` — Swift has no user-declared variance.

fun <T : Comparable<T>> clamp(value: T, low: T, high: T): T = maxOf(low, minOf(value, high))

interface Source<out T> { fun next(): T }

fun sumAll(sources: List<Source<Number>>): Double = sources.sumOf { it.next().toDouble() }

fun main() {
    println("${clamp(15, 0, 10)} ${clamp("m", "a", "f")}")
    val ints = object : Source<Int> { override fun next() = 2 }
    val doubles = object : Source<Double> { override fun next() = 0.5 }
    println(sumAll(listOf(ints, doubles)))
}
Result
10 f
2.5

Exceptions, require and runCatching

`throw` is an expression; `require` throws `IllegalArgumentException`; `runCatching` turns a throw into a `Result`.

class InvalidPort(text: String) : Exception("not a port: $text")

fun parsePort(text: String): Int {
    val n = text.toIntOrNull() ?: throw InvalidPort(text)
    require(n in 1..65535) { "out of range: $n" }
    return n
}

fun main() {
    for (input in listOf("8080", "http", "70000")) {
        val result = runCatching { parsePort(input) }
        println(result.fold({ "port $it" }, { "${it::class.simpleName}: ${it.message}" }))
    }
}
Result
port 8080
InvalidPort: not a port: http
IllegalArgumentException: out of range: 70000

Data classes and copies

`==` compares values, `===` identity; `copy()` is shallow, like a struct copy of a reference field.

data class Settings(val theme: String, val tags: List<String>)

fun main() {
    val a = Settings("dark", listOf("x"))
    val b = a.copy(theme = "light")
    println("$a $b")
    println("${a == a.copy()} ${a === a.copy()} ${a.tags === b.tags}")
}
Result
Settings(theme=dark, tags=[x]) Settings(theme=light, tags=[x])
true false true

Extensions and scope functions

`apply` configures and returns the receiver; `let` transforms and returns the lambda's result.

fun String.initials(): String =
    split(" ").filter { it.isNotEmpty() }.joinToString("") { it.first().uppercase() }

data class Request(var url: String = "", var retries: Int = 0)

fun main() {
    println("ada lovelace".initials())
    val request = Request().apply { url = "https://example.com"; retries = 3 }
    println(request.let { "${it.url} x${it.retries}" })
}

Combine → Flow

The same reactive vocabulary, built on suspension instead of demand.

CombineFlowNote
PublisherFlow<T> (cold)the block runs again for every collector
CurrentValueSubjectMutableStateFlowalways has a value; equal values are not re-emitted
PassthroughSubjectMutableSharedFlowno value; replay and buffers are configurable
sink + AnyCancellablecollect / launchIn(scope)the scope's end cancels the collection
switchToLatestflatMapLatestcancels the previous inner flow
zip / combineLatestzip / combine—
receive(on:)flowOn(dispatcher)changes the upstream context, not the collector's
share()shareIn / stateInturns a cold flow hot, with an explicit start policy

Cold flows

A `flow { }` does nothing until collected, and runs again for each collector.

import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking

fun numbers(): Flow<Int> = flow {
    println("start")
    for (i in 1..3) emit(i)
}

fun main() = runBlocking {
    numbers().map { it * 10 }.collect { println(it) }
    println(numbers().toList())
}
Result
start
10
20
30
start
[1, 2, 3]

StateFlow and SharedFlow

`StateFlow` holds the latest value and skips equal ones; `SharedFlow` broadcasts events.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val count = MutableStateFlow(0)
    val events = MutableSharedFlow<String>()

    val watcher = launch { count.collect { println("count = $it") } }
    val listener = launch { events.collect { println("event: $it") } }
    yield()                                    // let both collectors subscribe
    count.value = 1
    yield()
    count.value = 1                            // equal: not re-emitted
    events.emit("saved")
    yield()
    watcher.cancel()
    listener.cancel()
}
Result
count = 0
count = 1
event: saved

Operators that matter

`flatMapLatest` cancels stale work — the search-as-you-type operator.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runBlocking {
    flowOf("a", "ab", "abc")
        .onEach { delay(50) }                  // a keystroke every 50 ms
        .flatMapLatest { q -> flow { delay(500); emit("results for $q") } }   // a slow search
        .collect { println(it) }

    println(flowOf("ana", "bo").zip(flowOf(31, 27, 99)) { n, a -> "$n:$a" }.toList())
    println(flowOf(1, 1, 2, 2, 3).distinctUntilChanged().scan(0) { acc, x -> acc + x }.toList())
}
Result
results for abc
[ana:31, bo:27]
[0, 1, 3, 6]

Lifetime belongs to a scope

`launchIn(scope)` ties the collection to the scope; cancelling the scope ends it (the role of `AnyCancellable`).

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*

fun ticker(periodMs: Long): Flow<Int> = flow {
    var n = 0
    while (true) {
        emit(n++)
        delay(periodMs)
    }
}

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val screen = CoroutineScope(coroutineContext + Job())   // stand-in for viewModelScope
    val thirdTick = CompletableDeferred<Unit>()
    ticker(100).onEach { println("tick $it"); if (it == 2) thirdTick.complete(Unit) }.launchIn(screen)
    thirdTick.await()                                        // e.g. the screen goes away after three ticks
    screen.cancel()
    delay(200)
    println("after cancel: quiet")
}
Result
tick 0
tick 1
tick 2
after cancel: quiet

Bridging a listener API

`callbackFlow` registers on collect and unregisters in `awaitClose` when the collector stops.

import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.awaitClose
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.runBlocking

fun interface Listener { fun onReading(value: Int) }

class Sensor {                                 // a listener API you do not own
    fun register(listener: Listener) {
        Thread { for (v in listOf(10, 20, 30, 40)) listener.onReading(v) }.start()
    }
    fun unregister() = println("unregistered")
}

fun Sensor.readings(): Flow<Int> = callbackFlow {
    register { value -> trySend(value) }
    awaitClose { unregister() }
}

fun main() = runBlocking {
    println(Sensor().readings().take(3).toList())
}
Result
unregistered
[10, 20, 30]

Gotchas

The ones that cost a day.

  • collect suspends until the flow completes — a StateFlow never does, so the next line never runs.
  • Updating a StateFlow with a mutated list: equal by equals, so nothing is emitted. Emit a new list.
  • stateIn(scope, SharingStarted.WhileSubscribed(5_000), initial) for UI state: stops upstream work when nobody watches.
  • flowOn(Dispatchers.IO) for blocking upstream work; the collector keeps its own context.
  • catch { } handles upstream exceptions only — a throw in collect { } is not caught by it.

Flow Timing Operators — debounce, sample, timeout

debounce, sample, throttle by hand, delay, timeout, batching, drift-free tickers and backpressure — what each drops, proved under virtual time.

debounce — search as you type

`debounce` waits for silence, `distinctUntilChanged` skips a query that settles where it was, and `mapLatest` cancels a stale request and catches its failure inside, since a `catch` after it ends the stream.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import java.io.IOException

var calls = 0
suspend fun searchTracks(query: String): List<String> {
    delay(200)                                                 // the catalogue API...
    if (++calls == 1) throw IOException("503")                 // ...fails the first time
    return listOf("Beat It", "Beautiful Day", "Bean Bag").filter { it.startsWith(query, ignoreCase = true) }
}

@OptIn(FlowPreview::class, ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    // (pause before each keystroke in ms, the text): "bea", a pause, "beat" and back to "bea", "beau".
    // The box then closes: on completion debounce emits the last value at once, without waiting.
    val typing = listOf(0L to "b", 80L to "be", 80L to "bea", 500L to "beat", 120L to "bea", 600L to "beau")
    val queries = flow {
        for ((pause, text) in typing) {
            delay(pause)
            emit(text)
        }
    }

    queries
        .debounce(300)                                         // 300 ms of silence: they stopped typing
        .distinctUntilChanged()                                // "bea" -> "beat" -> "bea": same query, skip
        .onEach { println("${currentTime} ms: search '$it'") }
        .mapLatest { q ->                                      // a newer query cancels the running request
            try {                                              // caught INSIDE; a catch after it ends it all
                "results ${searchTracks(q)}"
            } catch (e: IOException) {
                "search failed (${e.message}): show Retry"
            }
        }
        .collect { println("${currentTime} ms: $it") }
}
Result
460 ms: search 'bea'
660 ms: search failed (503): show Retry
1380 ms: search 'beau'
1580 ms: results [Beautiful Day]

sample — one value per period from a fast source

Reach for `sample` when a source is faster than anyone can read (positions, sensors, download progress); it never waits for silence as `debounce` does.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import java.util.Locale

fun playbackPositionMs(): Flow<Long> = flow {                // the player reports about every frame
    var position = 0L
    while (true) {
        emit(position)
        delay(17)
        position += 17
    }
}

fun label(ms: Long) = "%d:%02d.%03d".format(Locale.ROOT, ms / 60_000, ms / 1_000 % 60, ms % 1_000)

@OptIn(FlowPreview::class, ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    var reported = 0
    playbackPositionMs()
        .onEach { reported++ }
        .sample(1_000)                                       // the label needs one value a second, not sixty
        .map(::label)
        .take(3)
        .collect { println("${currentTime} ms: label shows $it") }
    println("$reported positions reported, 3 rendered")
}

throttleFirst — written by hand

Flow ships no throttle operator, so this one takes the leading edge (buttons) and stamps each value on arrival, even while the handler is still busy.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import kotlin.time.*
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds

// First value, then nothing until the window has passed (Rx throttleFirst). Time is injected.
// channelFlow collects upstream in its own coroutine, so taps are stamped when they ARRIVE,
// even while the collector is still busy with the previous one.
fun <T> Flow<T>.throttleFirst(window: Duration, time: TimeSource = TimeSource.Monotonic) = channelFlow {
    var windowEnd: TimeMark? = null
    collect { value ->
        val end = windowEnd
        if (end == null || end.hasPassedNow()) {              // no window yet, or it is over
            windowEnd = time.markNow() + window
            send(value)
        }
    }
}

fun timed(vararg events: Pair<Long, String>) = flow {
    for ((pause, event) in events) {
        delay(pause)
        emit(event)
    }
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {                              // a double-tap must skip one track, not two
    timed(0L to "tap 1", 120L to "tap 2", 600L to "tap 3")
        .buffer()                                              // taps queue up, as with callbackFlow
        .throttleFirst(500.milliseconds, testTimeSource)       // Monotonic in the app, virtual time here
        .collect {
            println("${currentTime} ms: skip ($it)")
            delay(600)                                         // a 600 ms skip: tap 2 arrives meanwhile
        }
}

throttleLatest — written by hand

`conflate` plus a `delay` after each emit gives the first value at once and then the newest one per window, the shape a seek-bar drag needs.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import kotlin.time.Duration
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds

// First value at once, then the LATEST one per window: conflate keeps only the newest while we wait.
// (It also holds completion back by one window.)
fun <T> Flow<T>.throttleLatest(window: Duration): Flow<T> = conflate().transform {
    emit(it)
    delay(window)
}

fun timed(vararg events: Pair<Long, String>) = flow {
    for ((pause, event) in events) {
        delay(pause)
        emit(event)
    }
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {                                  // one seek per 200 ms at most, the newest
    timed(0L to "0:10", 50L to "0:12", 50L to "0:15", 50L to "0:19", 300L to "0:30")
        .throttleLatest(200.milliseconds)
        .collect { println("${currentTime} ms: seek to $it") }
}

Pacing with delay, timeout and withTimeoutOrNull

`transform { emit; delay }` paces a stream, `timeout` fails it when the gap between values grows too long, and `withTimeoutOrNull` bounds a single wait.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds

fun audioChunks(gapsMs: List<Long>): Flow<Int> = flow {           // chunks from the stream, with gaps
    gapsMs.forEachIndexed { i, gap ->
        delay(gap)
        emit(i)
    }
    awaitCancellation()                                          // a live stream never completes
}

@OptIn(FlowPreview::class, ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    // Pacing "Up next" banners: show each at once, then hold it 2 s (onEach { delay } would wait BEFORE each)
    flowOf("Up next: Beat It", "Up next: Beautiful Day")
        .transform {
            emit(it)
            delay(2_000)
        }
        .collect { println("${currentTime} ms: $it") }

    // timeout: no chunk for 5 s means the stream stalled; the flow fails, catch turns it into a value
    val start = currentTime
    audioChunks(listOf(100, 200, 6_000))
        .map { "chunk $it" }
        .timeout(5.seconds)
        .catch { e -> if (e is TimeoutCancellationException) emit("stalled: show Retry") else throw e }
        .collect { println("+${currentTime - start} ms: $it") }

    // withTimeoutOrNull: the first value, or give up
    val ready = withTimeoutOrNull(2.seconds) { audioChunks(listOf(3_000)).first() }
    println("player ready within 2 s? ${ready != null}")
}
Result
0 ms: Up next: Beat It
2000 ms: Up next: Beautiful Day
+100 ms: chunk 0
+300 ms: chunk 1
+5300 ms: stalled: show Retry
player ready within 2 s? false

Batching by time and size

The built-in `Flow.chunked(size)` (experimental in 1.10.2) counts only; analytics uploads need "3 events or 2 seconds, whichever first".

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import kotlin.time.Duration
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds

// Flush when the batch is full OR maxWait after its first item — whichever comes first.
fun <T> Flow<T>.chunkedByTime(maxSize: Int, maxWait: Duration): Flow<List<T>> = channelFlow {
    val batch = mutableListOf<T>()
    val lock = Mutex()                                           // the timer and the collector both flush
    var timer: Job? = null

    suspend fun flush(byTimer: Boolean = false) {                // always called holding the lock
        if (!byTimer) timer?.cancel()                            // a timer never cancels itself
        if (batch.isEmpty()) return
        send(batch.toList())
        batch.clear()
    }

    collect { item ->
        lock.withLock {
            batch += item
            if (batch.size == maxSize) flush()
            else if (batch.size == 1) timer = launch {
                delay(maxWait)
                lock.withLock { flush(byTimer = true) }
            }
        }
    }
    lock.withLock { flush() }                                    // upstream finished: send the rest
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    val pauses = listOf(0L, 100L, 100L, 100L, 100L, 4_100L, 10_000L)   // a burst of 5, then a trickle
    val plays = pauses.withIndex().asFlow()
        .onEach { delay(it.value) }
        .map { "play-${it.index}" }                              // "track played" analytics events
    plays.chunkedByTime(maxSize = 3, maxWait = 2.seconds)
        .collect { println("${currentTime} ms: upload $it") }

    println(flowOf(1, 2, 3, 4, 5).chunked(2).toList())             // built-in: by count only, experimental
}

A repeating flow without drift

Sleep until the next deadline rather than for the period, and skip the slots missed during a stall instead of replaying them (the `Job` version is in the Timers, Delays & Scheduled Work sheet; `channels.ticker` is `@ObsoleteCoroutinesApi`).

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import kotlin.time.*
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds

// Drifts: each tick waits `period` AFTER the collector finished with the previous one
fun naiveTicker(period: Duration): Flow<Int> = flow {
    var n = 0
    while (true) {
        emit(n++)
        delay(period)
    }
}

// No drift: ticks are due at start + k * period. After a stall (a slow collector, a GC pause,
// a sleeping device) the missed slots are skipped, not fired in a burst, and the phase is kept.
fun ticker(period: Duration, time: TimeSource = TimeSource.Monotonic): Flow<Int> = flow {
    val start = time.markNow()
    var n = 0
    var next = period
    while (true) {
        emit(n++)
        val now = start.elapsedNow()
        while (next <= now) next += period                     // late: skip the slots already missed
        delay(next - now)
    }
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    suspend fun Flow<Int>.tickTimes(work: (Int) -> Long): List<Long> {
        val t0 = currentTime
        return take(6).map { tick ->
            delay(work(tick))                                  // the collector's work for this tick, in ms
            currentTime - t0                                   // when that work was done
        }.toList()
    }
    println("naive:    ${naiveTicker(1.seconds).tickTimes { 30 }}")
    println("deadline: ${ticker(1.seconds, testTimeSource).tickTimes { 30 }}")
    println("stalled:  ${ticker(1.seconds, testTimeSource).tickTimes { if (it == 1) 4_500 else 30 }}")
}

deadline: [30, 1030, 2030, 3030, 4030, 5030]

conflate, buffer, collectLatest — and what each drops

When the collector is slower than the producer, choose who pays: the producer waits, the buffer grows, old values go, or old work is cancelled.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import java.util.Locale

// The waveform view: a new frame of levels every 100 ms, and drawing one takes 250 ms
fun levels(): Flow<Int> = flow {
    for (frame in 1..6) {
        emit(frame)
        delay(100)
    }
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    val drawn = mutableListOf<Int>()
    suspend fun draw(frame: Int) {
        delay(250)
        drawn += frame
    }
    suspend fun measure(name: String, run: suspend () -> Unit) {
        drawn.clear()
        val t0 = currentTime
        run()
        println("%-13s drew %-18s in %4d ms".format(Locale.ROOT, name, drawn, currentTime - t0))
    }

    measure("default") { levels().collect(::draw) }                // the producer waits for the drawer
    measure("buffer()") { levels().buffer().collect(::draw) }      // producer runs ahead; nothing dropped
    measure("conflate()") { levels().conflate().collect(::draw) }  // the drawer skips to the newest frame
    measure("collectLatest") { levels().collectLatest(::draw) }    // a new frame cancels the drawing
}
Result
default       drew [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] in 2100 ms
buffer()      drew [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6] in 1500 ms
conflate()    drew [1, 3, 5, 6]       in 1000 ms
collectLatest drew [6]                in  750 ms

Owning the collecting Job

Keep the `Job` from `launchIn`, make `start()` idempotent and `stop()` cancel it, so a second start never adds a collector and nothing runs after stop.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.flow.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*

class ProgressLabel(private val scope: CoroutineScope, private val positionsMs: Flow<Long>) {
    private var job: Job? = null                              // touched from one thread (the UI's)
    var text = "0:00"
        private set

    fun start() {
        if (job?.isActive == true) return                     // idempotent: never a second collector
        job = positionsMs
            .map { ms -> "%d:%02d".format(java.util.Locale.ROOT, ms / 60_000, ms / 1_000 % 60) }
            .distinctUntilChanged()                           // one update a second, not fifty
            .onEach { text = it }
            .launchIn(scope)                                  // the Job is the handle: keep it
    }

    fun stop() {
        job?.cancel()
        job = null
    }
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    var subscriptions = 0
    val positions = flow {                                    // the player: a position every 20 ms
        var ms = 0L
        while (true) {
            emit(ms)
            delay(20)
            ms += 20
        }
    }.onStart { subscriptions++ }

    val label = ProgressLabel(backgroundScope, positions)     // backgroundScope: cancelled when the test ends
    label.start()
    label.start()                                             // start() runs on every resume
    advanceTimeBy(66_000)                                     // 66 s of playback, in no real time
    println("${currentTime} ms: ${label.text}, subscriptions = $subscriptions")

    label.stop()
    advanceTimeBy(10_000)
    println("${currentTime} ms: ${label.text} (stopped: nothing collects)")
}
Result
66000 ms: 1:05, subscriptions = 1
76000 ms: 1:05 (stopped: nothing collects)

Virtual time: advanceTimeBy, runCurrent, advanceUntilIdle

`advanceTimeBy` runs the tasks due before its target, `runCurrent` those due at the current instant, and `advanceUntilIdle` stops once only `backgroundScope` work is left.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    var positionMs = 0L
    backgroundScope.launch {                                  // the player: a position every 20 ms
        while (true) {
            delay(20)
            positionMs += 20
        }
    }

    advanceTimeBy(65_000)                                     // runs every task due BEFORE 65 000 ms
    println("$currentTime ms: position $positionMs")
    runCurrent()                                              // ...and this runs the ones due AT 65 000 ms
    println("$currentTime ms: position $positionMs")
    advanceUntilIdle()                                        // background work alone is not waited for
    println("$currentTime ms: position $positionMs (it skips backgroundScope)")
}
Result
65000 ms: position 64980
65000 ms: position 65000
65000 ms: position 65000 (it skips backgroundScope)

Safety checklist for timing in Flow

The lifetime bugs outnumber the timing bugs.

  • Keep every Job that launchIn or launch returns; cancel it in stop(), and cancel before restarting so timers never pile up.
  • Test with runTest: delay is virtual, so a 5-minute timeout test takes milliseconds. Launch never-ending collectors in backgroundScope.
  • Inject a TimeSource into anything that compares time itself (throttleFirst, tickers); pass testTimeSource in tests.
  • Periodic work sleeps until the next deadline (start + k * period) and skips the slots it missed — never a fixed period after the work, never a burst of late ticks.
  • Catch inside mapLatest / flatMapLatest / transformLatest: a catch after the operator ends the whole stream on the first failure.
  • Mark preview and experimental operators honestly: @OptIn(FlowPreview::class) for debounce, sample, timeout; @OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class) for mapLatest, flatMapLatest, chunked.
  • debounce on a value that must arrive (a payment status, a final position): it drops every value but the last of a burst.
  • TimeSource.Monotonic or System.nanoTime() inside an operator you test with runTest: real time does not move with virtual time.
  • withTimeout throws TimeoutCancellationException, a CancellationException: a broad catch (e: Exception) that handles it also swallows real cancellation. Use withTimeoutOrNull, or catch the timeout type alone.
  • Flow has no throttle: write the one you mean and name it for its edge (throttleFirst, throttleLatest), or use sample when a fixed period is what you want.

Timers, Delays & Scheduled Work

One-shot delays, drift-free repeating loops, countdowns, polling, timeouts, retry with backoff, bounded parallelism, injected time — and the Android tools for work that outlives the screen.

  • jvm
  • android
  • kotlinx-coroutines-core
  • kotlinx-coroutines-test
  • kotlin >=2.0
  • kotlinx-coroutines >=1.10
  • jvm >=17
  • Kotlin/JVM with kotlinx.coroutines

Sources: Cancellation and timeouts — Kotlin docs · Time measurement — Kotlin docs · Background tasks overview — Android Developers

Which do I reach for?

Decide by how long the work must outlive the screen, then by how precise it must be.

ToolLives as long asPrecisionReach for it when
delay in a coroutine (viewModelScope, lifecycleScope)its scope: the screen or the ViewModelms, while the process runsbanners, debounce, countdowns, polling a visible screen — the default
Flow operators (debounce, sample, a ticker flow)the collecting Jobmsthe timing belongs to a stream (see Flow Timing Operators)
Handler(Looper.getMainLooper()).postDelayedthe process; remove callbacks yourselfms, uptime-based (pauses in deep sleep)Java or View code with no coroutines
ScheduledExecutorServiceuntil shutdown()ms, on its own threadsJVM servers and Java libraries; not java.util.Timer
WorkManagerprocess death and rebootsinexact; periodic work at least every 15 minsync, uploads, cleanup: must happen, may wait for network or charging
AlarmManager setAndAllowWhileIdleprocess death, not reboot (reschedule on boot)inexact, but fires in Dozea moment the user chose: a pickup reminder
AlarmManager.setAlarmClockprocess death, not reboot (reschedule on boot)exact, shown to the user, never movedalarm clock, calendar — exact time is the app's core function (USE_EXACT_ALARM)
Foreground servicewhile it shows a notificationcontinuousthe user is watching it happen: navigation, a workout, playback

A one-shot delay, restarted and cancelled — it is a Job

Keep the `Job`: cancel and relaunch it to restart the delay, and cancel it when the screen closes so nothing fires afterwards.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*

class BannerTimer(private val scope: CoroutineScope, private val log: (String) -> Unit) {
    private var hideJob: Job? = null

    fun show(text: String) {                               // one-shot delay, restarted by a new banner
        log("banner: $text")
        hideJob?.cancel()
        hideJob = scope.launch {
            delay(3_000)
            log("banner hidden")
        }
    }

    fun onScreenClosed() {
        hideJob?.cancel()                                  // nothing visual outlives the screen
    }
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    val banner = BannerTimer(this) { println("${currentTime} ms: $it") }
    banner.show("Coupon applied")
    advanceTimeBy(2_000)
    banner.show("Card saved")                              // before the first one hid: its timer restarts
    advanceTimeBy(4_000)
    banner.show("Order placed")
    advanceTimeBy(500)
    banner.onScreenClosed()                                // its hide timer is cancelled, not left behind
    advanceUntilIdle()
    println("${currentTime} ms: nothing left running")
}
Result
0 ms: banner: Coupon applied
2000 ms: banner: Card saved
5000 ms: banner hidden
6000 ms: banner: Order placed
6500 ms: nothing left running

A throttle is a Job that just waits

Refuse work while the cooldown `Job` is active, so a double tap submits one payment and a tap after the window submits the next.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*

class PayButton(private val scope: CoroutineScope, private val log: (String) -> Unit) {
    private var cooldown: Job? = null

    fun onTapped() {                                       // throttle, leading edge: one payment per 2 s
        if (cooldown?.isActive == true) {
            log("pay ignored (double tap)")
            return
        }
        log("payment submitted")
        cooldown = scope.launch { delay(2_000) }           // the window is a Job that just waits
    }
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    val pay = PayButton(this) { println("${currentTime} ms: $it") }
    pay.onTapped()
    advanceTimeBy(150)
    pay.onTapped()                                         // a double tap inside the window
    advanceTimeBy(2_000)
    pay.onTapped()                                         // the window is over: a real second payment
}
Result
0 ms: payment submitted
150 ms: pay ignored (double tap)
2150 ms: payment submitted

A debounced save that flushes when the screen closes

Debounce is a restartable one-shot delay; when the screen closes, save the pending text instead of cancelling it away (Flow's `debounce` is in the Flow Timing Operators sheet).

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*

class DeliveryNoteEditor(private val scope: CoroutineScope, private val save: (String) -> Unit) {
    private var pendingNote: String? = null
    private var saveJob: Job? = null

    fun onNoteEdited(note: String) {                       // debounce: save 1 s after the last keystroke
        pendingNote = note
        saveJob?.cancel()
        saveJob = scope.launch {
            delay(1_000)
            flush()
        }
    }

    fun onScreenClosed() {                                 // user data is flushed, not dropped
        saveJob?.cancel()
        flush()                                            // in an app: from a scope that outlives the screen
    }

    private fun flush() {
        pendingNote?.let(save)
        pendingNote = null
    }
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    val editor = DeliveryNoteEditor(this) { println("${currentTime} ms: saved '$it'") }
    for (text in listOf("Ring", "Ring the", "Ring the bell")) {
        editor.onNoteEdited(text)
        advanceTimeBy(300)
    }
    advanceTimeBy(2_000)                                   // one save, 1 s after the last keystroke
    editor.onScreenClosed()                                // left after it saved: nothing more to save
    editor.onNoteEdited("Leave at the door")
    advanceTimeBy(400)
    editor.onScreenClosed()                                // closed before the debounce fired: flushed
    advanceUntilIdle()
    println("${currentTime} ms: nothing left running")
}
Result
1600 ms: saved 'Ring the bell'
3300 ms: saved 'Leave at the door'
3300 ms: nothing left running
