A repeating timer without drift

`delay(period)` after the work makes every run late by the work's cost, while sleeping until the next slot keeps the rate and skips the slots a hung send missed (the `Flow` version is in the Flow Timing Operators sheet).

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import kotlin.time.*
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds

// Fixed delay: the period starts AFTER the work, so every send pushes all later ones back
fun CoroutineScope.fixedDelay(period: Duration, work: suspend () -> Unit) = launch {
    while (isActive) {
        work()
        delay(period)
    }
}

// Fixed rate: sleep until the next slot (start + k * period); slots missed while a send hung
// (or the device slept) are skipped, not fired in a burst
fun CoroutineScope.fixedRate(period: Duration, time: TimeSource, work: suspend () -> Unit) = launch {
    val start = time.markNow()
    var next = period
    while (isActive) {
        work()
        val now = start.elapsedNow()
        while (next <= now) next += period
        delay(next - now)
    }
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    val drifting = mutableListOf<Long>()                  // a location every 5 s; a send takes 120 ms
    val steady = mutableListOf<Long>()
    backgroundScope.fixedDelay(5.seconds) {
        drifting += currentTime
        delay(120.milliseconds)
    }
    backgroundScope.fixedRate(5.seconds, testTimeSource) {   // TimeSource.Monotonic in the app
        steady += currentTime
        delay(if (steady.size == 3) 7_000.milliseconds else 120.milliseconds)   // the 3rd send hangs 7 s
    }
    advanceTimeBy(20_001)                                 // both loops end with backgroundScope
    println("fixed delay sent at $drifting")
    println("fixed rate  sent at $steady")
}
Result
fixed delay sent at [0, 5120, 10240, 15360]
fixed rate  sent at [0, 5000, 10000, 20000]

A failed run does not end the schedule

Catch the expected failure inside the loop, never `Exception`, so one lost send is logged, the next slot still runs, and cancelling the loop still stops it.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import java.io.IOException
import kotlin.time.*
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds

// The fixed-rate loop from the card above, now with one failed run caught inside the loop
fun CoroutineScope.fixedRate(period: Duration, time: TimeSource, work: suspend () -> Unit) = launch {
    val start = time.markNow()
    var next = period
    while (isActive) {
        try {
            work()
        } catch (e: IOException) {                        // only the expected failure: never Exception
            println("send failed (${e.message}); the schedule goes on")
        }
        val now = start.elapsedNow()
        while (next <= now) next += period
        delay(next - now)
    }
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    val sent = mutableListOf<Long>()                      // a courier's location every 5 s
    val sending = backgroundScope.fixedRate(5.seconds, testTimeSource) {
        sent += currentTime
        delay(120.milliseconds)
        if (sent.size == 2) throw IOException("no signal")
    }
    advanceTimeBy(20_001)
    sending.cancel()                                      // the screen closes: the loop stops at its delay
    advanceTimeBy(10_000)
    println("sent at $sent, still running: ${sending.isActive}")
}
Result
send failed (no signal); the schedule goes on
sent at [0, 5000, 10000, 15000, 20000], still running: false

A countdown, and polling until a condition holds

A countdown is a loop of `delay`; polling is a loop that checks, waits and gives up under `withTimeoutOrNull`.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import kotlin.time.Duration
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds

// Countdown: "Resend code in 3 s… 2 s… 1 s…", then enable the button
suspend fun resendCountdown(from: Int, show: (String) -> Unit) {
    for (secondsLeft in from downTo 1) {
        show("Resend code in ${secondsLeft} s")
        delay(1.seconds)
    }
    show("Resend code")
}

enum class PaymentStatus(val isFinal: Boolean) {
    PENDING(false), AUTHORISED(false), SETTLED(true), DECLINED(true)
}

// Polling: ask every `interval` until the status is final, or give up after `limit`
suspend fun awaitFinalStatus(
    limit: Duration,
    interval: Duration,
    fetch: suspend () -> PaymentStatus,
): PaymentStatus? =
    withTimeoutOrNull(limit) {
        var status = fetch()
        while (!status.isFinal) {
            delay(interval)
            status = fetch()
        }
        status
    }

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    resendCountdown(3) { println("${currentTime} ms: $it") }

    val statuses = ArrayDeque(listOf(PaymentStatus.PENDING, PaymentStatus.AUTHORISED, PaymentStatus.SETTLED))
    val start = currentTime
    val settled = awaitFinalStatus(limit = 30.seconds, interval = 2.seconds) { statuses.removeFirst() }
    println("+${currentTime - start} ms: payment $settled")

    val stuck = awaitFinalStatus(limit = 10.seconds, interval = 2.seconds) { PaymentStatus.PENDING }
    println("+${currentTime - start} ms: payment ${stuck ?: "still pending: show 'We'll email you'"}")
}
Result

1000 ms: Resend code in 2 s
2000 ms: Resend code in 1 s
3000 ms: Resend code
+4000 ms: payment SETTLED
+14000 ms: payment still pending: show 'We'll email you'

A timeout per attempt, and retry with exponential backoff

Bound each attempt with `withTimeout`, wait 500 ms, 1 s, 2 s… between them, and let the last failure reach the caller.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import java.io.IOException
import kotlin.time.Duration
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds

suspend fun <T> retryWithBackoff(
    retries: Int = 3,
    perAttempt: Duration = 2.seconds,                      // a hung request counts as a failure
    onRetry: (attempt: Int, error: Exception, wait: Duration) -> Unit = { _, _, _ -> },
    block: suspend () -> T,
): T {
    var wait = 500.milliseconds                            // then 1 s, 2 s, … capped at 5 s
    for (attempt in 1..retries) {
        try {
            return withTimeout(perAttempt) { block() }
        } catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) {
            currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()       // the CALLER timed out: stop (next card)
            onRetry(attempt, e, wait)
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            onRetry(attempt, e, wait)
        }
        delay(wait)
        wait = (wait * 2).coerceAtMost(5.seconds)
    }
    return withTimeout(perAttempt) { block() }             // the last attempt's failure reaches the caller
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    val replies = ArrayDeque<suspend () -> String>(listOf(
        { awaitCancellation() },                           // the server never answers
        { throw IOException("503 Service Unavailable") },
        { delay(300); "order-1042" },
    ))
    val log = { n: Int, e: Exception, wait: Duration ->
        println("${currentTime} ms: attempt $n failed (${e::class.simpleName}), retry in $wait")
    }
    val orderId = retryWithBackoff(onRetry = log) { replies.removeFirst().invoke() }
    println("${currentTime} ms: placed $orderId")
}
Result
2000 ms: attempt 1 failed (TimeoutCancellationException), retry in 500ms
2500 ms: attempt 2 failed (IOException), retry in 1s
3800 ms: placed order-1042

A retry stops when its caller gives up

The caller's own timeout also arrives as a `TimeoutCancellationException`, so `ensureActive()` tells it apart from an attempt's and the retry stops without reporting a failed attempt.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import java.io.IOException
import kotlin.time.Duration
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.milliseconds
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds

suspend fun <T> retryWithBackoff(
    retries: Int = 3,
    perAttempt: Duration = 2.seconds,                      // a hung request counts as a failure
    onRetry: (attempt: Int, error: Exception, wait: Duration) -> Unit = { _, _, _ -> },
    block: suspend () -> T,
): T {
    var wait = 500.milliseconds                            // then 1 s, 2 s, … capped at 5 s
    for (attempt in 1..retries) {
        try {
            return withTimeout(perAttempt) { block() }
        } catch (e: TimeoutCancellationException) {
            currentCoroutineContext().ensureActive()       // the CALLER timed out or was cancelled: stop here
            onRetry(attempt, e, wait)
        } catch (e: IOException) {
            onRetry(attempt, e, wait)
        }
        delay(wait)
        wait = (wait * 2).coerceAtMost(5.seconds)
    }
    return withTimeout(perAttempt) { block() }             // the last attempt's failure reaches the caller
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    var reported = 0
    val log = { n: Int, e: Exception, wait: Duration ->
        reported++
        println("${currentTime} ms: attempt $n failed (${e::class.simpleName}), retry in $wait")
    }
    // The screen allows the whole operation 1 s: the caller's own timeout fires inside attempt 1
    val orderId = withTimeoutOrNull(1_000) {
        retryWithBackoff(onRetry = log) { awaitCancellation() }
    }
    println("${currentTime} ms: caller gave up (got $orderId), failed attempts reported: $reported")
}
Result
1000 ms: caller gave up (got null), failed attempts reported: 0

N jobs — serial, parallel, or at most K at once

`map` runs them one by one, `async` + `awaitAll` all at once, and a `Semaphore` caps how many hold a permit.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Semaphore
import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withPermit
import kotlinx.coroutines.test.*
import java.util.Locale

var running = 0
var peak = 0
suspend fun uploadPhoto(name: String): String {           // each receipt photo takes 300 ms
    running++
    peak = maxOf(peak, running)
    try { delay(300) } finally { running-- }
    return "$name ok"
}

@OptIn(ExperimentalCoroutinesApi::class)
fun main() = runTest {
    val photos = (1..6).map { "receipt-$it.jpg" }
    suspend fun measure(label: String, upload: suspend () -> List<String>) {
        peak = 0
        val t0 = currentTime
        val results = upload()
        val elapsed = currentTime - t0
        val line = "%-10s %d done in %4d ms, at most %d at once"
        println(line.format(Locale.ROOT, label, results.size, elapsed, peak))
    }

    measure("serial") { photos.map { uploadPhoto(it) } }
    measure("parallel") { coroutineScope { photos.map { async { uploadPhoto(it) } }.awaitAll() } }

    val permits = Semaphore(2)                             // the server allows two uploads per user
    measure("limited") {
        coroutineScope { photos.map { async { permits.withPermit { uploadPhoto(it) } } }.awaitAll() }
    }
}
Result
serial     6 done in 1800 ms, at most 1 at once
parallel   6 done in  300 ms, at most 6 at once
limited    6 done in  900 ms, at most 2 at once

Injecting time: Clock for when, TimeSource for how long

Code that reads the time takes it as a parameter — a fake `Clock` for instants, a `TestTimeSource` for durations — so tests never sleep (with `runTest`, pass its `testTimeSource`).

import kotlin.time.*
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.minutes
import kotlin.time.Duration.Companion.seconds

// Wall-clock time ("when"): a cart hold that expires at an instant shown to the user and stored
class CartHold(private val clock: Clock) {
    val expiresAt: Instant = clock.now() + 10.minutes
    fun isExpired() = clock.now() >= expiresAt
}

// Elapsed time ("how long"): monotonic, immune to the user changing the device clock
class ResendLimiter(private val time: TimeSource, private val cooldown: Duration) {
    private var lastSent: TimeMark? = null
    fun trySend(): Boolean {
        val last = lastSent
        if (last != null && last.elapsedNow() < cooldown) return false
        lastSent = time.markNow()
        return true
    }
}

class FakeClock(var now: Instant) : Clock { override fun now() = now }

fun main() {
    val clock = FakeClock(Instant.parse("2026-11-16T12:00:00Z"))   // Clock.System in the app
    val hold = CartHold(clock)
    clock.now += 9.minutes
    println("hold until ${hold.expiresAt}, expired after 9 min: ${hold.isExpired()}")
    clock.now += 1.minutes
    println("expired after 10 min: ${hold.isExpired()}")

    val time = TestTimeSource()                                     // TimeSource.Monotonic in the app
    val limiter = ResendLimiter(time, cooldown = 30.seconds)
    println("send: ${limiter.trySend()}, again at once: ${limiter.trySend()}")
    time += 30.seconds
    println("after 30 s: ${limiter.trySend()}")
}
Result
hold until 2026-11-16T12:10:00Z, expired after 9 min: false
expired after 10 min: true
send: true, again at once: false
after 30 s: true

The JVM's own scheduler, and the coroutine loop

`ScheduledExecutorService` still fits Java code and servers with no coroutines; `java.util.Timer` does not — one thread, and one exception kills every task.

ScheduledExecutorService
import java.util.concurrent.CountDownLatch
import java.util.concurrent.Executors
import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger

fun main() {
    val scheduler = Executors.newSingleThreadScheduledExecutor()
    val sent = AtomicInteger()
    val thirdSent = CountDownLatch(1)

    // scheduleAtFixedRate keeps the rate; scheduleWithFixedDelay drifts like a delay loop.
    // An exception thrown here silently cancels every later run.
    val reminders = scheduler.scheduleAtFixedRate({
        val n = sent.incrementAndGet()
        if (n <= 3) println("remind courier ($n)")
        if (n == 3) thirdSent.countDown()
    }, 0, 100, TimeUnit.MILLISECONDS)

    thirdSent.await()                                    // blocks a whole thread while waiting
    reminders.cancel(false)
    scheduler.shutdown()                                 // forget this and the JVM never exits
    println("stopped")
}
Coroutine loop
import kotlinx.coroutines.*

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val thirdSent = CompletableDeferred<Unit>()

    // A coroutine loop: cancellable at every delay, and an exception reaches the
    // parent instead of vanishing. (Fixed delay; use a deadline loop when rate matters.)
    val reminders = launch {
        var n = 0
        while (isActive) {
            n++
            println("remind courier ($n)")
            if (n == 3) thirdSent.complete(Unit)
            delay(100)
        }
    }

    thirdSent.await()                                    // suspends; the thread is free meanwhile
    reminders.cancelAndJoin()
    println("stopped")
}
Result
remind courier (1)
remind courier (2)
remind courier (3)
stopped

Work that outlives the screen: WorkManager and AlarmManager

WorkManager for work that must happen eventually (it persists across reboots), an inexact alarm for a moment the user chose, and an exact alarm only when exact time is the app's core function.

// WorkManager: work that must happen eventually; it survives process death and reboots
class SyncOrdersWorker(context: Context, params: WorkerParameters) : CoroutineWorker(context, params) {
    override suspend fun doWork(): Result = try {
        (applicationContext as OrdersApplication).orderRepository.syncPending()
        Result.success()
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        if (runAttemptCount < 5) Result.retry() else Result.failure()   // retry follows the backoff below
    }
}

fun scheduleOrderWork(context: Context) {
    val online = Constraints.Builder().setRequiredNetworkType(NetworkType.CONNECTED).build()
    val sync = PeriodicWorkRequestBuilder<SyncOrdersWorker>(15, TimeUnit.MINUTES)   // 15 min is the minimum
        .setConstraints(online)
        .setBackoffCriteria(BackoffPolicy.EXPONENTIAL, 30, TimeUnit.SECONDS)
        .build()
    val upload = OneTimeWorkRequestBuilder<UploadReceiptWorker>().setConstraints(online).build()
    WorkManager.getInstance(context).apply {               // unique names: one copy, not one per app start
        enqueueUniquePeriodicWork("order-sync", ExistingPeriodicWorkPolicy.KEEP, sync)
        enqueueUniqueWork("receipt-1042", ExistingWorkPolicy.KEEP, upload)
    }
}

// AlarmManager: a moment the user chose. A reminder is fine inexact; it still fires in Doze.
fun schedulePickupReminder(context: Context, orderId: Int, atMillis: Long) {
    val intent = Intent(context, PickupReminderReceiver::class.java).putExtra("orderId", orderId)
    val flags = PendingIntent.FLAG_IMMUTABLE or PendingIntent.FLAG_UPDATE_CURRENT
    val pending = PendingIntent.getBroadcast(context, orderId, intent, flags)   // one alarm per order
    val alarms = context.getSystemService(AlarmManager::class.java)
    alarms.setAndAllowWhileIdle(AlarmManager.RTC_WAKEUP, atMillis, pending)
}

// Exact time only when it IS the app's core function (an alarm clock, a calendar): such an app
// declares USE_EXACT_ALARM (granted on install, Play-policy restricted). Other apps need
// SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM, denied by default for new installs targeting API 33+ on Android 14+:
// they check canScheduleExactAlarms() and degrade.
fun scheduleWakeUpAlarm(alarms: AlarmManager, atMillis: Long, ring: PendingIntent, showAlarm: PendingIntent) {
    alarms.setAlarmClock(AlarmManager.AlarmClockInfo(atMillis, showAlarm), ring)   // shown, never moved
}
Result

Order sync runs about every 15 minutes whenever the device is online, retrying with exponential backoff; the receipt upload runs once when online; the pickup reminder arrives near its time even in Doze; the wake-up alarm rings at its exact time and shows in the status bar.

Setup
  1. An Android project with androidx.work:work-runtime 2.9 or later (since 2.9 work-runtime-ktx is empty: CoroutineWorker lives in work-runtime)
  2. An OrdersApplication holding an orderRepository with suspend fun syncPending(), an UploadReceiptWorker, and a PickupReminderReceiver declared in AndroidManifest.xml
  3. For scheduleWakeUpAlarm: an alarm-clock or calendar app declares USE_EXACT_ALARM (granted on install, Play-policy restricted); any other app declares SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM and checks canScheduleExactAlarms() first

Excerpt, not compiled or run here: it needs an Android app (needs the Android SDK and androidx.work).

  • android.app.AlarmManager
  • kotlin >=2.0

Rules and pitfalls

Most timer bugs are lifetime bugs.

  • Store every timer's Job, cancel it before restarting, and launch it in a scope that ends with its owner (viewModelScope, lifecycleScope).
  • Periodic work sleeps until the next slot, catches its expected failure per run (never Exception, which also catches cancellation), and skips the runs it missed.
  • When the screen closes, cancel the timers that only change what is shown, but flush pending user data (a debounced save) from a scope that outlives the screen.
  • Inject time — a Clock for instants, a TimeSource for durations, a CoroutineScope for delay — so runTest makes a 10-minute test instant.
  • Retry only failures that can succeed later (timeouts, IOException, 503), cap the wait, and add random jitter in production so clients do not retry in lockstep.
  • Thread.sleep in a coroutine blocks the thread other coroutines need; GlobalScope.launch { while (true) … } outlives the screen.
  • System.currentTimeMillis() differences for elapsed time: the user or NTP can move the wall clock. Use TimeSource.Monotonic.
  • A PeriodicWorkRequest below 15 minutes, or exact alarms for routine sync or reminders: WorkManager raises the interval to the minimum, and SCHEDULE_EXACT_ALARM is denied by default for new installs targeting API 33+ on Android 14+, and can be revoked.
  • Alarms are cleared on reboot and WorkManager work is not; enqueueUnique…Work keeps one copy instead of one per app start.

Shared Mutable State — Mutex, Confinement, Actors

Three ways to keep coroutines on many threads from racing — none of them checked by the compiler.

  • jvm
  • android

Sources: Shared mutable state and concurrency — Kotlin docs

Swift isolation → Kotlin

Swift proves data-race freedom at compile time; Kotlin leaves it to discipline and these tools.

SwiftKotlinDifference
actorstate owned by one coroutine that reads a channel (below)one message at a time, start to finish: no reentrancy at its suspension points
actor (serial executor)a limitedParallelism(1) dispatcherserial only between suspension points: other work interleaves at an await, as on a Swift actor
actor-isolated mutationMutex.withLock { }suspends while waiting, never blocks a thread
Sendable—no compiler check: immutable data (val, read-only collections) by convention
@MainActorDispatchers.Maina dispatcher choice, not a type-system guarantee
atomic countersjava.util.concurrent.atomic.*same as Synchronization.Atomic

Mutex and atomics

100,000 increments from many threads. A plain `count++` would lose updates; both of these do not.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex
import kotlinx.coroutines.sync.withLock
import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val mutex = Mutex()
    var guarded = 0
    val atomic = AtomicInteger()
    withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {         // a pool of threads
        repeat(1_000) {
            launch {
                repeat(100) {
                    mutex.withLock { guarded++ }
                    atomic.incrementAndGet()
                }
            }
        }
    }
    println("guarded=$guarded atomic=${atomic.get()}")
}
Result
guarded=100000 atomic=100000

`limitedParallelism(1)` gives a serial view of a shared pool — the closest thing to a serial executor.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*

val counterContext = Dispatchers.Default.limitedParallelism(1)

fun main() = runBlocking {
    var count = 0                               // only ever touched on counterContext
    withContext(Dispatchers.Default) {
        repeat(1_000) { launch { withContext(counterContext) { count++ } } }
    }
    println(count)
}

An actor from a channel

One coroutine owns the state and handles one message at a time; replies come back through `CompletableDeferred`.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import kotlinx.coroutines.channels.Channel

sealed interface AccountMsg {
    data class Deposit(val amount: Int) : AccountMsg
    data class Balance(val reply: CompletableDeferred<Int>) : AccountMsg
}

fun CoroutineScope.account(): Channel<AccountMsg> {
    val inbox = Channel<AccountMsg>(Channel.UNLIMITED)
    launch {
        var balance = 0
        for (msg in inbox) when (msg) {
            is AccountMsg.Deposit -> balance += msg.amount
            is AccountMsg.Balance -> msg.reply.complete(balance)
        }
    }
    return inbox
}

fun main() = runBlocking {
    val account = account()
    coroutineScope {
        repeat(100) { launch(Dispatchers.Default) { account.send(AccountMsg.Deposit(10)) } }
    }
    val reply = CompletableDeferred<Int>()
    account.send(AccountMsg.Balance(reply))
    account.close()                             // the actor drains its inbox, then stops
    println(reply.await())
}
Result
1000

Rules

Without a compiler check, the design has to make races impossible.

  • Prefer immutable data passed between coroutines: val properties, read-only collections, data class copies.
  • Expose state as StateFlow and mutate it only with update { } — an atomic compare-and-set.
  • synchronized or ReentrantLock around a suspension point: the lock is held while the coroutine is parked.
  • @Volatile makes writes visible, not compound updates atomic: x++ still races.

Writing atomically

Write a temporary sibling, `force(true)` it to the device, then `ATOMIC_MOVE` over the target.

import java.nio.ByteBuffer
import java.nio.channels.FileChannel
import java.nio.file.Files
import java.nio.file.Path
import java.nio.file.StandardCopyOption
import java.nio.file.StandardOpenOption
import kotlin.io.path.*

fun writeAtomically(target: Path, text: String) {
    val temp = Files.createTempFile(target.parent, ".${target.name}", ".tmp")   // same file system
    FileChannel.open(temp, StandardOpenOption.WRITE).use { channel ->
        val buffer = ByteBuffer.wrap(text.toByteArray())
        while (buffer.hasRemaining()) channel.write(buffer)
        channel.force(true)                    // on the device before the move publishes it
    }
    Files.move(temp, target, StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE)
}

fun main() {
    val dir = createTempDirectory("atomic")
    val settings = dir / "settings.json"
    writeAtomically(settings, """{"theme":"dark"}""")
    writeAtomically(settings, """{"theme":"light"}""")
    println(settings.readText())
    dir.toFile().deleteRecursively()
}
Result
{"theme":"light"}

Streaming a large file line by line

`useLines` hands a lazy sequence and closes the file afterwards; one line is in memory at a time.

import kotlin.io.path.*

fun main() {
    val log = createTempFile("app", ".log")
    log.bufferedWriter().use { out ->
        for (i in 0 until 10_000) out.appendLine("${if (i % 10 == 0) "ERROR" else "INFO"} event $i")
    }
    val errors = log.useLines { lines -> lines.count { it.startsWith("ERROR") } }
    println("$errors errors")
    log.deleteExisting()
}

An append-only journal

One JSON object per line — appending never rewrites what is already there.

import kotlin.io.path.*

fun main() {
    val journal = createTempFile("journal", ".jsonl")
    for (event in listOf("start", "save", "stop")) journal.appendText("{\"event\":\"$event\"}\n")
    println(journal.readLines().map { it.substringAfter(":\"").removeSuffix("\"}") })
    journal.deleteExisting()
}
Result
[start, save, stop]

Walking a directory tree

`walk()` is lazy and depth-first; it is still marked experimental, hence the opt-in.

import kotlin.io.path.*

@OptIn(ExperimentalPathApi::class)
fun main() {
    val root = createTempDirectory("tree")
    (root / "src/main").createDirectories()
    (root / "src/main/App.kt").writeText("fun main() {}")
    (root / "README.md").writeText("# demo")
    val sources = root.walk().filter { it.extension == "kt" }.map { it.relativeTo(root).invariantSeparatorsPathString }
    println(sources.toList())
    root.deleteRecursively()
}

[src/main/App.kt]

Where things belong

The JVM gives you a temp directory and a home directory; everything else is a convention you resolve once, at startup.

LocationHow to get itSurvivesUse for
TemporarycreateTempDirectory("app") (under java.io.tmpdir)until you delete it — or the OS cleans /tmpscratch files for one operation; delete in finally
User homePath(System.getProperty("user.home"))yesthe root to build the per-OS data directory from — never write straight into it
Per-user app datano JDK API: $XDG_DATA_HOME (default ~/.local/share/<app>) on Linux, ~/Library/Application Support/<app> on macOS, %LOCALAPPDATA% on Windows (%APPDATA% only for small settings that should roam)yessettings, databases, state you must keep
Per-user caches~/.cache/<app> ($XDG_CACHE_HOME), ~/Library/Caches/<app>, %LOCALAPPDATA%until the user or a cleaner removes itre-creatable data: thumbnails, downloads you can fetch again
Working directoryPath("").toAbsolutePath() (user.dir)—never assume it: it is wherever the process was started. Resolve against an explicit root
Classpath resourcesjavaClass.getResourceAsStream("/seed.json")read-only, inside the jarshipped defaults; not a Path — it may live inside a zip
Androidcontext.filesDir / context.cacheDir (and noBackupFilesDir)filesDir until uninstall (and in Auto Backup unless excluded); cacheDir may be cleared by the system when storage is lowapp-private data / re-creatable caches; no permission needed

Read strategy by file size

The API you choose is a memory decision — pick it from the size and the access pattern, not from habit.

The fileAPIWhat sits in memory
small (up to a few MB), needed wholereadText() / readLines() / readBytes()the whole file
any size, read once in orderuseLines { } / bufferedReader() / inputStream().buffered()one line or one buffer at a time
any size, a record by numberan offset index + RandomAccessFile.seek or FileChannel.read(buffer, position)8 bytes of index per record
huge and read-mostly, random accessFileChannel.map(MapMode.READ_ONLY, position, size)pages the OS faults in on demand; one MappedByteBuffer covers at most 2 GB, so map in slices

Path over String

Build paths with `resolve` (`/`) and `normalize`, never concatenation — and refuse a user-supplied name that escapes its directory.

import java.nio.file.Path
import kotlin.io.path.*

/** Resolves an untrusted file name inside `root`, refusing blanks, `../` and absolute paths. */
fun safeChild(root: Path, untrustedName: String): Path {
    require(untrustedName.isNotBlank()) { "empty file name" }
    val candidate = root.resolve(untrustedName).normalize()
    // A lexical check: when entries can be symlinks (an unpacked zip), also require
    // candidate.parent.toRealPath().startsWith(root.toRealPath()).
    require(candidate.startsWith(root.normalize())) { "outside the export directory: $untrustedName" }
    return candidate
}

fun main() {
    val root = Path("exports")                          // relative here only so the output is portable
    val report = root / "2026" / "orders report.csv"    // `/` is resolve(): one separator, spaces kept
    println(report.invariantSeparatorsPathString)
    println("${report.name} | ${report.nameWithoutExtension} | ${report.extension} | ${report.parent?.name}")
    println(Path("exports/2026/../2025/./q4.csv").normalize().invariantSeparatorsPathString)
    println(root.relativize(report).invariantSeparatorsPathString)

    println(safeChild(root, "q4.csv").invariantSeparatorsPathString)
    for (attack in listOf("../../etc/passwd", "/etc/passwd", "")) {
        println(runCatching { safeChild(root, attack) }.exceptionOrNull()?.message)
    }
    // "exports" + "/" + name breaks on Windows separators, doubled slashes and names containing "/".
}

Real durability: force, and syncing the directory

A payments ledger that must survive a power cut the moment `append` returns: force the file, and fsync the directory when the name is new.

import java.io.IOException
import java.nio.ByteBuffer
import java.nio.channels.FileChannel
import java.nio.file.Path
import java.nio.file.StandardOpenOption.*
import kotlin.io.path.*

// flush()          -> the OS page cache: survives the process crashing, not the machine
// force(false)     -> the file's content on the device
// force(true)      -> content and metadata (size, timestamps) — an append changes the size
// directory force  -> the directory entry itself: a new file's name, or a rename
// macOS: the JDK's force() issues F_FULLFSYNC, so it reaches the medium, not just the drive cache.

fun syncDirectory(dir: Path) {
    val channel = try {
        FileChannel.open(dir, READ)
    } catch (e: IOException) {
        return                                            // Windows cannot open a directory as a channel
    }
    channel.use { it.force(true) }                        // a failure here is real: let it reach the caller
}

fun appendDurably(ledger: Path, line: String) {
    val isNew = ledger.notExists()
    FileChannel.open(ledger, CREATE, WRITE, APPEND).use { channel ->
        val bytes = ByteBuffer.wrap("$line\n".encodeToByteArray())
        while (bytes.hasRemaining()) channel.write(bytes)
        channel.force(true)
    }
    if (isNew) syncDirectory(ledger.parent)               // same after an ATOMIC_MOVE into the directory
}

fun main() {
    val dir = createTempDirectory("ledger")
    try {
        val ledger = dir / "payments.log"
        appendDurably(ledger, "pay-1 captured 42.00")
        appendDurably(ledger, "pay-2 captured 9.99")
        println(ledger.readLines())
    } finally {
        dir.toFile().deleteRecursively()
    }
}
Result
[pay-1 captured 42.00, pay-2 captured 9.99]

Streaming a large write

Export 200 000 orders without holding them: a lazy Sequence through a 256 KB buffer, forced to the device and published atomically when complete.

import java.nio.channels.FileChannel
import java.nio.file.Files
import java.nio.file.Path
import java.nio.file.StandardCopyOption
import java.nio.file.StandardOpenOption
import kotlin.io.path.*

data class OrderRow(val id: Int, val customer: String, val cents: Long)

fun exportCsv(rows: Sequence<OrderRow>, target: Path) {
    val temp = Files.createTempFile(target.parent, ".${target.name}", ".tmp")
    try {
        // The 256 KB buffer sits below the text encoder, so the file sees one write per ~256 KB, not per row.
        Files.newOutputStream(temp).buffered(256 * 1024).bufferedWriter().use { out ->
            out.appendLine("id,customer,cents")
            for (row in rows) out.appendLine("${row.id},${row.customer},${row.cents}")
        }
        FileChannel.open(temp, StandardOpenOption.WRITE).use { it.force(true) }   // on the device first
        Files.move(temp, target, StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE)
    } finally {
        temp.deleteIfExists()                                         // still there only if something failed
    }
}

fun main() {
    val dir = createTempDirectory("export")
    try {
        val target = dir / "orders.csv"
        val rows = generateSequence(1) { it + 1 }.take(200_000)
            .map { OrderRow(it, "customer-${it % 1000}", it * 125L) }
        exportCsv(rows, target)
        println("${target.useLines { it.count() }} lines")
        println("directory holds ${dir.listDirectoryEntries().map { it.name }}")              // no temp left
        println(target.useLines { it.drop(1).first() })
    } finally {
        dir.toFile().deleteRecursively()
    }
}

Algorithm — external merge sort

Sort a file bigger than memory: sorted runs of a chunk each, then a k-way merge through a heap — O(n log n) time, O(chunk + k) memory.

import java.io.BufferedReader
import java.nio.file.Path
import java.util.PriorityQueue
import kotlin.io.path.*
import kotlin.random.Random

fun makeRuns(input: Path, size: Int, dir: Path): List<Path> = input.useLines { lines ->
    lines.chunked(size).mapIndexed { i, chunk -> (dir / "run-$i.txt").apply { writeLines(chunk.sorted()) } }
        .toList()
}

fun mergeRuns(runs: List<Path>, output: Path) {         // thousands of runs: merge ~100 per pass
    val readers = ArrayList<BufferedReader>()
    try {
        runs.mapTo(readers) { it.bufferedReader() }            // in the try: a failed open closes the rest
        val heads = PriorityQueue<Pair<String, BufferedReader>>(compareBy { it.first })
        for (reader in readers) reader.readLine()?.let { heads += it to reader }
        output.bufferedWriter().use { out ->
            while (heads.isNotEmpty()) {
                val (line, reader) = heads.poll()                      // the smallest line of all runs
                out.appendLine(line)
                reader.readLine()?.let { heads += it to reader }
            }
        }
    } finally {
        readers.forEach { it.close() }
    }
}

fun main() {
    val dir = createTempDirectory("sort")
    try {
        val input = dir / "order-ids.txt"
        input.writeLines((1..10_000).shuffled(Random(7)).map { "order-" + it.toString().padStart(5, '0') })
        val runs = makeRuns(input, size = 1_000, dir = dir)
        val output = dir / "sorted.txt"
        mergeRuns(runs, output)
        val sorted = output.useLines { lines -> lines.zipWithNext().all { (a, b) -> a <= b } }
        println("${runs.size} runs, sorted=$sorted")
    } finally {
        dir.toFile().deleteRecursively()                               // the runs too
    }
}

Algorithm — an offset index for random access

Jump to line n of a 100 000-line export without reading what precedes it: index the line starts once, then seek.

import java.io.RandomAccessFile
import java.nio.file.Path
import kotlin.io.path.*

/** Line-start offsets in one buffered pass: 8 bytes per line once built (a boxed list while building). */
fun buildIndex(file: Path): LongArray {
    val starts = mutableListOf(0L)
    file.inputStream().use { input ->
        val chunk = ByteArray(64 * 1024)
        var position = 0L
        while (true) {
            val n = input.read(chunk)
            if (n == -1) break
            for (i in 0 until n) if (chunk[i] == '\n'.code.toByte()) starts += position + i + 1
            position += n
        }
    }
    if (starts.last() == file.fileSize()) starts.removeAt(starts.lastIndex)   // no line after a final \n
    return starts.toLongArray()
}

fun RandomAccessFile.lineAt(index: LongArray, n: Int): String {      // fixed-width: offset = n × size
    val end = if (n + 1 < index.size) index[n + 1] else length()
    val bytes = ByteArray((end - index[n]).toInt())
    seek(index[n])
    readFully(bytes)
    return bytes.decodeToString().removeSuffix("\n").removeSuffix("\r")    // LF or CRLF
}

fun main() {
    val dir = createTempDirectory("index")
    try {
        val export = dir / "orders.csv"
        export.writeLines((0 until 100_000).map { "order-$it,${if (it % 3 == 0) "shipped" else "open"}" })
        val index = buildIndex(export)
        RandomAccessFile(export.toFile(), "r").use { file ->         // keep it open across lookups
            val lines = listOf(0, 41_999, 99_999).map { file.lineAt(index, it) }
            println("${index.size} lines: ${lines.joinToString(" | ")}")
        }
    } finally {
        dir.toFile().deleteRecursively()
    }
}

Algorithm — tail, the last n lines

The last lines of a multi-gigabyte log by reading 8 KB blocks backwards — the same answer as `tail -n` for LF, CRLF, blank lines and empty files.

import java.io.RandomAccessFile
import java.nio.file.Path
import kotlin.io.path.*

/** Reads backwards until more than `count` newlines are in hand. Cost O(tail), not O(file). */
fun lastLines(file: Path, count: Int): List<String> {
    if (count <= 0) return emptyList()
    return RandomAccessFile(file.toFile(), "r").use { raf ->
        if (raf.length() == 0L) return emptyList()
        var offset = raf.length()
        val blocks = ArrayDeque<ByteArray>()                     // prepend without re-copying the tail
        var newlines = 0
        while (offset > 0 && newlines <= count) {
            val block = ByteArray(minOf(8192L, offset).toInt())
            offset -= block.size
            raf.seek(offset)
            raf.readFully(block)
            newlines += block.count { it == '\n'.code.toByte() }
            blocks.addFirst(block)
        }
        val text = blocks.fold(ByteArray(0)) { acc, block -> acc + block }.decodeToString()
        // Only the final terminator ends a line; earlier blank lines are lines too.
        text.removeSuffix("\n").removeSuffix("\r").split("\r\n", "\n").takeLast(count)
    }
}

fun main() {
    val dir = createTempDirectory("tail")
    try {
        val log = dir / "access.log"
        log.writeText((1..5_000).joinToString("") { "GET /orders/$it\r\n" })     // CRLF, as on Windows
        val notes = (dir / "notes.txt").apply { writeText("first\nsecond\n\n") }
        val empty = (dir / "empty.txt").apply { writeText("") }
        println(lastLines(log, 2))                                   // across many 8 KB blocks
        // `tail -n 2` of notes.txt is "second" and the blank line, so an empty string comes last.
        println("${lastLines(notes, 2)} ${lastLines(notes, 0)} ${lastLines(empty, 3)}")
    } finally {
        dir.toFile().deleteRecursively()
    }
}

[second, ] [] []

Algorithm — dedupe and checksum

Two one-pass utilities for an access log: keep the first occurrence of each line, and a streaming SHA-256 that never loads the file.

import java.nio.file.Path
import java.security.MessageDigest
import java.util.HexFormat
import kotlin.io.path.*

/** Copies the first occurrence of each line. Memory O(distinct lines): beyond that, external-sort first. */
fun dedupe(input: Path, output: Path): Int {
    val seen = HashSet<String>()
    output.bufferedWriter().use { out ->
        input.useLines { lines -> lines.filter(seen::add).forEach { out.appendLine(it) } }
    }
    return seen.size
}

/** Constant memory however big the file: feed the digest one buffer at a time. */
fun sha256(file: Path): String {
    val digest = MessageDigest.getInstance("SHA-256")
    file.inputStream().use { input ->
        val buffer = ByteArray(64 * 1024)
        while (true) {
            val n = input.read(buffer)
            if (n == -1) break
            digest.update(buffer, 0, n)
        }
    }
    return HexFormat.of().formatHex(digest.digest())
}

fun main() {
    val dir = createTempDirectory("log")
    try {
        val log = dir / "access.log"
        log.writeText((1..5_000).joinToString("") { "GET /orders/${it % 300} 200\n" })
        println("${dedupe(log, dir / "unique.log")} distinct lines of 5000")
        println(sha256(log))
    } finally {
        dir.toFile().deleteRecursively()
    }
}
Result

Attributes & permissions

Read size and type in one call, and create a token file owner-only from the first byte — chmod after writing leaves a window.

import java.nio.file.Files
import java.nio.file.LinkOption.NOFOLLOW_LINKS
import java.nio.file.attribute.BasicFileAttributes
import java.nio.file.attribute.PosixFilePermissions
import kotlin.io.path.*

fun main() {
    val dir = createTempDirectory("attrs")
    try {
        val report = (dir / "report.csv").apply { writeText("id,total\n1,42\n") }

        // One call, one stat: size, type and times together. NOFOLLOW_LINKS, or a link reports its target.
        val attrs = report.readAttributes<BasicFileAttributes>(NOFOLLOW_LINKS)
        println("${attrs.size()} bytes, regular=${attrs.isRegularFile}, symlink=${attrs.isSymbolicLink}")

        if ("posix" in dir.fileSystem.supportedFileAttributeViews()) {
            // The mode is set by the create itself, so no other user can ever open the token.
            val ownerOnly = PosixFilePermissions.asFileAttribute(PosixFilePermissions.fromString("rw-------"))
            val token = Files.createFile(dir / "refresh.token", ownerOnly)
            token.writeText("placeholder-not-a-real-token")
            println("token ${PosixFilePermissions.toString(token.getPosixFilePermissions())}")

            report.setPosixFilePermissions(PosixFilePermissions.fromString("rw-r--r--"))
            println("report ${PosixFilePermissions.toString(report.getPosixFilePermissions())}")
        } else {
            println("no POSIX permissions here (Windows): use AclFileAttributeView")
        }
    } finally {
        dir.toFile().deleteRecursively()
    }
}

File locking

A single-instance guard for a sync job — and why a file lock is no help between threads of the same JVM.

import java.nio.channels.FileChannel
import java.nio.channels.OverlappingFileLockException
import java.nio.file.Path
import java.nio.file.StandardOpenOption.*
import kotlin.io.path.*

/** Runs `block` only if no other PROCESS holds the lock; returns null when one does. */
fun <T> withInstanceLock(lockFile: Path, block: () -> T): T? =
    FileChannel.open(lockFile, CREATE, WRITE).use { channel ->
        val lock = channel.tryLock() ?: return null
        lock.use { block() }
    }

fun main() {
    val dir = createTempDirectory("lock")
    try {
        val lockFile = dir / "sync.lock"
        println(withInstanceLock(lockFile) { "synced 12 orders" })

        // The lock belongs to the whole JVM: a second attempt from this JVM throws instead of waiting.
        withInstanceLock(lockFile) {
            try {
                withInstanceLock(lockFile) { "never runs" }
            } catch (e: OverlappingFileLockException) {
                println("same JVM: ${e::class.simpleName}")
            }
        }
    } finally {
        dir.toFile().deleteRecursively()
    }
}
// Locks are advisory on most Unix systems and unreliable on network file systems. Closing ANY channel to
// the file may release this JVM's lock: one channel per file, and a Mutex between threads. Never delete
// the lock file — a waiter may already hold a channel to it and would lock a file nobody else can see.

Concurrency: files are blocking work

Load a week of order files in parallel without blocking the caller: blocking I/O on Dispatchers.IO, with the parallelism bounded.

import kotlinx.coroutines.*
import java.nio.file.Path
import kotlin.io.path.*

/** Main-safe: the function moves its own blocking work, and takes the dispatcher so tests can swap it. */
suspend fun totalCents(file: Path, io: CoroutineDispatcher = Dispatchers.IO): Long = withContext(io) {
    file.useLines { lines -> lines.drop(1).sumOf { it.substringAfterLast(',').toLong() } }
}

fun main() = runBlocking<Unit> {
    val dir = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) { createTempDirectory("io") }
    try {
        val files = withContext(Dispatchers.IO) {
            (1..7).map { day ->
                val rows = (1..100).joinToString("\n") { "$it,${it * day}" }
                (dir / "orders-$day.csv").apply { writeText("id,cents\n$rows") }
            }
        }
        val disk = Dispatchers.IO.limitedParallelism(4)                 // at most 4 files open at once
        println(files.map { async { totalCents(it, disk) } }.awaitAll())
        val worker = withContext(disk) { Thread.currentThread().name }
        println("read on a worker thread: ${worker.startsWith("DefaultDispatcher-worker")}")
    } finally {
        withContext(Dispatchers.IO + NonCancellable) { dir.toFile().deleteRecursively() }
    }
}
// On Android the caller is usually Dispatchers.Main (the UI thread): StrictMode flags disk reads there.

[5050, 10100, 15150, 20200, 25250, 30300, 35350]
read on a worker thread: true

  • Kotlin/JVM with kotlinx.coroutines

Sources: Coroutine context and dispatchers — Kotlin docs

Error handling

Catch the specific `java.nio.file` exception instead of checking first — the check is stale before you act on it.

SituationExceptionNote
File or parent missingNoSuchFileException.file names the path; legacy java.io streams throw FileNotFoundException instead
Target already existsFileAlreadyExistsExceptionfrom createFile, createDirectory, CREATE_NEW, and move / copy without REPLACE_EXISTING
No permissionAccessDeniedExceptionalso a read-only file or directory
Deleting a non-empty directoryDirectoryNotEmptyExceptionwalk and delete children first, or deleteRecursively()
Listing a file as a directoryNotDirectoryExceptionfrom listDirectoryEntries / newDirectoryStream
ATOMIC_MOVE impossibleAtomicMoveNotSupportedExceptionthe temp file is on another file store — create it beside the target
Bytes are not valid UTF-8MalformedInputExceptionFiles.readString, Files.readAllLines, Path.readLines() and Path.useLines throw; Path.readText() and the java.io.File helpers (File.readText, File.readLines) silently substitute U+FFFD
Disk full, I/O errorIOException / FileSystemExceptionno dedicated type: log .reason and the path
Any of the aboveFileSystemExceptionthe parent of every java.nio.file case above: .file, .otherFile, .reason
Legacy java.io.Filenone — returns falsedelete(), mkdirs(), renameTo() hide the reason; prefer Files / kotlin.io.path

Testing file code

JUnit's `@TempDir` gives each test a fresh directory and deletes it afterwards, so file tests can run in parallel.

import org.junit.jupiter.api.Assertions.assertEquals
import org.junit.jupiter.api.Test
import org.junit.jupiter.api.assertThrows
import org.junit.jupiter.api.io.TempDir
import java.nio.file.Files
import java.nio.file.NoSuchFileException
import java.nio.file.Path
import java.nio.file.StandardCopyOption
import kotlin.io.path.*

/** The code under test: a temp sibling, then an atomic rename; the temp never outlives a failure. */
fun writeAtomically(target: Path, text: String) {
    val temp = Files.createTempFile(target.parent, ".${target.name}", ".tmp")
    try {
        temp.writeText(text)
        Files.move(temp, target, StandardCopyOption.ATOMIC_MOVE)
    } finally {
        temp.deleteIfExists()
    }
}

class SettingsStoreTest {
    @TempDir
    lateinit var dir: Path

    @Test
    fun `atomic write replaces the file and leaves no temp files`() {
        val settings = dir / "settings.json"
        writeAtomically(settings, """{"theme":"dark"}""")
        writeAtomically(settings, """{"theme":"light"}""")
        assertEquals("""{"theme":"light"}""", settings.readText())
        assertEquals(listOf("settings.json"), dir.listDirectoryEntries().map { it.name })
    }

    @Test
    fun `reading a missing file throws NoSuchFileException`() {
        assertThrows<NoSuchFileException> { (dir / "missing.json").readText() }
    }
}
Result

Both tests pass; JUnit creates and deletes a separate directory for each.

  1. A Gradle JVM project with testImplementation(platform("org.junit:junit-bom:5.10.5")), testImplementation("org.junit.jupiter:junit-jupiter") and tasks.test { useJUnitPlatform() }
  2. Put the class under src/test/kotlin and run ./gradlew test

Rules that prevent data loss

The JVM adds a few of its own.

  • Close every stream with use { } — it is defer for Closeable.
  • Replace a file with a temporary sibling + ATOMIC_MOVE; never truncate the original first.
  • Java's FileReader / InputStreamReader without a charset used the platform default before JDK 18; Kotlin's readText() / readLines() default to UTF-8 already.
  • ATOMIC_MOVE over an existing target is implementation-specific: POSIX rename replaces, other file systems may throw.
  • On Android, app-private files go under context.filesDir; shared storage goes through the Storage Access Framework.

The decision table, translated.

SwiftUIComposeLives until
@Stateremember { mutableStateOf(x) }the composable leaves the composition
@SceneStorage (survives recreation)rememberSaveable { … }the saved-state registry is cleared (also survives rotation)

@Observable modelViewModel exposing StateFlowthe screen's back-stack entry is destroyed

remember, rememberSaveable and hoisting

A stateless composable takes the value and an event; the caller owns the state.

@Composable
fun Counter(count: Int, onIncrement: () -> Unit) {        // stateless: easy to preview and test
    Button(onClick = onIncrement) { Text("Clicked $count times") }
}

@Composable
fun CounterScreen() {
    var count by rememberSaveable { mutableIntStateOf(0) }   // survives recomposition and rotation
    Counter(count = count, onIncrement = { count++ })
}
Result

The button's label counts up on each tap and keeps its value when the device rotates.

  2. Call the screen from setContent { } in your ComponentActivity, then run the app on a device or emulator

ViewModel + StateFlow, collected with the lifecycle

One immutable UI state, updated atomically; the screen collects it only while it is at least STARTED.

data class SearchUiState(val query: String = "", val results: List<String> = emptyList(), val loading: Boolean = false)

class SearchViewModel(private val repo: SearchRepository) : ViewModel() {
    private val _state = MutableStateFlow(SearchUiState())
    val state: StateFlow<SearchUiState> = _state.asStateFlow()
    private var searchJob: Job? = null

    fun onQueryChange(query: String) {
        _state.update { it.copy(query = query, loading = true) }
        searchJob?.cancel()                                  // a newer query supersedes the old one
        searchJob = viewModelScope.launch {                  // cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared
            val results = repo.search(query)
            _state.update { it.copy(results = results, loading = false) }
        }
    }
}

@Composable
fun SearchScreen(vm: SearchViewModel) {
    val state by vm.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
    Column {
        TextField(value = state.query, onValueChange = vm::onQueryChange)
        if (state.loading) CircularProgressIndicator()
        state.results.forEach { Text(it) }
    }
}
Result

Typing updates the field at once, shows a spinner, then the results of the latest query only.

Setup
  1. An Android Studio project with the Compose template, plus androidx.lifecycle:lifecycle-viewmodel-compose and lifecycle-runtime-compose
  2. A SearchRepository with suspend fun search(query: String): List<String>, passed to the ViewModel through a factory or your DI container

Async work tied to the screen

`LaunchedEffect(key)` starts when the composable enters, restarts when the key changes and is cancelled when it leaves — `.task(id:)`.

@Composable
fun Profile(userId: String, load: suspend (String) -> String) {
    var name by remember(userId) { mutableStateOf<String?>(null) }   // reset for a new user
    LaunchedEffect(userId) {
        name = load(userId)
    }
    Text(name ?: "Loading…")
}
Result

Shows "Loading…", then the name; switching userId cancels the old load and starts a new one.

Identity and lifetime rules

Most Compose state bugs are one of these.

  • Mutating a list inside mutableStateOf(list) — Compose sees the same object and does not recompose. Assign a new list, or use mutableStateListOf.
  • Side effects (network, logging, writes) directly in a composable body: it runs on every recomposition.
  • Give items(…, key = { it.id }) stable keys so state follows the item, not the position.
  • derivedStateOf { } for values computed from state that changes more often than the result.
  • Configuration changes recreate the activity: remember resets, rememberSaveable and the ViewModel survive.

SwiftUIComposeNote

A component — inputs, modifier and a slot

Data and events in as parameters, `modifier` as the first optional one, and a composable lambda (slot) for the part callers customise.

data class Order(val id: String, val customer: String, val totalCents: Long,
                 val status: OrderStatus, val placedAt: Instant)

enum class OrderStatus { Pending, Shipped, Delivered }

@Composable
fun OrderRow(
    order: Order,
    onClick: () -> Unit,
    modifier: Modifier = Modifier,                    // the caller decides size and outer spacing
    trailing: @Composable RowScope.() -> Unit = {},   // a slot: price, chip, menu — the caller chooses
) {
    Row(
        modifier = modifier
            .fillMaxWidth()
            .clickable(onClick = onClick)
            .padding(horizontal = 16.dp, vertical = 12.dp),
        verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically,
        horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(12.dp),
    ) {
        Column(Modifier.weight(1f)) {
            Text(order.customer, style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleMedium)
            Text("#${order.id}", style = MaterialTheme.typography.bodySmall)
        }
        trailing()
    }
}

@Preview(showBackground = true)
@Composable
private fun OrderRowPreview() {
    val placedAt = Instant.parse("2026-11-16T09:30:00Z")
    val order = Order("1042", "Grace Hopper", 4_250, OrderStatus.Shipped, placedAt)
    MaterialTheme {
        OrderRow(order, onClick = {}) {
            Text(NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(Locale.US).format(order.totalCents / 100.0))
        }
    }
}

Modifier order decides the result

Each modifier wraps everything after it — clip before background, clickable before the inner padding (a real pay action would be a `Button`; this shows the order).

Padding outside the target, background unclipped
@Composable
fun PayButton(onPay: () -> Unit) {
    Text(
        text = "Pay now",
        modifier = Modifier
            .padding(16.dp)                  // space first…
            .clickable(onClick = onPay)      // …so the padding is not tappable
            .background(MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primaryContainer)
            .clip(RoundedCornerShape(12.dp)) // too late: the background is already drawn square
            .padding(horizontal = 24.dp, vertical = 12.dp),
    )
}
Shape first, whole pill tappable
@Composable
fun PayButton(onPay: () -> Unit, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
    Text(
        text = "Pay now",
        modifier = modifier                  // outer spacing comes from the caller
            .clip(RoundedCornerShape(12.dp)) // background and ripple follow the shape
            .background(MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primaryContainer)
            .clickable(role = Role.Button, onClick = onPay)   // TalkBack says "button"
            .padding(horizontal = 24.dp, vertical = 12.dp),
    )
}
Result

Left: a square background and a ripple that stops short of the 16 dp margin. Right: a rounded pill whose whole area — padding included — responds to the tap and is announced as a button.

Row, Column, Box — arrangement, alignment, sizing, weight

`weight` shares the leftover space, `fillMaxWidth` takes the offered width, `Box` stacks and aligns children on top of each other.

@Composable
fun OrderHeader(order: Order, itemCount: Int, total: String, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
    Column(
        modifier = modifier.fillMaxWidth().padding(16.dp),
        verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(8.dp),       // gaps between children
    ) {
        Row(verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically) {
            Box(contentAlignment = Alignment.Center) {             // avatar with a status dot on top
                Text(
                    text = order.customer.take(1),
                    modifier = Modifier
                        .size(40.dp)
                        .background(MaterialTheme.colorScheme.secondaryContainer, CircleShape)
                        .wrapContentSize(),                     // centre the letter inside the 40 dp circle
                )
                Box(
                    Modifier.align(Alignment.BottomEnd).size(10.dp)
                        .background(MaterialTheme.colorScheme.primary, CircleShape),
                )
            }
            Spacer(Modifier.width(12.dp))
            Text(
                text = order.customer,
                modifier = Modifier.weight(1f),                  // takes what the avatar leaves
                maxLines = 1,
                overflow = TextOverflow.Ellipsis,
            )
        }
        Row(Modifier.fillMaxWidth(), horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.SpaceBetween) {
            Text("$itemCount items", style = MaterialTheme.typography.bodyMedium)
            Text(total, style = MaterialTheme.typography.titleMedium)
        }
    }
}
Result

An avatar circle with a dot at its bottom-right, the customer name ellipsised to the remaining width, and a second row with the item count at the start and the total at the end.

Shaping a lazy list — headers, entries and unique keys (runs on the JVM)

The ViewModel builds the rows and their keys in plain Kotlin; a key used twice makes `LazyColumn` throw, so overlapping pages are de-duplicated first, keeping the newer copy.

import java.time.Instant
import java.time.LocalDate
import java.time.ZoneId

data class Order(val id: String, val customer: String, val status: String, val placedAt: Instant)

sealed interface OrderListItem {
    data class Header(val day: LocalDate) : OrderListItem
    data class Entry(val order: Order) : OrderListItem
}

// The LazyColumn key: unique across the whole list (prefixed by kind), stable, and a saveable String
val OrderListItem.key: String
    get() = when (this) {
        is OrderListItem.Header -> "day-$day"
        is OrderListItem.Entry -> "order-${order.id}"
    }

val OrderListItem.contentType: String
    get() = if (this is OrderListItem.Header) "header" else "order"

fun buildItems(orders: List<Order>, zone: ZoneId): List<OrderListItem> =
    orders
        .associateBy { it.id }.values                  // a later page repeats an order: the newer copy wins
        .sortedByDescending { it.placedAt }
        .groupBy { it.placedAt.atZone(zone).toLocalDate() }   // the user's day, not UTC
        .flatMap { (day, ofDay) -> listOf(OrderListItem.Header(day)) + ofDay.map(OrderListItem::Entry) }

fun main() {
    val page1 = listOf(
        Order("1043", "Adele", "pending", Instant.parse("2026-11-16T08:15:00Z")),
        Order("1042", "Grace", "pending", Instant.parse("2026-11-15T23:40:00Z")),   // the 16th in Madrid
    )
    val page2 = listOf(
        Order("1042", "Grace", "shipped", Instant.parse("2026-11-15T23:40:00Z")),   // changed since page 1
        Order("1041", "Ada", "delivered", Instant.parse("2026-11-15T09:05:00Z")),
    )
    val items = buildItems(page1 + page2, ZoneId.of("Europe/Madrid"))
    val keys = items.map { it.key }
    require(keys.size == keys.toSet().size) { "duplicate LazyColumn keys: $keys" }
    for (item in items) {
        val status = (item as? OrderListItem.Entry)?.order?.status.orEmpty()
        println("${item.contentType.padEnd(6)} ${item.key.padEnd(16)} $status".trimEnd())
    }
}
Result
header day-2026-11-16
order  order-1043       pending
order  order-1042       shipped
header day-2026-11-15
order  order-1041       delivered

LazyColumn and LazyVerticalGrid with keys and content types

`key` keeps state and animations with the item when it moves; `contentType` lets Compose reuse a row only for a row of the same shape.

@Composable
fun OrderList(items: List<OrderListItem>, onOpen: (String) -> Unit, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
    val dayFormat = remember { DateTimeFormatter.ofLocalizedDate(FormatStyle.MEDIUM) }
    LazyColumn(
        modifier = modifier,
        contentPadding = PaddingValues(vertical = 8.dp),         // scrolls under, unlike Modifier.padding
    ) {
        items(items, key = { it.key }, contentType = { it.contentType }) { item ->
            when (item) {
                is OrderListItem.Header -> Text(
                    text = dayFormat.format(item.day),
                    style = MaterialTheme.typography.labelLarge,
                    modifier = Modifier.padding(16.dp).animateItem(),   // headers move with their rows
                )
                is OrderListItem.Entry -> OrderRow(
                    order = item.order,
                    onClick = { onOpen(item.order.id) },
                    modifier = Modifier.animateItem(),
                )
            }
        }
    }
}

@Composable
fun ProductGrid(products: List<Product>, modifier: Modifier = Modifier) {
    LazyVerticalGrid(
        columns = GridCells.Adaptive(minSize = 160.dp),           // as many 160 dp+ columns as fit
        modifier = modifier,
        contentPadding = PaddingValues(16.dp),
        horizontalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(12.dp),
        verticalArrangement = Arrangement.spacedBy(12.dp),
    ) {
        items(products, key = { it.sku }) { product -> ProductCard(product) }
    }
}
Result

Day headers and order rows that only compose what is on screen; inserting or reordering orders animates rows and headers (animateItem, foundation 1.7+). The grid shows two columns on most phones (one below about 364 dp, where 2 × 160 + 12 + 32 no longer fits) and more on wider windows.

Scaffold and the Material 3 building blocks

`Scaffold` places the app bar, FAB and snackbars, and hands you the padding that keeps content clear of them.

@OptIn(ExperimentalMaterial3Api::class)   // TopAppBar and scroll behaviours: experimental in material3 1.4
@Composable
fun OrdersScreen(
    state: OrdersUiState,
    onOpen: (String) -> Unit,
    onNewOrder: () -> Unit,
    onRefresh: () -> Unit,
) {
    val snackbarHostState = remember { SnackbarHostState() }
    val scrollBehavior = TopAppBarDefaults.enterAlwaysScrollBehavior()
    LaunchedEffect(state.errorMessage) {
        state.errorMessage?.let { snackbarHostState.showSnackbar(it) }
    }
    Scaffold(
        modifier = Modifier.nestedScroll(scrollBehavior.nestedScrollConnection),   // the bar hides on scroll
        topBar = {
            TopAppBar(
                title = { Text("Orders") },
                actions = {
                    IconButton(onClick = onRefresh) {
                        Icon(painterResource(R.drawable.refresh_24), contentDescription = "Refresh")
                    }
                },
                scrollBehavior = scrollBehavior,
            )
        },
        floatingActionButton = {
            ExtendedFloatingActionButton(
                text = { Text("New order") },
                icon = { Icon(painterResource(R.drawable.add_24), contentDescription = null) },
                onClick = onNewOrder,
            )
        },
        snackbarHost = { SnackbarHost(snackbarHostState) },
    ) { innerPadding ->
        OrderList(state.items, onOpen, Modifier.padding(innerPadding))   // or the bar covers row one
    }
}
Result

An app bar titled Orders with a refresh action that hides on scroll, a New order FAB at the bottom end, the list between them clear of the system bars, and a snackbar whenever errorMessage changes to a value.

Navigation Compose with type-safe routes and arguments

`@Serializable` routes with `NavHost` (Navigation 2.8+) — the path for existing apps and Fragment interop; Compose-only apps can start on Navigation 3 (next card).

@Serializable data object Orders

@Serializable data class OrderDetail(val orderId: String)

@Composable
fun ShopNavHost(navController: NavHostController = rememberNavController()) {
    NavHost(navController = navController, startDestination = Orders) {
        composable<Orders> {
            val viewModel: OrdersViewModel = viewModel()
            val state by viewModel.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
            OrdersScreen(
                state = state,
                onOpen = { id -> navController.navigate(OrderDetail(orderId = id)) },
                onNewOrder = { /* navigate to checkout */ },
                onRefresh = viewModel::refresh,
            )
        }
        composable<OrderDetail> { backStackEntry ->
            val route: OrderDetail = backStackEntry.toRoute()          // typed argument, no Bundle keys
            OrderDetailScreen(orderId = route.orderId, onBack = { navController.popBackStack() })
        }
    }
}

class OrderDetailViewModel(savedStateHandle: SavedStateHandle) : ViewModel() {
    private val orderId = savedStateHandle.toRoute<OrderDetail>().orderId   // the same typed route
}

// After checkout: show the new order, and make Back return to the list, not to the checkout
fun NavController.showPlacedOrder(id: String) = navigate(OrderDetail(id)) {
    popUpTo<Orders>()
    launchSingleTop = true
}
Result

The list opens first; tapping an order pushes its detail with the id as a typed argument; after checkout, Back from the new order returns straight to the list.

Setup

Navigation 3 — a back stack you own

What the docs now recommend for Compose-only apps: the back stack is a saveable list of `NavKey`s, navigating is adding or removing a key, and `NavDisplay` shows the top one.

@Serializable data object Orders : NavKey

@Serializable data class OrderDetail(val orderId: String) : NavKey

@Composable
fun ShopNavDisplay() {
    val backStack = rememberNavBackStack(Orders)        // survives rotation and process death
    NavDisplay(
        backStack = backStack,
        onBack = { backStack.removeLastOrNull() },
        entryDecorators = listOf(
            rememberSaveableStateHolderNavEntryDecorator(),   // rememberSaveable state per entry
            rememberViewModelStoreNavEntryDecorator(),        // viewModel() scoped to the entry
        ),
        entryProvider = entryProvider {
            entry<Orders> {
                val viewModel: OrdersViewModel = viewModel()
                val state by viewModel.state.collectAsStateWithLifecycle()
                OrdersScreen(
                    state = state,
                    onOpen = { id -> backStack.add(OrderDetail(orderId = id)) },   // navigate: push a key
                    onNewOrder = { /* push a Checkout key */ },
                    onRefresh = viewModel::refresh,
                )
            }
            entry<OrderDetail> { key ->
                OrderDetailScreen(orderId = key.orderId, onBack = { backStack.removeLastOrNull() })
            }
        },
    )
}

// After checkout: drop any open detail and the checkout, then show the new order above the list
fun MutableList<NavKey>.showPlacedOrder(id: String) {
    removeAll { it != Orders }
    add(OrderDetail(id))
}
Result

The list opens first; tapping an order pushes its detail; system Back pops it; the stack and each entry's saved state come back after process death, and an entry's ViewModel is cleared when its key leaves the stack.

Local state, animate*AsState, AnimatedContent, AnimatedVisibility, updateTransition

`expanded` is UI-only state the card owns with `rememberSaveable` (screen state belongs in a ViewModel — kt-compose-state), and it drives every animation here.

@Composable
fun ExpandableOrder(order: Order) {
    var expanded by rememberSaveable { mutableStateOf(false) }   // local; survives rotation and scrolling
    val transition = updateTransition(targetState = expanded, label = "order card")
    val elevation by transition.animateDp(label = "elevation") { if (it) 6.dp else 1.dp }
    val arrowRotation by transition.animateFloat(label = "arrow") { if (it) 180f else 0f }
    val colors = MaterialTheme.colorScheme
    val badgeColor by animateColorAsState(                        // a single value
        targetValue = if (order.status == OrderStatus.Delivered) colors.primaryContainer
            else colors.tertiaryContainer,
        label = "badge colour",
    )
    Card(
        onClick = { expanded = !expanded },
        elevation = CardDefaults.cardElevation(defaultElevation = elevation),
    ) {
        Row(Modifier.padding(16.dp), verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically) {
            Text(order.customer, Modifier.weight(1f))
            AnimatedContent(                                       // swapped content: the label slides in
                targetState = order.status,
                modifier = Modifier
                    .drawBehind { drawRoundRect(badgeColor, cornerRadius = CornerRadius(size.height / 2)) }
                    .padding(horizontal = 12.dp, vertical = 4.dp),
                transitionSpec = { (fadeIn() + slideInVertically { it / 2 }) togetherWith fadeOut() },
                label = "status",
            ) { status -> Text(status.name, style = MaterialTheme.typography.labelMedium) }
            Icon(
                painter = painterResource(R.drawable.expand_more_24),
                contentDescription = if (expanded) "Collapse" else "Expand",
                modifier = Modifier.graphicsLayer { rotationZ = arrowRotation },
            )
        }
        AnimatedVisibility(visible = expanded) {           // in a Column: fades and expands vertically
            OrderLineItems(order, Modifier.padding(start = 16.dp, end = 16.dp, bottom = 16.dp))
        }
    }
}
Result

A status change cross-fades the badge colour and slides the new label in; a tap raises the card, turns the arrow and expands the line items, all from one expanded flag kept across rotation.

Keeping recomposition cheap

Cache expensive work with `remember(keys)`, dampen fast state with `derivedStateOf`, and read fast-changing values in lambda modifiers so only layout or draw re-runs.

@Composable
fun OrderHistory(orders: List<Order>, onOpen: (String) -> Unit) {
    val listState = rememberLazyListState()
    val scope = rememberCoroutineScope()
    val newestFirst = remember(orders) { orders.sortedByDescending { it.placedAt } }   // when orders change
    val showJumpToTop by remember {
        derivedStateOf { listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 3 }   // recompose when this flips, not per pixel
    }
    Box {
        Column {
            CollapsingTitle(fade = {                         // a lambda: read later, in the draw phase
                if (listState.firstVisibleItemIndex > 0) 1f else listState.firstVisibleItemScrollOffset / 300f
            })
            LazyColumn(state = listState) {
                items(newestFirst, key = { it.id }) { order ->
                    OrderRow(order, onClick = { onOpen(order.id) })
                }
            }
        }
        AnimatedVisibility(showJumpToTop, Modifier.align(Alignment.BottomEnd).padding(16.dp)) {
            SmallFloatingActionButton(onClick = { scope.launch { listState.animateScrollToItem(0) } }) {
                Icon(painterResource(R.drawable.arrow_upward_24), contentDescription = "Back to top")
            }
        }
    }
}

@Composable
private fun CollapsingTitle(fade: () -> Float) {
    Text(
        text = "Order history",
        style = MaterialTheme.typography.headlineSmall,
        modifier = Modifier
            .padding(16.dp)
            .graphicsLayer { alpha = 1f - fade().coerceIn(0f, 1f) },   // no recomposition per frame
    )
}
Result

Scrolling fades the title and shows a back-to-top button past the fourth row without recomposing the screen on every scroll frame; the sort by placedAt runs only when orders changes.

What recomposes, and how to keep it cheap

The rules worth saying out loud in a review or an interview; the key and `derivedStateOf` rules are on kt-compose-state.

  • Strong skipping is on by default since Kotlin 2.0.20: stable parameters are compared with equals, unstable ones (List, classes from modules without the Compose compiler) with ===. Pass the same instance when nothing changed; never build a new list in the composable body.
  • @Immutable on a class that holds a large list makes every skip check an element-by-element equals — it can cost more than the recomposition it saves.
  • list.indexOf(item) inside items { } scans the whole list for every composed row; use itemsIndexed. And give mixed rows a contentType.
  • State that changes every frame (scroll, animation) belongs in lambda modifiers — offset { }, graphicsLayer { }, drawBehind { } — so Compose skips composition and goes straight to layout or draw.
  • Writing to state after reading it in the same composition (a backwards write) schedules another recomposition — forever. Write state only from events and effects.
  • Ship a Baseline Profile (the androidx.baselineprofile Gradle plugin, a Macrobenchmark BaselineProfileRule, androidx.profileinstaller): ART pre-compiles startup and scroll paths, about 30% faster from the first launch.
  • Judging performance on a debug build: Compose is interpreted and unminified there. Measure a release build with R8 enabled.
  • Layout Inspector's recomposition counts and the Compose compiler reports show which composables do not skip and which classes are inferred unstable.

Activity and Fragment lifecycle in one table

Where each kind of work belongs; the `Lifecycle.State` column is what `repeatOnLifecycle` and `collectAsStateWithLifecycle` key on.

CallbackCalled onState afterDo here
onCreateActivity, FragmentCREATEDread arguments and saved state, get the ViewModel (by viewModels()); an Activity calls setContentView
onCreateViewFragmentview: INITIALIZEDbuild or inflate the view tree and return it — nothing else
onViewCreatedFragmentview: INITIALIZED (→ CREATED at onViewStateRestored)wire listeners and adapters, start collecting with viewLifecycleOwner
onStartActivity, FragmentSTARTEDvisible: repeatOnLifecycle(STARTED) blocks start here
onResumeActivity, FragmentRESUMEDin front and interactive: camera, sensors, exclusive resources
onPauseActivity, Fragmentback to STARTEDlosing focus but often still visible (multi-window): release exclusive resources
onStopActivity, Fragmentback to CREATEDinvisible: STARTED collectors are cancelled; persist drafts
onSaveInstanceStateActivity, Fragment—small UI state into the Bundle (it must survive process death)
onDestroyViewFragmentview: DESTROYEDdrop the binding and every view reference; the fragment itself may live on in the back stack
onDestroyActivity, FragmentDESTROYEDfinishing or a configuration change (isChangingConfigurations); the ViewModel survives the latter

Building the view tree in code

Create views with a `Context`, give each its `LayoutParams` from the parent's type, add them, and set listeners — no XML.

class OrdersActivity : AppCompatActivity() {
    private val viewModel: OrdersViewModel by viewModels()
    private val Int.dp: Int get() = (this * resources.displayMetrics.density).roundToInt()

    override fun onCreate(savedInstanceState: Bundle?) {
        super.onCreate(savedInstanceState)
        enableEdgeToEdge()                          // enforced from target SDK 35: we handle the insets below
        val root = LinearLayout(this).apply { orientation = LinearLayout.VERTICAL }
        val search = EditText(this).apply {
            id = R.id.orders_search                 // a stable id: the typed text survives rotation
            hint = "Search orders"
            doAfterTextChanged { text -> viewModel.onQueryChange(text?.toString().orEmpty()) }
        }
        val list = RecyclerView(this).apply {
            layoutManager = LinearLayoutManager(context)
            adapter = OrdersAdapter(onOpen = ::openOrder)
        }
        val refresh = MaterialButton(this).apply {
            text = "Refresh"
            setOnClickListener { viewModel.refresh() }
        }
        root.addView(search, LinearLayout.LayoutParams(MATCH_PARENT, WRAP_CONTENT))
        root.addView(list, LinearLayout.LayoutParams(MATCH_PARENT, 0, 1f))    // weight 1: what is left
        val end = LinearLayout.LayoutParams(WRAP_CONTENT, WRAP_CONTENT).apply { gravity = Gravity.END }
        root.addView(refresh, end)
        ViewCompat.setOnApplyWindowInsetsListener(root) { view, insets ->
            val types = WindowInsetsCompat.Type.systemBars() or WindowInsetsCompat.Type.displayCutout() or
                WindowInsetsCompat.Type.ime()            // the keyboard too: the larger bottom wins
            val bars = insets.getInsets(types)
            view.updatePadding(                     // clear of the bars, the cutout and the keyboard
                left = bars.left + 16.dp,
                top = bars.top + 16.dp,
                right = bars.right + 16.dp,
                bottom = bars.bottom,
            )
            insets
        }
        setContentView(root)
    }

    private fun openOrder(id: String) = startActivity(OrderDetailActivity.intent(this, id))
}
Result

A search field below the status bar, a scrolling order list that fills the remaining height, and a Refresh button at the bottom end above the navigation bar; while the keyboard is open the list and button sit above it; typing filters through the ViewModel, and the text is restored after rotation.

  2. res/values/ids.xml with <item name="orders_search" type="id"/>; OrdersAdapter from the RecyclerView card; an OrderDetailActivity whose companion has intent(context, orderId)
  3. android:windowSoftInputMode="adjustResize" on the activity in the manifest, so the window receives IME insets
