The plain-JVM catalog: ResourceBundle + MessageFormat

`ChoiceFormat` ranges (`0#`, `1#`, `1<`) are written per language by the translator — fine for English and Spanish, while Russian or Arabic need CLDR plural categories (ICU, or Android quantity strings, which is also what Android uses instead of this JVM-only demo).

import java.net.URLClassLoader
import java.nio.file.Files
import java.text.MessageFormat
import java.util.Locale
import java.util.ResourceBundle

// What the build ships: one UTF-8 .properties file per locale, each holding only what differs.
// In a MessageFormat pattern an apostrophe is written '' ("You''ve"); a trailing \ continues the line.
val catalogs = mapOf(
    "Messages.properties" to """
        greeting=Hello, {0}!
        cart=You''ve got {1,choice,0#no items|1#one item|1<{1,number,integer} items} in your cart, {0}.
    """.trimIndent(),
    "Messages_es.properties" to """
        greeting=¡Hola, {0}!
        cart={0}, {1,choice,0#no tienes artículos|1#tienes un artículo|\
            1<tienes {1,number,integer} artículos} en el carrito.
    """.trimIndent(),
    "Messages_es_MX.properties" to "greeting=¡Qué onda, {0}!",
)

fun main() {
    val dir = Files.createTempDirectory("i18n")
    catalogs.forEach { (name, text) -> Files.writeString(dir.resolve(name), text) }
    // Without this Control a missing locale falls back to the JVM's default locale first: machine-dependent.
    val control = ResourceBundle.Control.getNoFallbackControl(ResourceBundle.Control.FORMAT_PROPERTIES)
    URLClassLoader(arrayOf(dir.toUri().toURL())).use { loader ->
        for (tag in listOf("en-US", "es-ES", "es-MX", "fr-FR")) {
            val locale = Locale.forLanguageTag(tag)
            val bundle = ResourceBundle.getBundle("Messages", locale, loader, control)
            fun text(key: String, vararg args: Any): String =
                MessageFormat(bundle.getString(key), locale).format(args)
            println("$tag  ${text("greeting", "Ana")}")
            // fr-FR falls back to the root (English) text but still groups digits the French way,
            // with U+202F NARROW NO-BREAK SPACE on JDK 21; pass bundle.locale to match the text instead.
            for (count in listOf(0, 1, 2500)) println("$tag  ${text("cart", "Ana", count)}")
        }
    }
    dir.toFile().deleteRecursively()
}
Result
en-US  Hello, Ana!
en-US  You've got no items in your cart, Ana.
en-US  You've got one item in your cart, Ana.
en-US  You've got 2,500 items in your cart, Ana.
es-ES  ¡Hola, Ana!
es-ES  Ana, no tienes artículos en el carrito.
es-ES  Ana, tienes un artículo en el carrito.
es-ES  Ana, tienes 2.500 artículos en el carrito.
es-MX  ¡Qué onda, Ana!
es-MX  Ana, no tienes artículos en el carrito.
es-MX  Ana, tienes un artículo en el carrito.
es-MX  Ana, tienes 2,500 artículos en el carrito.
fr-FR  Hello, Ana!
fr-FR  You've got no items in your cart, Ana.
fr-FR  You've got one item in your cart, Ana.
fr-FR  You've got 2 500 items in your cart, Ana.

  2. Save as main.kt; run kotlinc main.kt -include-runtime -d main.jar && java -jar main.jar — it writes its catalogs to a temp directory and deletes them

Dates and times with a pinned Locale and ZoneId

Keep an `Instant` and render it in the user's zone with a localized style or skeleton, never a hard-coded `"MM/dd/yyyy"` — on Android, where `ofLocalizedPattern` does not exist, `DateFormat.getBestDateTimePattern(locale, "yMMMEd")` plays the skeleton's role.

import java.time.Instant
import java.time.ZoneId
import java.time.format.DateTimeFormatter
import java.time.format.FormatStyle
import java.util.Locale

fun main() {
    val placedAt = Instant.parse("2026-11-16T18:30:00Z")          // store and send instants in UTC
    val customers = listOf(
        "en-US" to "America/New_York",
        "en-GB" to "Europe/London",
        "de-DE" to "Europe/Berlin",
        "ja-JP" to "Asia/Tokyo",
    )
    for ((tag, zone) in customers) {
        val locale = Locale.forLanguageTag(tag)
        val local = placedAt.atZone(ZoneId.of(zone))               // render in the user's zone
        val date = DateTimeFormatter.ofLocalizedDate(FormatStyle.MEDIUM).withLocale(locale)
        // A skeleton names the fields; the locale decides their order and punctuation (JDK 19+).
        val skeleton = DateTimeFormatter.ofLocalizedPattern("yMMMEd").withLocale(locale)
        val time = DateTimeFormatter.ofLocalizedTime(FormatStyle.SHORT).withLocale(locale)
        println("$tag  ${local.format(date)} | ${local.format(skeleton)} | ${local.format(time)}")
    }
    // Since JDK 20 (CLDR 42) en-US puts U+202F NARROW NO-BREAK SPACE before "PM": never match it with " ".
    val usTime = placedAt.atZone(ZoneId.of("America/New_York"))
        .format(DateTimeFormatter.ofLocalizedTime(FormatStyle.SHORT).withLocale(Locale.US))
    println("narrow no-break space: ${'\u202F' in usTime}")
}
Result
en-US  Nov 16, 2026 | Mon, Nov 16, 2026 | 1:30 PM
en-GB  16 Nov 2026 | Mon, 16 Nov 2026 | 18:30
de-DE  16.11.2026 | Mo., 16. Nov. 2026 | 19:30
ja-JP  2026/11/17 | 2026年11月17日(火) | 3:30
narrow no-break space: true
Setup

  2. Save as main.kt; run kotlinc main.kt -include-runtime -d main.jar && java -jar main.jar — it writes its catalogs to a temp directory and deletes them

Numbers, money, percentages — and sorting by locale

Set the currency from the amount and the format from the reader (the spaces before `€`, `%` and `Mio.` in German are NO-BREAK SPACEs), and on Android, which lacks `getCompactNumberInstance`, use `android.icu.text.CompactDecimalFormat`.

import java.text.Collator
import java.text.NumberFormat
import java.text.ParsePosition
import java.util.Currency
import java.util.Locale

fun parseAmount(text: String, locale: Locale): Number? {
    val position = ParsePosition(0)
    // Grouping off for typed input: an English-style "12.34" must not become 1234, a factor of 100.
    val format = NumberFormat.getNumberInstance(locale).apply { isGroupingUsed = false }
    val number = format.parse(text, position)
    return number?.takeIf { position.index == text.length }
}

fun main() {
    val total = 1234567.891
    val euro = Currency.getInstance("EUR")                         // the currency is data, not the locale's
    for (tag in listOf("en-US", "de-DE", "ja-JP")) {
        val locale = Locale.forLanguageTag(tag)
        val number = NumberFormat.getNumberInstance(locale).apply { maximumFractionDigits = 2 }
        val money = NumberFormat.getCurrencyInstance(locale).apply {
            // Setting the currency does NOT update the fraction digits: ja-JP (yen) would print €1,234,568.
            currency = euro
            maximumFractionDigits = euro.defaultFractionDigits
        }
        val percent = NumberFormat.getPercentInstance(locale).apply { minimumFractionDigits = 1 }
        val compact = NumberFormat.getCompactNumberInstance(locale, NumberFormat.Style.SHORT)
        val parts = listOf(
            number.format(total),
            money.format(total),
            percent.format(0.075),
            compact.format(1_250_000),
        )
        println("$tag  " + parts.joinToString(" | "))
    }
    // Parsing is per locale too, and parse() stops at the first character it cannot read: demand it all.
    println(listOf("12.34", "1.2.3", "12,5", "1.234,5", "1234,5").map { parseAmount(it, Locale.GERMANY) })

    val cities = listOf("Zürich", "Århus", "Oslo", "Ängelholm", "Zagreb")
    println(cities.sortedWith(Collator.getInstance(Locale.GERMAN)))
    println(cities.sortedWith(Collator.getInstance(Locale.forLanguageTag("sv-SE"))))
}
Result
en-US  1,234,567.89 | €1,234,567.89 | 7.5% | 1M
de-DE  1.234.567,89 | 1.234.567,89 € | 7,5 % | 1 Mio.
ja-JP  1,234,567.89 | €1,234,567.89 | 7.5% | 125万
[null, null, 12.5, null, 1234.5]
[Ängelholm, Århus, Oslo, Zagreb, Zürich]
[Oslo, Zagreb, Zürich, Århus, Ängelholm]

Relative time, units and lists: android.icu.text

The JDK has no relative-time or unit formatter (and `java.text.ListFormat` only from JDK 22), while Android ships ICU's (API 24+, `ListFormatter` 26+) with every locale's grammar.

import android.icu.text.ListFormatter
import android.icu.text.MeasureFormat
import android.icu.text.RelativeDateTimeFormatter
import android.icu.text.RelativeDateTimeFormatter.Direction
import android.icu.text.RelativeDateTimeFormatter.RelativeUnit
import android.icu.util.Measure
import android.icu.util.MeasureUnit
import java.util.Locale

// "in 3 days" / "dans 3 jours" / "через 3 дня" — the plural form comes from the locale
fun deliveryEta(daysAway: Int, locale: Locale): String =
    RelativeDateTimeFormatter.getInstance(locale)
        .format(daysAway.toDouble(), Direction.NEXT, RelativeUnit.DAYS)

// "2.5 kg" / "2,5 kg"
fun parcelWeight(kilograms: Double, locale: Locale): String =
    MeasureFormat.getInstance(locale, MeasureFormat.FormatWidth.SHORT)
        .format(Measure(kilograms, MeasureUnit.KILOGRAM))

// "Ana, Bo, and Chen" / "Ana, Bo y Chen"
fun recipients(names: List<String>, locale: Locale): String =
    ListFormatter.getInstance(locale).format(names)
Result

For Locale.US the three calls give "in 3 days", "2.5 kg" and "Ana, Bo, and Chen"; for Spanish, "dentro de 3 días", "2,5 kg" and "Ana, Bo y Chen".

Setup
  1. An Android project with minSdk 26 or later (or guard ListFormatter with Build.VERSION.SDK_INT >= 26)
  2. Call the functions from a composable or a ViewModel with the current locale from LocalConfiguration.current.locales[0]

Per-app language preferences

`AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales` syncs with the Android 13+ system setting and works back to older versions; let AGP generate the `LocaleConfig`.

import androidx.appcompat.app.AppCompatDelegate
import androidx.core.os.LocaleListCompat

@Composable
fun LanguagePicker(supported: List<String> = listOf("en", "es", "sr-Latn")) {
    // null is "follow the system language": an empty locale list.
    val current = AppCompatDelegate.getApplicationLocales().get(0)?.toLanguageTag()
    val choices: List<String?> = listOf(null) + supported
    Column(Modifier.selectableGroup()) {                          // TalkBack announces one radio group
        choices.forEach { tag ->
            val label = if (tag == null) {
                stringResource(R.string.use_system_language)
            } else {
                Locale.forLanguageTag(tag).let { it.getDisplayName(it) }   // each name in its own language
            }
            ListItem(
                headlineContent = { Text(label) },
                leadingContent = { RadioButton(selected = tag == current, onClick = null) },
                modifier = Modifier.selectable(selected = tag == current, role = Role.RadioButton) {
                    val locales = tag?.let { LocaleListCompat.forLanguageTags(it) }
                        ?: LocaleListCompat.getEmptyLocaleList()
                    // Main thread: recreates the activity and resolves every stringResource again.
                    AppCompatDelegate.setApplicationLocales(locales)
                },
            )
        }
    }
}

// Android 13+ without AppCompat, e.g. in a settings screen:
// context.getSystemService(LocaleManager::class.java).applicationLocales = LocaleList.forLanguageTags("es")
Result

TalkBack reads the rows as one radio group; picking "español" recreates the activity in Spanish and shows the same choice under Settings › Apps › Language, and "Use system language" is selected whenever no app language is set.

Setup
  1. An Android project with androidx.appcompat:appcompat 1.6 or later; the activity hosting Compose must extend AppCompatActivity
  2. In build.gradle.kts: android { androidResources { generateLocaleConfig = true } } (AGP 8.1+), and res/resources.properties with unqualifiedResLocale=en-US
  3. For Android 12 and lower, declare <service android:name="androidx.appcompat.app.AppLocalesMetadataHolderService" android:enabled="false" android:exported="false"> with <meta-data android:name="autoStoreLocales" android:value="true" /> in the manifest

Right-to-left, pseudolocales and testing a locale

Use start/end and auto-mirrored icons, wrap embedded opposite-direction text, then look at `ar-XB` and `en-XA` before any translation exists.

import androidx.compose.ui.test.junit4.v2.createComposeRule

@Composable
fun OrderTopBar(order: Order, onBack: () -> Unit) {
    Row(Modifier.padding(start = 4.dp, end = 16.dp), verticalAlignment = Alignment.CenterVertically) {
        IconButton(onClick = onBack) {
            // AutoMirrored flips in RTL; Icons.Filled.ArrowBack is deprecated for that reason.
            Icon(Icons.AutoMirrored.Filled.ArrowBack, contentDescription = stringResource(R.string.back))
        }
        // An LTR order code inside Arabic or Hebrew text keeps its order once wrapped; pass the
        // composition's direction, because getInstance() alone reads Locale.getDefault().
        val rtl = LocalLayoutDirection.current == LayoutDirection.Rtl
        val code = BidiFormatter.getInstance(rtl).unicodeWrap(order.code)
        Text(stringResource(R.string.order_title, code), Modifier.weight(1f))
    }
}

@Preview(name = "Default")
@Preview(name = "Arabic", locale = "ar")                       // the mirrored layout, side by side
@Composable
private fun OrderTopBarPreview() = OrderTopBar(Order(code = "ORD-1042"), onBack = {})

class OrderTopBarRtlTest {
    @get:Rule val composeRule = createComposeRule()

    @Test
    fun backButtonSitsOnTheRightInRtl() {
        composeRule.setContent {
            CompositionLocalProvider(LocalLayoutDirection provides LayoutDirection.Rtl) {
                OrderTopBar(Order(code = "ORD-1042"), onBack = {})
            }
        }
        val back = composeRule.onNodeWithContentDescription("Back").fetchSemanticsNode().boundsInRoot
        val title = composeRule.onNodeWithText("ORD-1042", substring = true).fetchSemanticsNode().boundsInRoot
        assertTrue(back.left > title.left)
    }
}
Result

The preview pane shows the bar mirrored for Arabic (on a device, AR (XB) mirrors it the same way and English (XA) shows stretched, bracketed text); the test passes because the back button is laid out to the right of the title in RTL.

Setup
  1. An Android project with Compose, androidx.compose.ui:ui-test-junit4 1.11+ (BOM 2026.04.01) for the v2 test rule, and android:supportsRtl="true" on the <application>
  2. Enable pseudolocales in debug builds: android { buildTypes.getByName("debug") { isPseudoLocalesEnabled = true } }; on the device turn on Developer options and reboot, then pick English (XA) or AR (XB) in Settings › System › Languages

Rules and pitfalls

The bugs translators and RTL users report first.

  • Concatenating getString(R.string.hello) + " " + name: the translator cannot reorder it and pseudolocales show it as two bracketed pieces. One string, positional %1$s.
  • Hard-coded formats ("MM/dd/yyyy", "$" + price, "%.2f"): wrong order, separator and symbol for most users. Use localized styles, skeletons and NumberFormat.
  • String.format("%.2f", x) without a Locale uses the device's: 1,50 in Germany breaks CSV, URLs and SQL. Locale.ROOT for machine text, the user's locale for display.
  • "title".uppercase() is locale-invariant — wrong for a Turkish heading (TİTLE); Java's String.toUpperCase() (an error in Kotlin 2.1+, still there in Java code) uses the default locale — wrong for keys on a Turkish device. Choose on purpose.
  • Testing count == 1 for the singular: Russian, Polish, Arabic and Welsh need more forms. Always go through <plurals> or PluralRules.
  • Pin Locale and ZoneId in every test; a formatter that reads the defaults passes on your laptop and fails on CI.
  • Keep the default values/strings.xml complete — a key missing there crashes with Resources.NotFoundException in a locale nobody tested.
  • Locale.getDefault() is the system language; with per-app languages the app's own is LocalConfiguration.current.locales[0] (Compose) or resources.configuration.locales[0].
  • Give text room: German and Finnish run 30–40% longer, and en-XA shows where a fixed width or maxLines = 1 will clip.

UI & End-to-End Testing

Compose UI tests that render, act and assert through semantics, Espresso for Views, UI Automator across apps and system UI, waiting without sleeps, fakes behind Hilt, robots, JVM versus device — and a suite that does not flake.

  • Jetpack Compose
  • androidx.compose.ui:ui-test-junit4
  • Espresso
  • UI Automator

The tools, by what they drive

Most UI tests should be Compose or Espresso tests on one screen; keep a few UI Automator or Maestro journeys for what crosses the app's boundary.

A Compose UI test that renders, interacts and asserts

Set the content with a fake behind the ViewModel, act like a user, assert on text, descriptions and roles — never on internal state.

import androidx.compose.ui.test.junit4.v2.createComposeRule
import java.util.Currency
import java.util.Locale

class CartScreenTest {
    @get:Rule val composeRule = createComposeRule()

    @Test
    fun removingAnItemUpdatesTheTotal() {
        val cart = FakeCartRepository(listOf(CartItem("Running shoes", 8990), CartItem("Socks", 990)))
        // The test pins the formatter, so the expected text never depends on the device's locale.
        val money = MoneyFormatter(Locale.US, Currency.getInstance("EUR"))
        composeRule.setContent { AppTheme { CartScreen(CartViewModel(cart, money)) } }

        composeRule.onNodeWithText("Total: ${money.format(9980)}").assertIsDisplayed()

        composeRule.onNode(hasContentDescription("Remove Socks") and hasClickAction())
            .performClick()

        composeRule.onNodeWithText("Socks").assertDoesNotExist()
        composeRule.onNodeWithTag("cart-total").assertTextEquals("Total: ${money.format(8990)}")
        composeRule.onNode(hasRole(Role.Button) and hasText("Checkout")).assertIsEnabled()
    }
}

// There is no built-in role matcher; this is the documented way to match a property.
fun hasRole(role: Role): SemanticsMatcher = SemanticsMatcher.expectValue(SemanticsProperties.Role, role)
Result

The test passes once the row is removed and the total recomputed; a missing content description or a renamed button fails it with the semantics tree printed.

Setup
  1. androidTestImplementation("androidx.compose.ui:ui-test-junit4") and debugImplementation("androidx.compose.ui:ui-test-manifest") with Compose BOM 2026.04.01 or later (ui-test 1.11+, which has the junit4.v2 rules)
  2. Put the class under src/androidTest/kotlin and run ./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest — or under src/test/kotlin with Robolectric and ./gradlew testDebugUnitTest

Excerpt, not compiled or run here: it needs an Android test host (an instrumented test on a device or emulator, or Robolectric on the JVM).

Find nodes by semantics and test tags, never by layout

Match what a user perceives — text, content description, role, state; fall back to `Modifier.testTag` only where nothing perceivable identifies the node.

By position
// The third child of the root: breaks when a banner is added.
composeRule.onRoot().onChildren()[2].onChildAt(0).performClick()

// Which "Remove"? Index order is layout order, and lists are lazy.
composeRule.onAllNodesWithText("Remove")[1].performClick()

// Icons have no text: this never matches, so the test author adds a sleep and gives up.
composeRule.onNodeWithText("Remove Socks").assertExists()
Thread.sleep(2_000)
By meaning
// Perceivable first: the description TalkBack reads, plus "it is clickable".
composeRule.onNode(hasContentDescription("Remove Socks") and hasClickAction()).performClick()

// Lazy lists: scroll the container to the node instead of indexing children.
composeRule.onNodeWithTag("cart-list").performScrollToNode(hasText("Gift card"))

// A test tag where nothing a user perceives identifies the node.
composeRule.onNodeWithTag("cart-total").assertTextContains("€89.90", substring = true)

// Debug a failing finder by printing the tree, not by guessing.
composeRule.onRoot(useUnmergedTree = true).printToLog("CartScreenTest")
Result

The selectors on the right survive layout changes and double as an accessibility check; the ones on the left break on the next redesign.

  2. Put the class under src/androidTest/kotlin and run ./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest — or under src/test/kotlin with Robolectric and ./gradlew testDebugUnitTest

Synchronise without sleeps: the test clock, waitUntil, idling resources

Compose waits for recomposition and animations itself; for work it cannot see, wait on a condition or register an idling resource — and drive time with `mainClock`.

@Test
fun undoBannerHidesAfterFourSeconds() {
    composeRule.mainClock.autoAdvance = false              // the test owns Compose time
    composeRule.setContent { OrderRow(order, onArchive = {}) }
    composeRule.onNodeWithContentDescription("Archive ORD-1042").performClick()

    composeRule.mainClock.advanceTimeBy(3_900)            // the banner's LaunchedEffect { delay(4_000) }
    composeRule.onNodeWithText("Undo").assertIsDisplayed()
    composeRule.mainClock.advanceTimeBy(200)
    composeRule.onNodeWithText("Undo").assertDoesNotExist()
}

@Test
fun ordersAppearAfterTheRepositoryLoads() {
    composeRule.setContent { OrdersScreen(viewModel) }
    // Work on another dispatcher is invisible to Compose: wait for its visible result (wall-clock timeout).
    composeRule.waitUntil(timeoutMillis = 5_000) {
        composeRule.onAllNodesWithText("ORD-1042", substring = true).fetchSemanticsNodes().isNotEmpty()
    }
}

// Or tell the rule when your own background work is busy, once, in @Before:
class RepositoryIdling(private val repository: FakeOrderRepository) : IdlingResource {
    // inFlightRequests is an AtomicInteger: the fake changes it on another dispatcher.
    override val isIdleNow: Boolean get() = repository.inFlightRequests.get() == 0
}
// composeRule.registerIdlingResource(RepositoryIdling(repository))
// Views: IdlingRegistry.getInstance().register(countingIdlingResource) for Espresso
Result

Both tests finish in well under a second of real time: the first steps the virtual clock across the 4 s delay, the second returns as soon as the order is on screen.

  2. Put the class under src/androidTest/kotlin and run ./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest — or under src/test/kotlin with Robolectric and ./gradlew testDebugUnitTest

Espresso for Views, with RecyclerView actions

`onView` cannot reach an off-screen row; `RecyclerViewActions` scrolls to the matching item and acts on it.

@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
class OrderHistoryViewsTest {
    @get:Rule val activityRule = ActivityScenarioRule(OrderHistoryActivity::class.java)

    @Test
    fun openingAnOrderBelowTheFoldShowsItsDetails() {
        onView(withId(R.id.order_list)).perform(
            RecyclerViewActions.actionOnItem<OrderAdapter.OrderViewHolder>(
                hasDescendant(withText("ORD-1042")), click(),        // scrolls to the row first
            ),
        )
        onView(withId(R.id.order_title)).check(matches(withText("ORD-1042")))
        onView(withContentDescription(R.string.track_parcel)).check(matches(isDisplayed()))

        pressBack()
        onView(withId(R.id.order_list)).check(matches(isDisplayed()))
    }

    @Test
    fun swipingTheFirstRowArchivesIt() {
        onView(withId(R.id.order_list)).perform(
            RecyclerViewActions.actionOnItemAtPosition<OrderAdapter.OrderViewHolder>(0, swipeLeft()),
        )
        onView(withText("ORD-1043")).check(doesNotExist())
    }
}
Result

Espresso waits for the main thread's message queue and every registered idling resource before each action, so the scroll, click and back navigation run in order with no sleeps.

Setup
  1. androidTestImplementation("androidx.test.espresso:espresso-core"), espresso-contrib (for RecyclerViewActions) and androidx.test.ext:junit
  2. Run with ./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest

An end-to-end journey across the system UI with UI Automator

UI Automator sees every window — the launcher, the notification shade, permission dialogs — so the journey can leave the app and come back.

@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
class ShippingNotificationJourneyTest {
    private val app = "com.example.shop"

    @Test
    fun tappingTheShippedNotificationOpensTheOrder() = uiAutomator {
        watchFor(PermissionDialog) { clickAllow() }                      // POST_NOTIFICATIONS, if asked
        startApp(app)
        onElement { viewIdResourceName == "orders-list" }                  // a Compose testTag

        // The code path the push handler calls in production, triggered from the test.
        val context = InstrumentationRegistry.getInstrumentation().targetContext
        ShippingNotifier(context).notifyShipped(orderId = "ORD-1042")

        pressHome()                                                        // leave the app
        device.openNotification()                                          // the system shade
        onElement(timeoutMs = 15_000) { textAsString()?.contains("ORD-1042 has shipped") == true }.click()

        waitForAppToBeVisible(app)
        onElement { textAsString() == "Shipped" }                          // the order screen, deep-linked
    }
}
Result

The test leaves the app, opens the notification shade, taps the real notification and lands on the order screen showing "Shipped"; each onElement polls up to its timeout instead of sleeping.

Setup
  1. androidTestImplementation("androidx.test.uiautomator:uiautomator:2.4.1") and androidx.test.ext:junit
  2. In the app, once near the root: Modifier.semantics { testTagsAsResourceId = true } so test tags are visible as resource ids
  3. Run with ./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest on an API 33+ device or emulator

Isolate network and state with a fake behind Hilt

Replace the data layer once for every instrumented test with `@TestInstallIn`; the screen, ViewModel and navigation stay real, and the fake decides what the network does.

import androidx.compose.ui.test.junit4.v2.createAndroidComposeRule

@Module
@TestInstallIn(components = [SingletonComponent::class], replaces = [OrdersDataModule::class])
abstract class FakeOrdersModule {
    @Binds abstract fun bindRepository(fake: FakeOrderRepository): OrderRepository
}

@Singleton
class FakeOrderRepository @Inject constructor() : OrderRepository {
    val orders = MutableStateFlow(listOf(Order(code = "ORD-1042", status = OrderStatus.Shipped)))
    @Volatile var failNextRefresh = false              // set on the test thread, read on the repository's

    override fun observeOrders(): Flow<List<Order>> = orders
    override suspend fun refresh() {
        if (failNextRefresh) {
            failNextRefresh = false
            throw IOException("offline")
        }
    }
}

@HiltAndroidTest
class OrdersOfflineTest {
    @get:Rule(order = 0) val hiltRule = HiltAndroidRule(this)
    @get:Rule(order = 1) val composeRule = createAndroidComposeRule<MainActivity>()
    @Inject lateinit var repository: FakeOrderRepository

    @Before fun inject() = hiltRule.inject()

    @Test
    fun failedRefreshKeepsCachedOrdersAndOffersRetry() {
        repository.failNextRefresh = true
        composeRule.onNodeWithContentDescription("Refresh orders").performClick()
        composeRule.onNodeWithText("ORD-1042", substring = true).assertIsDisplayed()
        composeRule.onNodeWithText("Retry").assertIsDisplayed()
    }
}
Result

The real screen shows the cached order and a Retry button after the fake throws; no request leaves the device, and each test starts from cleared app data.

Setup
  1. androidTestImplementation("com.google.dagger:hilt-android-testing:2.57.1") and kspAndroidTest("com.google.dagger:hilt-android-compiler:2.57.1")
  2. A runner returning HiltTestApplication from newApplication, set as testInstrumentationRunner in defaultConfig
  3. Fresh app state per test: testInstrumentationRunnerArguments["clearPackageData"] = "true" with testOptions { execution = "ANDROIDX_TEST_ORCHESTRATOR" } and androidTestUtil("androidx.test:orchestrator:1.6.1")

The robot (screen-object) pattern

One robot per screen owns its selectors; tests read as the user's steps, and a redesign is fixed in one file.

import androidx.compose.ui.test.junit4.v2.createComposeRule

class CartRobot(private val rule: ComposeContentTestRule) {
    fun assertTotal(total: String) = apply {
        rule.onNodeWithTag("cart-total").assertTextEquals("Total: $total")
    }
    fun removeItem(name: String) = apply {
        rule.onNode(hasContentDescription("Remove $name") and hasClickAction()).performClick()
    }
    fun checkout(): CheckoutRobot {
        rule.onNode(hasText("Checkout") and hasClickAction()).performClick()
        return CheckoutRobot(rule)
    }
}

class CheckoutRobot(private val rule: ComposeContentTestRule) {
    fun assertShown() = apply { rule.onNode(hasText("Payment") and isHeading()).assertIsDisplayed() }
}

fun ComposeContentTestRule.cart(steps: CartRobot.() -> Unit): CartRobot = CartRobot(this).apply(steps)

class CheckoutJourneyTest {
    @get:Rule val composeRule = createComposeRule()

    @Test
    fun removeSocksThenCheckOut() {
        composeRule.setContent { ShopApp(FakeAppGraph(locale = Locale.US)) }   // fakes and a pinned locale
        composeRule.cart {
            assertTotal("€99.80")
            removeItem("Socks")
            assertTotal("€89.90")
        }.checkout().assertShown()
    }
}
Result

The test reads as the journey; when the total moves to a new component only CartRobot.assertTotal changes.

  2. Put the class under src/androidTest/kotlin and run ./gradlew connectedDebugAndroidTest — or under src/test/kotlin with Robolectric and ./gradlew testDebugUnitTest

Where tests run: the JVM with Robolectric, or a managed device

Run the same Compose tests on the JVM on every commit and on emulators that AGP provisions in CI; keep device-only checks (accessibility checks, UI Automator) on the device run.

// app/build.gradle.kts
android {
    testOptions {
        unitTests.isIncludeAndroidResources = true          // Robolectric needs the merged resources
        animationsDisabled = true                           // instrumented runs: no animation timing
        managedDevices {
            localDevices {
                create("pixel6api34") {
                    device = "Pixel 6"
                    apiLevel = 34
                    systemImageSource = "aosp"              // "google" if the app needs Play services
                }
            }
        }
    }
}
dependencies {
    testImplementation("org.robolectric:robolectric:4.16.1")      // 4.16+ runs SDK 36, on JDK 21
    testImplementation("androidx.compose.ui:ui-test-junit4")
    debugImplementation("androidx.compose.ui:ui-test-manifest")
}

// src/test/kotlin — the same test body, on the JVM (createComposeRule from ...test.junit4.v2)
@RunWith(AndroidJUnit4::class)
@Config(qualifiers = "w411dp-h891dp-xxhdpi")                // a pinned screen, not the default one
class CartScreenRobolectricTest {
    @get:Rule val composeRule = createComposeRule()
    // … the tests from CartScreenTest
}

// ./gradlew testDebugUnitTest              JVM + Robolectric: seconds, every commit
// ./gradlew pixel6api34DebugAndroidTest    an emulator AGP creates, snapshots and tears down
Result

testDebugUnitTest runs the screen tests without a device; pixel6api34DebugAndroidTest boots a clean emulator, runs the instrumented suite and writes an HTML report.

Setup
  1. Android Gradle Plugin 8.1 or later (managedDevices { localDevices { } } arrived in 8.1); GMD needs API 27+ system images
  2. JDK 21 for the unit-test JVM: Robolectric 4.16+ runs SDK 36 and needs Java 21 for it
  3. The Compose test from this sheet, in src/test/kotlin for Robolectric and src/androidTest/kotlin for the device

The flake checklist

A UI test that fails one run in fifty is worse than none; go down this list first.

  • Thread.sleep or delay in a test: too short on CI, too slow everywhere. Use waitUntil, onElement(timeoutMs), idling resources or mainClock.
  • Selecting by index, child position or coordinates. Select by text, content description, role or testTag; scroll lazy lists with performScrollToNode.
  • Real network, real clock, real accounts: replace the data layer with a fake (@TestInstallIn) or a local MockWebServer, and inject the clock.
  • Start every test from known state: clearPackageData with the orchestrator, a fresh fake per test, no order between tests.
  • Disable animations on devices (testOptions { animationsDisabled = true }, or the three developer-option scales to 0) and pin locale, time zone, font scale and screen size.
  • Wait on the result the user sees ("ORD-1042" on screen), not on a proxy (a spinner disappearing) — the proxy can flicker.
  • Compose 1.11 deprecated androidx.compose.ui.test.junit4.createComposeRule and createAndroidComposeRule: the junit4.v2 versions used here run coroutines on a StandardTestDispatcher, which queues them instead of running them at once — a test that relied on the old immediate behaviour needs waitForIdle() or mainClock steps.
  • Quarantine a flaky test with an issue link instead of retrying it silently; AGP and Firebase Test Lab retries hide real races.
  • Most coverage belongs in fast Compose/Robolectric tests of one screen; keep only a handful of UI Automator journeys for what crosses apps or system UI.

Modularization — Gradle Modules & Visibility

Gradle modules as the unit, `implementation` and `internal` as the walls, feature / data / core layers with api–impl pairs, convention plugins and a version catalog, navigation that never crosses features, and KMP source sets.

  • jvm
  • android
  • kotlin >=2.2.10
  • gradle >=9.1
  • android-gradle-plugin >=9.0
  • hilt >=2.59
  • a Gradle multi-module build (Kotlin DSL); Android modules use the Android Gradle plugin

Sources: Guide to Android app modularization — Android Developers · Common modularization patterns — Android Developers · Structuring projects with Gradle — Gradle docs · The Java Library plugin (api and implementation) — Gradle docs · Visibility modifiers — Kotlin docs

Why modularize, and the unit of modularity

Have concrete reasons ready; "cleanliness" is not one.

  • Build time — Gradle recompiles only the changed module and the modules whose compile classpath it is on; modules build in parallel and hit the build cache one by one.
  • Enforced boundaries — internal is invisible outside its module and an implementation dependency is invisible to consumers, so the architecture is compiler-checked, not a wiki page.
  • Ownership — one team per feature/* folder, routed by CODEOWNERS; fewer merge conflicts in one giant module.
  • Reuse — the same :core:* modules feed a phone app, a Wear or TV app module, a benchmark module, or a KMP shared module.
  • The unit is the Gradle module (a project with its own build.gradle.kts): a Kotlin/JVM library, an Android library, or the Android app. Packages inside one module enforce nothing beyond private.
  • Cost: configuration per module, DI wiring across module edges, slower Gradle configuration with hundreds of modules, and a graph someone must keep acyclic.

settings.gradle.kts and a feature module's build file

`settings.gradle.kts` declares the modules; a feature's build file names only what it uses — the shared Android, Compose and Hilt setup lives in a convention plugin.

// settings.gradle.kts
pluginManagement {
    includeBuild("build-logic")                       // convention plugins (see below)
    repositories { google(); mavenCentral(); gradlePluginPortal() }
}
dependencyResolutionManagement {
    repositoriesMode.set(RepositoriesMode.FAIL_ON_PROJECT_REPOS)   // repositories in one place only
    repositories { google(); mavenCentral() }
}
rootProject.name = "shop"
include(":app")
include(":feature:orders", ":feature:checkout")
include(":core:model", ":core:data:api", ":core:data:impl")
include(":core:database", ":core:network", ":core:designsystem", ":core:testing")

// feature/orders/build.gradle.kts
plugins {
    id("shop.android.feature")                        // SDK levels, Compose, Hilt: declared once
}

android {
    namespace = "com.example.shop.feature.orders"
}

dependencies {
    implementation(project(":core:data:api"))         // the contract, never :core:data:impl
    implementation(project(":core:designsystem"))
    testImplementation(project(":core:testing"))      // fakes of the api interfaces
    // never: implementation(project(":feature:checkout"))
}
Result

Gradle configures the ten modules (plus the empty parent projects :core, :core:data and :feature); building :feature:orders compiles it against :core:data:api, :core:model and :core:designsystem only — a change in :core:data:impl does not recompile it.

Setup
  1. A Gradle multi-module Android project (Android Studio's template, Gradle wrapper 9.1 or later, which AGP 9 requires), with the convention plugins and version catalog shown further down
  2. Run ./gradlew :feature:orders:assembleDebug to build one module and only what it depends on

Excerpt, not compiled or run here: it needs a Gradle multi-module project (needs Gradle, the Android Gradle plugin and the Android SDK).

`internal` is the wall — and where it stops

Expose an interface and a factory, keep the implementation `internal`; but `internal` is a Kotlin compile-time rule, so Java code and reflection still see a public class with mangled member names.

// ---- :core:data — one Gradle module, here one file ----
interface OrderRepository {                                   // public: the module's contract
    fun recentOrderIds(): List<String>
}

internal class CachedOrderRepository(private val source: () -> List<String>) : OrderRepository {
    private var cache: List<String>? = null
    override fun recentOrderIds() = cache ?: source().also { cache = it }
    internal fun evictAll() { cache = null }                  // tests in this module may call it
}

fun orderRepository(): OrderRepository =                     // the only way in from outside
    CachedOrderRepository { listOf("A-1", "A-2") }

// ---- a consumer in another module sees OrderRepository and orderRepository(), nothing else ----
fun main() {
    println(orderRepository().recentOrderIds())

    // The limit: on the JVM the internal class is public and its internal members are renamed
    // `name$module` — callable from Java and reflection, so never treat internal as security.
    val compiled = Class.forName("CachedOrderRepository")
    println(java.lang.reflect.Modifier.isPublic(compiled.modifiers))
    println(compiled.declaredMethods.map { it.name }.filter { it.startsWith("evict") })
}
Result
[A-1, A-2]
true
[evictAll$main]
Setup
  1. A Kotlin 2.x compiler (kotlinc) and JDK 17 or later
  2. Save as main.kt; run kotlinc main.kt -d out && kotlin -cp out MainKt (one file is one module, named main)

Ran with kotlinc 2.4.21, JVM 21.0.12.1 on 2026-11-16: the output matched the result shown.

Feature, data and core modules — and the dependency rule

Arrows point from `:app` to features to core, never sideways between features and never back up.

ModuleContainsMay depend onMust not depend on
:appApplication, the NavHost, DI wiring, build variantsevery feature and :impl module— (nothing depends on :app)
:feature:ordersscreens, view models, its route and graph builder:core:*:api, :core:model, :core:designsystemother features, any :impl module
:core:data:apirepository interfaces (pure Kotlin/JVM):core:model, kotlinx-coroutines-coreAndroid, :impl, features
:core:data:implRoom, Retrofit, data sources, the DI bindings:core:data:api, :core:database, :core:networkfeatures
:core:modeldata classes shared by everyone (pure Kotlin/JVM)the standard libraryeverything else
:core:designsystemtheme, tokens and shared composablesComposedata and feature modules
:core:testingfakes of the api interfaces, test rules:core:*:api— added only with testImplementation

api–impl pairs, `api` versus `implementation`, explicit API mode

`api` puts a dependency on every consumer's compile classpath — use it only for types that appear in your public signatures; everything else is `implementation`, invisible to consumers and no reason to recompile them.

// core/data/api/build.gradle.kts — pure Kotlin: interfaces and the types in their signatures
plugins {
    `java-library`
    alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.jvm)
}
kotlin {
    explicitApi()                              // public declarations need `public` and an explicit type
}
dependencies {
    api(project(":core:model"))                // Order is in OrderRepository's signatures: consumers need it
    api(libs.kotlinx.coroutines.core)          // so is Flow
}

// core/data/impl/build.gradle.kts — the heavy part, hidden behind the api module
plugins {
    id("shop.android.library")
    alias(libs.plugins.ksp)
    alias(libs.plugins.hilt)
}
android { namespace = "com.example.shop.core.data.impl" }
dependencies {
    implementation(project(":core:data:api"))
    implementation(libs.retrofit)              // never on a consumer's compile classpath
    implementation(libs.androidx.room.runtime)
    ksp(libs.androidx.room.compiler)
    // src/main: internal classes + a Hilt @Module that @Binds OrderRepository to them
}

// app/build.gradle.kts — the composition root is the only module that sees implementations
dependencies {
    implementation(project(":feature:orders"))
    implementation(project(":feature:checkout"))
    implementation(project(":core:data:impl"))
    // a variant can swap it: releaseImplementation(:impl) + debugImplementation(:core:data:fake)
}
Result

Features compile against interfaces only; editing a Room query rebuilds :core:data:impl and :app but no feature module, and a public declaration without an explicit visibility in :core:data:api fails compilation.

Setup
  1. A Gradle multi-module Android project (Android Studio's template, Gradle wrapper 9.1 or later, which AGP 9 requires), with the convention plugins and version catalog shown further down
  2. Run ./gradlew :feature:orders:assembleDebug to build one module and only what it depends on

Excerpt, not compiled or run here: it needs a Gradle multi-module project (needs Gradle, the Android Gradle plugin and the Android SDK).

Convention plugins and a version catalog

Versions live once in `libs.versions.toml`; build logic lives once in `build-logic` as precompiled script plugins, applied by id — so forty modules cannot drift apart.

# gradle/libs.versions.toml
[versions]
agp = "9.0.0"
kotlin = "2.4.21"
hilt = "2.59.2"
retrofit = "3.0.0"

[libraries]
android-gradlePlugin = { module = "com.android.tools.build:gradle", version.ref = "agp" }
kotlin-gradlePlugin = { module = "org.jetbrains.kotlin:kotlin-gradle-plugin", version.ref = "kotlin" }
retrofit = { module = "com.squareup.retrofit2:retrofit", version.ref = "retrofit" }
junit = { module = "junit:junit", version = "4.13.2" }

[plugins]
kotlin-jvm = { id = "org.jetbrains.kotlin.jvm", version.ref = "kotlin" }
hilt = { id = "com.google.dagger.hilt.android", version.ref = "hilt" }   # 2.59+ is the first for AGP 9
# ...the other aliases used on this page (ksp, room, ktor) follow the same shape

// build-logic/settings.gradle.kts — an included build reads the same catalog
dependencyResolutionManagement {
    repositories { google(); mavenCentral() }
    versionCatalogs { create("libs") { from(files("../gradle/libs.versions.toml")) } }
}

// build-logic/build.gradle.kts
plugins { `kotlin-dsl` }

dependencies {
    implementation(libs.android.gradlePlugin)
    implementation(libs.kotlin.gradlePlugin)    // AGP 9 alone brings KGP 2.2.10; this pins the catalog's
}

// build-logic/src/main/kotlin/shop.android.library.gradle.kts — the plugin id is the file name
plugins { id("com.android.library") }          // AGP 9 compiles Kotlin itself: no kotlin-android plugin

val libs = extensions.getByType<VersionCatalogsExtension>().named("libs")

android {
    compileSdk = 36
    defaultConfig { minSdk = 24 }
}

dependencies {
    "testImplementation"(libs.findLibrary("junit").get())
}
// shop.android.feature.gradle.kts applies shop.android.library plus Compose and Hilt the same way
Result

Every module that applies id("shop.android.library") gets the same SDK levels and test dependencies; bumping a version is a one-line change in the catalog.

Setup
  1. A Gradle multi-module Android project (Android Studio's template, Gradle wrapper 9.1 or later, which AGP 9 requires), with the convention plugins and version catalog shown further down
  2. Run ./gradlew :feature:orders:assembleDebug to build one module and only what it depends on

Navigation between feature modules that never meet

Each feature exposes its route, a `navigateTo…` function and a graph builder that takes callbacks, and only `:app` depends on both and connects them, passing ids rather than objects.

// ---- :feature:orders — knows nothing about checkout ----
@Serializable data object OrdersRoute

fun NavGraphBuilder.ordersScreen(onCheckout: (orderId: String) -> Unit) {
    composable<OrdersRoute> { OrdersScreen(onCheckout = onCheckout) }
}

// ---- :feature:checkout ----
@Serializable data class CheckoutRoute(val orderId: String)

fun NavController.navigateToCheckout(orderId: String) = navigate(CheckoutRoute(orderId))

fun NavGraphBuilder.checkoutScreen(onDone: () -> Unit) {
    composable<CheckoutRoute> { entry ->
        val route = entry.toRoute<CheckoutRoute>()     // in a view model: savedStateHandle.toRoute()
        CheckoutScreen(orderId = route.orderId, onDone = onDone)
    }
}

// ---- :app — the only module that depends on both features ----
@Composable
fun ShopNavHost(navController: NavHostController = rememberNavController()) {
    NavHost(navController, startDestination = OrdersRoute) {
        ordersScreen(onCheckout = navController::navigateToCheckout)
        checkoutScreen(onDone = { navController.popBackStack(OrdersRoute, inclusive = false) })
    }
}
Result

Tapping an order in the orders screen opens checkout for that order id, and finishing checkout pops back to the list — with no Gradle dependency between the two feature modules.

  2. Each section below lives in the module named in its comment

Kotlin Multiplatform source sets

In a KMP module the source set is the boundary: `commonMain` cannot touch the JDK or Android, and each platform source set supplies its own dependencies and `actual`s.

// shared/build.gradle.kts
plugins { alias(libs.plugins.kotlin.multiplatform) }

kotlin {
    jvm()                                          // desktop and server
    iosArm64()
    iosSimulatorArm64()
    // Android target: apply com.android.kotlin.multiplatform.library (AGP's KMP library plugin)
    explicitApi()

    sourceSets {
        commonMain.dependencies { implementation(libs.kotlinx.coroutines.core) }
        commonTest.dependencies { implementation(kotlin("test")) }
        jvmMain.dependencies { implementation(libs.ktor.client.okhttp) }
        iosMain.dependencies { implementation(libs.ktor.client.darwin) }
    }
}

// shared/src/commonMain/kotlin/Currency.kt
public expect fun currencySymbol(isoCode: String): String

// shared/src/jvmMain/kotlin/Currency.jvm.kt
public actual fun currencySymbol(isoCode: String): String = java.util.Currency.getInstance(isoCode).symbol

// shared/src/iosMain/kotlin/Currency.ios.kt supplies its actual from Foundation's NSNumberFormatter.
// Prefer an interface in commonMain, injected per platform, when the platform part has state.
Result

commonMain compiles once for every target; jvmMain and iosMain each add their own HTTP engine and actual, and a JDK call in commonMain fails to compile.

Setup
  1. A Gradle project with the org.jetbrains.kotlin.multiplatform plugin; iOS targets build only on macOS with Xcode
  2. Run ./gradlew :shared:allTests

Choosing a strategy

Start with the cheapest shape that solves today's pain; split again when build time or ownership hurts.

StrategyLooks likeUse when
One module:app with packagesa prototype or a solo developer; nothing is enforced but private
Layer modules:ui, :domain, :dataa small team that wants the layering checked; every feature still touches all three
Feature + core modules:feature:orders, :core:data, :core:designsystemseveral teams or a growing app — Google's and Now in Android's default
Feature + api–impl pairs:core:data:api / :core:data:implslow builds or swappable implementations: an implementation change no longer recompiles features
KMP shared module:shared with commonMainsharing domain and data code with iOS, desktop or a server
Included builds / published artifactsincludeBuild("../payments-sdk"), Maven coordinatesgenuine reuse across products or repositories; adds versioning and release work

Pitfalls

The ones that undo the benefits.

  • Cycles — Gradle rejects them; the fix is moving the shared type down into :core:model or extracting an api module, never merging the two.
  • A god :common / :core:utils module — everything depends on it, so every change to it rebuilds the world. Split by what changes together.
  • Over-modularizing — a module per class costs configuration time, DI wiring and Android library overhead; prefer plain Kotlin/JVM modules where there is no Android code.
  • api everywhere — it leaks transitive dependencies onto every consumer and turns a one-module change into a cascade of recompiles.
  • Feature depends on feature — navigate through :app or an api module instead, and pass ids, not objects.
  • Treating internal as security — it is a compile-time rule; Java and reflection reach it. Keep secrets off the device instead.
  • Fail the build when the graph breaks the rule (a dependency-analysis or module-graph check in CI); a diagram in a wiki never holds.
  • Give every api module a fake in :core:testing and every feature a test source set; a feature should build and test without any :impl module.

Coverage against the Swift Catalog

Every Swift topic, and what this catalog has for it — an equivalent, a partial counterpart, or the reason there is none.

How to read the matrix

Nothing here is a translation made to fill a gap.

  • equivalent — a sheet here covers the same concept and shares its concept id, so the language selector lands on it from the Swift sheet.
  • partial — a sheet here covers part of it under its own concept id, so the selector does not land on it: the Here column names it and the reason says what is missing.
  • no counterpart — nothing here; the reason says whether the topic does not exist in this language or is simply not written yet.
